Am 30.06.23 um 13:30 schrieb Daniel Antal:
Hi James and Tile,

Yes, we had an agreement, and I also had an agreement with James. Tile was supposed to work for me for 100  euros per hour, and I do not know how many hours you worked, because Tile was available at random hours and it was unclear how he is contributing at most time. James also told me that he will take over some of the costs.  This is the cost I want him to take over, not Gabija's.

Without knowing how much and what I will be paying for, I will return whatever invoice you are sending to me.

I also must add that both of your contributions were rather reducing the value of the proposal than adding to it.  Neither of you were available, and when I wanted to take out Sinus from the proposal, James asked me not to do it and took an oath that we will get your part that day.  With Istvan we did not really go to bed that night and did not get it. At the last moment, at the request of Tile, we even wrote him into the application!  Overall I think it went against the quality of the proposal, which would be stronger without leaving both of you in.

To me writing this proposal cost already a lot of money, James promised to pitch in, and I want him to reimburse fully or partly Tile's invoice. It can be done directly to Reprex or to Tile. I would like to know what is James's promised contribution, and I would like to offer that amount to Tile. I suggest that we set this to 8 hours, i.e. 800 EUR + VAT.

Best regards,
Daniel

Daniel

From: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
Sent: Friday, August 4, 2023 12:35 PM
To: Joost Poort &lt;j.p.poort@uva.nl&gt;; James Rhys Edwards &lt;JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&gt;
Subject: ABM model

Hi James and Joost,

I read Giulio's proposal and this is my short assessment.  This model has nothing to do with the Tx.1 and Tx.2 task-streams, so perhaps this would fit into the T4.3 novel data uses. To me, this work has nothing to do with the WP1 current description, so it does not contradict anything either, it can be an achievement.  This is an entire separate model from the market comparator model, it is certainly not a valuation model.

These ABM models are mainly not used in economics, although they have been used in finance, and they require plenty of consistent data.  What data is unclear to me, as I do not state what ABM model they will specify, I do not see what is the outcome they want to model, however, I assume that the data needs to be very extensive and may partly overlap with our data targets, but may lead to completely different data needs.

The way this document could me made use of if we would get a more structured proposal of
- What will be the models input, output and potential policy use
- What data is needed precisely
- Who and at what cost will gather that data.

My fear is that if we get a novel model which has scientific value, but at an expense of others that are needed, and it increases our resource needs significantly on the data collection side than we cause more headache than we solve anything.

To me, this could be something in WP4 if actually feasible, as we discussed preliminiary a month ago with James, but I absolutely cannot relate this work with whatever we do in WP1 or as a matter of fact WP2.

As a last word, my problem is with Giulio's ideas is that he signed up for a data collection task and he comes up with exntensive data consumer tasks.  So the more you give way to his ideas, the bigger of our unfilled data gap, because he generates novel data needs that nobody even thought of.

Best regards,


Daniel Antal, CFA
co-founder

Hi Joost and James,

And really the very last, to make sense of the forwarded mail.  If you look below, basically I distributed the tasks into two groups: minium requirement was that they can take over with EUBA that Bologna essential tasks, and everything else was supposed to an incentive for them to add their optional research.  So, the EUBA and SSSA contribution was calculated with a hefty extra PM number above the originally envisioned Bologna PMs, because they promised to take over research less interesting to them and add on top theirs (on theirs I think Caterina is included, because we added a good few PMs with saying that Giulios'work will benefit that one, too, as diversity requires data not only legal analysis.)

From the correspondence it is clear that the orphaned tasks were the minimum requirement to take them into the grant, and for example, the MSME surveying and enterprise surveying was optional that Arianna chose personally to be added. Of course, that only made sense with the gross value added calculations (that is where it is needed) which was supposed to be an EUBA accompanying addition.

However, EUBA never added anybody to the project who can do GVA calculations from enterprise surveys and SSSA's enterprise survey expert was never in the picture in the last months.  This is typically a task that I can do and prefer to with a research assistant, because the tackling of the survey items, documentation, etc, can be a laborious work but somebody familiar with it can do it easily alone, or I can instruct somebody who is interested, just it is a lot of nitty-gritty detail to get it practically done.

I also see a potentially disastrous editing error from later, because here we explicitly talk about Use of non DCF valuation models, as described in the current work plan here [we plan to use almost all recognized copyright valuation models, which are extensions of the general IP valuation models.]   and Giulio was constantly arguing for DCF models.

In my experience, DCF models are used either as a theoretical construction to check the consistency of one's model, like in equity or bond pricing, or in project finance with well-described and not numerous DCFs,  or with long historical time series and risk metrics. Here we still talked about non DCF models because in my professional life I never saw enough DCF/risk metrics to be applicable in music.  I also spent a lot of time explaining to Giulio and Daniele that while theoretically you can work with accruals of royalty accounts, attributing actual cash flows and accruals to a time line is extremely difficult and makes the use of DCF models particularly difficult in practice.   It is explicitly stated in one of the documents shared with them why accruals in royalty accounting is such a big issue in itself. (it means that SOZA or Spotify pay out royalty when they meet a minimum threshold, because often the bank and accounting cost would be greater than the periodic royalty.  So they pay when an asset reached 10 euros.  Which can be 1 months or 15 months or more.  Just by observing the payout we cannot automatically treat it as a July 2023 payout if it is accrued over 15 months. )

I am giving these illustrations to say that they received very sufficient information and even information on their ideas whenever I found them to be impractical for research.

Best regards,
Daniel

Cc: James Rhys Edwards &lt;JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&lt;mailto:JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&gt;&gt;

 Dear Giulio, Arianna,
I would like to set up a call with you for Monday afternoon or Tuesday when we would try to finalize, at least orally, your contribution to the Horizon Europe call, and the budget.   Unfortunately, I have not received a lot of input from some partners, and next week will be Easter, so we have 4 working days to finalize the work planning.  Our grantwriters work in the HE forms, we have this dynamic document that we will continue to work on during the weekend.
I am available on Monday afternoon, or Tuesday, I know that Cate is not much available on Monday, but I think that these tasks have no legal aspect, and whenever we can talk, we should as the time is very-very tight.
https://horizon.dataobservatory.eu/consortium.html
username:bologna
password:Horizon_Europe_2022
We have four Work Packages, each of them having a methodology and indicator design output, a data collection, processing and presentation, and policy/business use cases with scientific relevance.
The data collection, processing, presentation will be mainly done by Sinus, Reprex, and the University of Turku in all work packages.
Minimum contributions
Your economic contributions could be placed in order or priority: 1) Music economy, 2) Innovation 3) Music and society.  Caterina will lead and work WP Diversity, where your input will be indirect.
There is some degree of freedom in the output regarding policy relevant outputs, but on the methodological front we must cover the following:
-   participation in indicator design, following the Eurostat methodology (with various feedback cycles from end users) and any methodology that you think is the best practice regarding the data gaps identified in the Feasibility Study for the European Music Observatory&lt;https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/a756542a-249d-11eb-9d7e-01aa75ed71a1/language-en&gt;.  pp 31-38.
- creation of a dynamic portfolio selection algorithm that creates basket of recordings that well represent various music content segments, such as “Italian emerging artists”  or “Swedish perennial artist”.
- creation of a streaming index methodology, with periodic (monthly) rebalancing of the basket, that calculates the representative volume (number of streams, number of followers) and representative price (representative song revenue / representative number of streams) for each content segment.
- This will be an input into DCF valuation models.
Optional / to be discussed
Apart from this, I would like to distribute tasks between you and the Economic University of Bratislava related to these economics competences:

-          Generally, we need to design many indicators, so split up data gaps,

-          Use of non DCF valuation models, as described in the current work plan here [we plan to use almost all recognized copyright valuation models, which are extensions of the general IP valuation models.]

-          Economic contributions to the national economy: gross value added, employment, tax base effects (we currently use and input-output model, further methods can be considered)

-          ESG sustainability reporting (using auxiliary tables / satellite accounts for greenhouse gases, and potentially gender inequality and some governance measures.)

-          Experience in designing small enterprise and microenterprise / professional surveys

-          Handling survey bias in enterprise surveys and some special-purpose surveys.
It is desirable to have team members, or at least research assistants who can work in R.  The research infrastructure that we have to access streaming data, or to make the I-O models work, all to harmonize survey data are all written in the R language.
Of course, this is not a necessity in methodology, indicator design, and finalizing some final policy/scientific outputs, but because we want to make most outputs reproducible, the best way is to work in R for those outputs.  If we must, we can add Python or C++ bits for the reproducible parts.
Best regards,

Dear Tomáš,

Thank you for this – I’ve gone through the table and indicated my opinion.

Re: the Hungarian and Bulgarian Statistical offices, I tend to agree with the recommendation that we adopt a sharp focus on Slovakia in this meeting, and organize a second workshop with our other target country stakeholders. At that time, hopefully, we may have other interested parties as well.

Re: the Consortium, ARTISJUS and MUSICAUTOR should probably attend, and perhaps UTU as well. Then we would have all WP leads in one place, and could double-purpose the trip for an in-person WP leader meeting.

FYI, I am on holiday from 17-27 August. Please CC @Richard Wages&lt;mailto:Richard.Wages@sinus-institut.de&gt; and @Isabella Tautscher&lt;mailto:Isabella.Tautscher@sinus-institut.de&gt; in any emails to me. I’m available by mobile for emergencies.

Thank you again and best regards,
James

Subject: RE: Bratislava workshop planning

Dear all,

I am getting back to you with respect to Bratislava workshop as promised.
I spent today an hour with the new Director of IKP Mr. Čas, who seems to be very cooperative.

According to his schedule, we should aim either for September 20, 21 or 25. We can agree on the final date during next week once Mr. Bieščad returns to office.

We agreed that from our side:

  *   we will send him next week a proposed list of attendees/ institutions we would like to invite
  *   we will send him early September a one pager on the proposed agenda
  *   we will set up the meeting venue

From their side:

  *   they will help us to get invitations to the right people
  *   they will prepare a short presentation on current state of play of their work including policy goals, methodology, indicators design and gaps, surveying overview
  *   they welcome our project and are aware of the fact that at some point we can do some of their work which they see as a big help (there are only 4 employees at the Institute who cover all CCIs)

It would be good to have a short call during next week to agree on the above and move forward. I can be pretty flexible between Tuesday and Friday.

Have a nice weekend!

Tomáš

<!-- source: OpenMuse_20261009-2156/OpenMuse/messages/202308161436-Re_ Open Music Europe -- proposed amendment to mov-882.txt -->

Hi Daniel,

Note I have removed the Consortium from CC because I do not want to waste their time.

The text of my Fri 7/14/2023 5:39 PM email to the entire Consortium, announcing the vote in accordance with the Consortium Agreement, follows. Note that we gave partners significantly longer than the allotted 10 calendar days to vote – many chose not to. That is their right.

While it’s true that REPREX didn’t mail in a vote, you did indicate to me in a call with Istvan the way that you wanted to vote, and I recorded it. So you did indeed get a vote.

Anyway. I am going on holiday from 17-27 August, and like you, I need this holiday. So unless it is a genuine emergency, I would strongly prefer not to have work-related contact until 28 August.



==Text of Fri 7/14/2023 announcement==

Dear Open Music Europe Consortium,
Please find attached the REPREX proposal to shift T6.3, the Data Management Plan, into Work Package 5. Please return your vote for or against the proposal, or your decision to abstain, within 10 calendar days, i.e., by Mon, 24 July 2023. Requests for clarification of the proposal itself should be directed to REPREX, while requests for clarification of the opinion stated in the section “Feedback by the partners affected” should be directed at SINUS.
Below are the relevant provisions of the Consortium Agreement.
Thank you, and best regards,
James
==
6.2.2.7 Decisions without a meeting
Any decision may also be taken without a meeting if

  1.  the Coordinator circulates to all Members of the General Assembly a suggested decision with a deadline for responses of at least 10 calendar days after receipt by a Party and
  2.  the decision is agreed by 51 % of all Parties.
The Coordinator shall inform all the Parties of the outcome of the vote.
A veto according to Section 6.2.4 may be submitted up to 15 calendar days after receipt of this information.
The decision will be binding after the Coordinator sends a notification to all Members. The Coordinator will keep records of the votes and make them available to the Parties on request.

Dear Open Music Europe consortium,

I am writing to pass along the results of the vote taken on the proposed amendment (attached) to move T6.3, the Data Management Plan, from WP6 into WP5. For the proposal to be taken up, 51% of all GA votes would need to be cast in favour. The results follow:

Voted yes: 2
Voted no: 8
Abstained: 1
Did not vote: 5

Accordingly, the task will stay in WP6.

Please note that I will be on holiday from 17 to 27 August. Please CC @Richard Wages&lt;mailto:Richard.Wages@sinus-institut.de&gt; and @Isabella Tautscher&lt;mailto:Isabella.Tautscher@sinus-institut.de&gt; in any emails to me. I will also be off all other channels (in the mountains).

Thank you and best regards,
James

  2.  the decision is agreed by 51 % of all Parties.
The Coordinator shall inform all the Parties of the outcome of the vote.
A veto according to Section 6.2.4 may be submitted up to 15 calendar days after receipt of this information.
The decision will be binding after the Coordinator sends a notification to all Members. The Coordinator will keep records of the votes and make them available to the Parties on request.

Subject: D1.1 technical and workflow probelms

Dear Colleagues,
Yesterday we had a recap of why there are problems with the T1.1 and we came back again to a few issues that kill plenty of time, and should not be done at the expense of senior researchers.  It is about the Word template, the spelling and citations. For the record, I would like to give a more thorough recap that can be used to avoid future problems.  I added Christoph from Synyo to this thread.
The Word template suffers from the same problems that I identified in February and what Richard also keeps repeating.  It could be fixed in an hour by somebody who is knowledgeable about Word. I do not think that we can work in Word, but we must be able to finalise and revise deliverables in Word.

-          The heading numbers is inconsistent, and the „multi-level number” is mis-set

-          The page numbering is not correctly set

-          There appear to be unnecessary section breaks.


I do not work in Word, but apart from final formatting, I think that interoperability means that nobody is forced to do so. However, Word is a quasi-standard, and my software, as many other software, can work with standard Word files.  In my case, I just have to show a correctly formatted file to my software, it will read the metadata of the file (the formatting) and then create a new Word file with the exact same formatting. So the problem is not who is using Word (and I could talk about the differences of a Windows, Mac and Cloud Word) but if we start from a correctly formatted template or not.
Spelling.  My text went through three layers of spelling and grammar checks, however, the last minute deliveries of parts in bad formats obviously resulted in a more chaotic text. Nevertheless, I also encountered some problems that Richard stated, and more.  While we are expected to use British spelling,  direct quotation of international treaties and other sources must not alter the spelling.  So you cannot put through an American or old international text through a 2023 British spell-check.  I did change back to original text spelling some texts at least twice.  The International Labour Organization uses a spelling that is old American in its name, so neither British nor American. I cited several American texts, which used the American standard academic spelling of their issue year.  But my original text went through three layers of current British English spelling.  So, just putting through a Word document on a spell checker is not enough, however, with your own text it is a bare minimum. The correct workflow is, as I continue with OPA/FAIR is to separately collect your tables, datasets, charts, citations and references.  For example changing the spelling of a direct quote makes it impossible to find in an ebook. Changing the title of a Slovak document to English makes it absolutely impossible to find.  There are ways how to cite a non-English text in English. In my case, I used title = "Original title" and subtitle [translated title] notation in brackets.  Whatever format you use, you must beware that while our original document must be 2023 British spelling, we work with different languages and source countries, and in music research we may also encounter Canadian English original texts, as Canada is very strong in music research.
This leads to the third problem, references, which also connects to the use of OPA and FAIR.  It is a minimum requirement in any academic writing that the sources can be identified, and in OPA and FAIR it is also a requirement that they can be connected in a machine-readable format to the new text. We agreed on a very simple rule: all references find their way to the shared Zotero, and then they are exported to BibLatex, which is an interoperable, standard citations format that can be translated to any machine-readable or academic publisher required formatting.
To me, filling out the reference database is the very first step in a reproducible research workflow, and it is the bare minimum of reviewable work. Any academic writers, who will be reviewed by a task leader, internal and external peer review must make their work reviewable, and correct referencing is a first step.  When we agree on a literature review, we first put the documents into a database, and then we check if we reviewed at least the originally stated documents. Many of the documents that should have been reviewed and interpreted were not in the reference database, never found their way to the bibliography file, and I spent even my first day of the vacation to try desperately to find references in a language that I do not speak and cannot write.
In an OPA/FAIR compliant work, we have a reference if we have it in a machine readable file. Zotero can export to such a file, and it is widely used by academics.  It is machine readable if the document can be associated with an URI or URL; the URI can be a DOI, ISBN and in some cases an ISSN.  It can be cited in a document (depending on the citation format) if it has a name (person or institution) as an author and a year or a date. Zotero, and endless citation management programs correctly cite references once the references are set.  To me, putting the reviewable documents into the reference database is always the first step of research, and not the last, partly, because it will cause last minute headbach, but also because it makes the review and direction by a more senior academic practically impossible.
Last, but not least, all OPA/FAIR compliant research must be properly documented.  All charts, tables, and datasets must have an individual reference number (preferably a DOI), an author (with co-authors and other contributors) and a title.  This must be placed in a repository with standardized file structure and names.  I do believe that this compliance cannot be reached in Word, but even if it could, these steps are again not only important to make the work machine-readable, findable, accessible, interoperable, but first and foremost to allow internal and external peer-review and reuse.

If anything is not clear here, just let me know how to make this clearer in the reference text https://contributors.dataobservatory.eu/

Best regards,
Daniel

I spent today an hour with the new Director of IKP Mr. Čas, who seems to be very cooperative.



According to his schedule, we should aim either for September 20, 21 or 25. We can agree on the final date during next week once Mr. Bieščad returns to office.



We agreed that from our side:

-          we will send him next week a proposed list of attendees/ institutions we would like to invite

-          we will send him early September a one pager on the proposed agenda

-          we will set up the meeting venue



From their side:

-          they will help us to get invitations to the right people

-          they will prepare a short presentation on current state of play of their work including policy goals, methodology, indicators design and gaps, surveying overview

-          they welcome our project and are aware of the fact that at some point we can do some of their work which they see as a big help (there are only 4 employees at the Institute who cover all CCIs)



It would be good to have a short call during next week to agree on the above and move forward. I can be pretty flexible between Tuesday and Friday.



Have a nice weekend!



Tomáš





Tomáš Mikš

Hi all,



Thank you for the productive call!



To prepare for our Eurostat microdata application, we need the most recent codebooks and questionnaires for:



  *   EU-LFS
  *   EU-SILC – also specifically 2006 and 2015 - Social and cultural participation (ilc_scp)
  *   AES – also specifically 2007 and 2011 (there may have also been an AES module on culture post-2012 when the ESSnet-Culture recommendations were published – we must check)
  *   HBS
  *   ICT
  *   HETUS



We should tender the microdata application as a research network consisting of EUBA, UVA, SSSA, and UTU (and possibly SINUS if we are recognized in time, otherwise we will tender separately for the SILC and AES data alone).
To prepare specifically for the Slovakia workshop, we also need:



  *   KULT-5-01 and KULT-19 methodological notes (as we already have for KULT-16-01)
  *   ROČ 1-01 and ROČ 2-01 questionnaires
  *   ROČ 2-01 and NSNO 1-01 sampling method
  *   To ask in workshop: response rates



We can use the Eurostat microdata application as a “template” for our Slovakian statistical authority microdata application. This should be ready to hand over to them on Thursday.



Re: the post-workshop with the other CMOs, I will prepare a partner survey on surveys (similarly to the one Magali sent around for D2.1 about airplay quotas, etc.). Basically, we will ask what national-level surveying programmes exist in the target countries, for links to codebooks and questionnaires, and about microdata access procedures. We can introduce the topic during the post-workshop, and I will send out the survey after. I imagine microdata access on a national level will become easier once we have been granted access by Eurostat.



@EUBA, let’s plan on lunch and a one-hour meeting to go over any questions on the Slovak surveying program on 19 Sept.



@Daniel and @Joost, separately SINUS will need the codebooks and questionnaires for the CEEMID surveys and UVA anti-piracy survey, respectively. However, this is lower priority.



@Richard and @Daniel, I’ll see you at 09:00 in the call with Joost tomorrow.



Please note all templates are here: https://cloud.sinus-institut.de/ws-OpenMusE/templates



Thank you again, and best regards,
James

Subject: Culture spending / royal castle

Hi Marcel,

I tried to look up for you the spending on the Royal Castle district in Hungary, but of course, it is impossible, it is hidden in hundreds of pockets.  The official estimate of the program was about 0.65 bn euro in 2014 and the unofficial at that time 3 billion.

Because they restore the historic defence ministry building and move the defence ministry there, of course, it is a state secret what goes there. Etc.

The official part that went to the cultural heritage budget in 2021 was around 250 million for the year 2020. There is a corruption research NGO, called K-monitor that has a special project and website trying to track the costs.

In 2021 the official budget was 1 billion euros (over several years), but that again excluded plenty of hidden items.

If you look only at the photos you can imagine the scale of the building.

https://mfor.hu/cikkek/makro/ha-torik-ha-szakad-befejezik-a-gigantikus-epitkezeseket-a-varban.html
https://www.valaszonline.hu/2023/02/03/budai-var-kulugyminiszterium-honved-foparancsnoksag-jozsef-fohercegi-palota-szent-gyorgy-ter-disz-rekonstrukciol-visszaepites-hauszmann-program/
https://adatbazis.k-monitor.hu/adatbazis/aktak/hauszmann-program-es-a-miniszteriumok-varba-koltozese

The main company that is building is owned by Orban's neighbor in his village, who is widely seen as the custordian of his unofficial assets.

Best regards,

Dear Marcel and Tomas,

I checked my calendar for travel, and I think that even though I have an invitation to the SOZA gala ceremony, that is not the best day to travel. I could best spend 9 or 10 October in Bratislava (Mon-Tue) or 13 (Fri), but Fridays are not always the best to meet civil servants.  Alternatively, perhaps I could make 6 October (Fri), or 18 Oct (Wed).

My absolutely fixed days are 2-4 Oct and 11-12 Oct and 16-17 Oct when I absolutely cannot make this trip.

In my opinion, the earlier would be better, because I am meeting another bit EU consortium, Polifonia, on 17 October in Bologna, and if we would have clearer plans by then with SOZA and Hudobne centrum, we would be able to sell a technical assistance cooperation to them, which is not so relevant for IKP, but it is very relevant for our linked open data infrastructure.

Hi Marcel and Tomas,

 I would also try to have a meaningful meeting with Hudobne centrum, and we could review things with Tomas or all three of us on 13 October in a Zoom call. @marcel.cas@culture.gov.sk&lt;mailto:marcel.cas@culture.gov.sk&gt; , you told me that it would be more appropriate to talk to Sivlia's boss than her about these things, and we are already in touch with a Ms Janka Horecká, but I am not sure if she is the best contact.

Hey Daniel,

These dates you are mentioning below are for the planned meeting with the statistical office (ŠÚ SR) or with Hudobné centrum (HC)?

Marcel

From: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
Sent: Wednesday, September 27, 2023 9:00 AM
To: Mikš Tomáš &lt;Tomas.Miks@soza.sk&gt;
Cc: Čas Marcel &lt;marcel.cas@culture.gov.sk&gt;
Subject: Re: Potential days in Bratislava

Good morning,

I will start a separate thread on Hudobné center.

What I am working on now is a 2 page document (in English) that could be shared with government statisticians, it will be based on Eurostat and European Statistical System or European Commission recommendations and guidelines on "using privately-held data for government statistics"; their use is increasingly common in environmental satellite accounts, for example. I will make this available in a first draft by the end of the week, but I think that it would be good if either Tomas or Marcel would draft an email in Slovak with roughly the following message.

On 21 September 2023 the Horizon Europe project "Open Music Europe" held a stakeholder consultation in Bratislava about the possibilities for improving the current Slovak cultural satellite accounts for cultural policy implementation, and to add details for further industries currently not covered by a separate account with the example of the music industry. These proposals are based on the best practices of using privately-held data in the making of official statistics, and sharing the results of open science with open statistics.  We would like to seek a meeting on behalf of Open Music Europe (as a potential data and know-how provider), IKP (as a potential user of the improved statistical indicators) and statistical office about the possibilities of providing data via a so-called SBR satellite to the office for the improvement of its satellite accounts. On behalf of "Open Music Europe", Daniel Antal, CFA would travel to Bratislava from the Netherlands; he is the responsible task leader for data management in this project, and he is the author of the Slovak music industry report which pioneered the use of privately-held data for public policy purposes.  Mr. Antal does not speak Slovak, but we are happy to facilitate conversation in a mix of English and Slovak.

As Tomas sent out the invitations to the Workshop, he could send this, or IKP in a government capacity, I think it is equally good.  The preferred dates would be Oct 10 (afternoon), Oct 11 or Oct 13.  About the hour, I must make sure that it does not conflict with the final hours of the Open Music Europe consortium project management board which is not yet know but will be on Oct 10 or 11.

Best regards,
Daniel

Good morning,

I will start a separate thread on Hudobné center.

What I am working on now is a 2 page document (in English) that could be shared with government statisticians, it will be based on Eurostat and European Statistical System or European Commission recommendations and guidelines on "using privately-held data for government statistics"; their use is increasingly common in environmental satellite accounts, for example. I will make this available in a first draft by the end of the week, but I think that it would be good if either Tomas or Marcel would draft an email in Slovak with roughly the following message.

On 21 September 2023 the Horizon Europe project "Open Music Europe" held a stakeholder consultation in Bratislava about the possibilities for improving the current Slovak cultural satellite accounts for cultural policy implementation, and to add details for further industries currently not covered by a separate account with the example of the music industry. These proposals are based on the best practices of using privately-held data in the making of official statistics, and sharing the results of open science with open statistics.  We would like to seek a meeting on behalf of Open Music Europe (as a potential data and know-how provider), IKP (as a potential user of the improved statistical indicators) and statistical office about the possibilities of providing data via a so-called SBR satellite to the office for the improvement of its satellite accounts. On behalf of "Open Music Europe", Daniel Antal, CFA would travel to Bratislava from the Netherlands; he is the responsible task leader for data management in this project, and he is the author of the Slovak music industry report which pioneered the use of privately-held data for public policy purposes.  Mr. Antal does not speak Slovak, but we are happy to facilitate conversation in a mix of English and Slovak.

As Tomas sent out the invitations to the Workshop, he could send this, or IKP in a government capacity, I think it is equally good.  The preferred dates would be Oct 10 (afternoon), Oct 11 or Oct 13.  About the hour, I must make sure that it does not conflict with the final hours of the Open Music Europe consortium project management board which is not yet know but will be on Oct 10 or 11.

Best regards,
Daniel

Subject: Re: WP2

Hi James,

Thank you very much. I can be available the day before if the other CMOs will be there, too. I think that it would be helpful if I could review on Monday the work so far available to work a bit on the agenda and make it appealing for Artisjus to attend.

There is also an applicant to the stakeholder network, Dikh TV &amp; Radio. It is the first roma commercial music tv &amp; radio that is broadcasted in 6 countries, including SK &amp; HU. They’d like to join Listen Local (WP2) and be a media partner. I think it would boost or almost invisible communications activity and it would hit two birds with a proverbial stone.

I am wondering what is the procedure for this and if we could perhaps sign an MoU with them on the day before?

I’ll talk on Wednesday with Johannes/SYNYO from a comms perspective about this but this would make a precedent with our stakeholder network.

The reason why I am asking is that the owner of this roma commercial media is also the owner of the market leader Hungarian music radio, and they are among the biggest tv/transmission clients of both Artisjus and SOZA (they are also very big in Romania.) somehow I feel that it would add some appealto Artisjus.

This is a big company, as far as I know it is Romanian owned and headquartered in Budapest. They contacted me on a sustainability conference (they own nature channels) and when I realized that they make a private investment into roma music internationally I thought that they could put some blood into our media presence.

Hip-hop is the leading genre on streaming in both SK &amp; HU and many of the hiphop stars are of Roma origin with millions of views on their videos. They could really add a lot traffic to LL SK &amp; perhaps lure Artisjus into WP2. That would make the WP more active as they have more resources than SOZA amd Musicautor combined.

Best regards,
Daniel

Subject: Re: WP2

Hi James,

Thank you very much. I can be available the day before if the other CMOs will be there, too. I think that it would be helpful if I could review on Monday the work so far available to work a bit on the agenda and make it appealing for Artisjus to attend.

There is also an applicant to the stakeholder network, Dikh TV &amp; Radio. It is the first roma commercial music tv &amp; radio that is broadcasted in 6 countries, including SK &amp; HU. They’d like to join Listen Local (WP2) and be a media partner. I think it would boost or almost invisible communications activity and it would hit two birds with a proverbial stone.

I am wondering what is the procedure for this and if we could perhaps sign an MoU with them on the day before?

I’ll talk on Wednesday with Johannes/SYNYO from a comms perspective about this but this would make a precedent with our stakeholder network.

The reason why I am asking is that the owner of this roma commercial media is also the owner of the market leader Hungarian music radio, and they are among the biggest tv/transmission clients of both Artisjus and SOZA (they are also very big in Romania.) somehow I feel that it would add some appealto Artisjus.

This is a big company, as far as I know it is Romanian owned and headquartered in Budapest. They contacted me on a sustainability conference (they own nature channels) and when I realized that they make a private investment into roma music internationally I thought that they could put some blood into our media presence.

Hip-hop is the leading genre on streaming in both SK &amp; HU and many of the hiphop stars are of Roma origin with millions of views on their videos. They could really add a lot traffic to LL SK &amp; perhaps lure Artisjus into WP2. That would make the WP more active as they have more resources than SOZA amd Musicautor combined.

Best regards,
Daniel

Subject: Sustainability issues

Hi James,

I wonder if you have time before the workshop call to have a short chat on sustainability issues?  I am a bit cautious still, because we do not have formal notification, but we received an email that Reprex and its partners were selected by EIT's Breakthrough Lab for funding in this topic.

Our proposal was strictly for the film industry, and with partners only outside of OpenMuse, but the standardisation of European sustainability reporting and management in 2024/25 will be made in the same "Media and Communication" umbrella (to harmonize the European and American nomenclatures) for film and music. So there is absolutely no chance of double funding, however, work can directly benefit any academic or industry exploitation measures in OpenMuse.

If we actually get the contract, we will have a lot more resources for sustainability and we could connect your WP3 to this work, allowing us to have high-profile visibility and publications in 2024/25.

The reason why I am bringing this up is that the CSRD Directive will be high on the legislative agenda of the Slovak parliament after the elections, and perhaps introducing a few ideas in Bratislava could open more ears. Currently we expect that whatever we present about WP1 will only be interesting for statisticians, because the cultural ministry is interested in our diversity program.  Connecting to a different legislative/policy agenda may be wise if we are not entirely sure about WP2.

Diversity per se in the European sustainability framework has multiple meanings, and it falls partly under the social sustainability and partly the governance part of ESG. The reason why I left this out from the common thread is that I do not know where you are now with your WP3 and where you want to bring it.

Best regards,

Daniel Antal, CFA
co-founder

On 24 May 2023, at 12:23, Jacopo de Berardinis &lt;jacopo.deberardinis@kcl.ac.uk&lt;mailto:jacopo.deberardinis@kcl.ac.uk&gt;&gt; wrote:

Dear Daniel,

Thanks for considering our proposition and for all the pointers related to the potential concerns on Music Meta. This is very useful to us.

While we greatly appreciate the time you spent on understanding Music Meta, and the detail of your comments, we need to remark that the diagrams you found online hide a lot of complexity; and we would like to be given the opportunity to explain our work in the most constructive way before drawing possible conclusions. Our experience so far tells us that it is very common to disagree on “ontology designs” (at any stage), especially with domain experts; but when you bring people around the same table and explain the rationale of certain design choices — several concerns can be practically addressed, and solved. The latter is often triggered by the jargon and terminology used by ontology designers to represent certain domain-specific concepts. However, criticalities often come to the surface when ontology engineers try to use ontologies to semantically describe “example data” provided by the domain experts — which always offers valuable insights for further iterations.

So far, Music Meta has been a collaborative effort with domain experts such as musicologists, music librarians, archivists and cataloguers, music analysts, data engineers and so forth. Despite the cultural heritage influence in the model, we are still aligned to important contributions in the field which have already been applied to music industry, to some extent (e.g. The Music Ontology). Nevertheless, we found several critical issues with the existent contributions and collected evidence of these through a recent survey — which strikingly confirmed our expectations. The goal and the vision of Music Meta is to become a lingua franca for music metadata, regardless of the genre, historical period, datasets, stakeholders — and enable interoperability and expressivity at different level (both essential requirements to link music resources on the Web). This is why you see more abstract concepts in Music Meta (e.g. MusicEntity) but also hierarchical definitions (e.g. CreativeProcess) whenever the data you have available requires a more granular description of the music creation process for example (e.g. a piece may be composed in different places, times, and involve different people with different roles — assuming you have all this data to describe this). Nevertheless, you do not need to “use all the expressiveness” of the ontology if your data does not have such detail — because additional relationships will be created (at KG-creation time) to bypass these "highly expressive hubs”.

When it comes to modelling music industry data, you are right in concluding that the ontology is not complete yet; although I noticed that some classes that you mentioned are not in Music Meta (e.g. Musical Work, which is a very FRBR concept that is already in other music ontologies and comes with several limitations for the sake of interoperability). Music Meta is indeed an ongoing effort which fundamentally requires the integration of complementary perspectives to harmonise the cultural heritage view with music industry (our vision). Your comments already provide us with a useful resource to reflect on extending and improving our work; although I believe that you should be part of this process in a more systematic way. The challenge here is to find a way to make this exchange productive and useful for both parts. In line with your suggestions, we would like to propose this approach to kickstart this process:

- You provide a sample of music metadata from your dataset(s) that you consider as exhaustive and representative in regard to the modelling challenges you have brought to our attention (and more, if any). Any additional comment / explanation / supplementary information that could help us understand your data sample would be very much appreciated.

- Our ontology engineering team will then try to describe your data sample using Music Meta; which will presumably trigger further extensions, enhancements, and improvements in the ontology.

- We return an example of a Music Meta Knowledge Graph using your sample, which can then be scaled up. We will schedule a call to present this outcome and collect feedback from you for further iterations.

Though this process, which we will be following with other stakeholders in Polifonia as well, we will be able to improve and extend Music Meta in a way that can accommodate both music industry and cultural heritage perspectives to achieve our vision. What do you think about this workflow?

Looking forward to hearing from you.

Thanks,
Jacopo.



On 20 May 2023, at 11:19, Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&lt;mailto:daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;&gt; wrote:

Dear Jacopo,

Thank you for your quick reply.  I have identified myself with the Music Meta ontology in my presentation; however, the way I understand it, it is not suitable in this form; at least in our understanding, it goes against the conventions of the music industry and certainly does not allow the mapping to rights management databases; I think that it would be beneficial to start from a Music Meta Light that follows more the logic of the industry.

Hopefully my answer, while lengthy, will be useful for what I see as practical obstacles of using Music Meta, and also gives examples how Music Representation and Projection  could have a potentially globally unique use case.

We have legal access to about 80,000 sound recordings and are still searching for another 120,000 at least (we will certainly find some of them with the Slovak record labels, and others in the archive of the Slovak public broadcaster.)  These have various levels of documentation, and if somebody in the Polifonia consortium wants to extract features from them (about the contents), we can give legal access and computing capacity for free; we would only need guidance to create this dataset. Originally this was the intention to connect with Polifonia; and I think that this is the case at this moment still, because the Music Meta ontology, as you state, is an early-stage ontology and has no robust and numerous use cases. Music institutions, i.e. rights management agencies, publishers, labels and music archives could be a treasure trove of information.

Still, I do not see an obvious way to start applying this ontology to their databases.

 - Music content, audio and symbolic —&gt; Music Representation and Projection modules (we also have support for music annotations, datasets, and algorithms)

The problem I see here is that we have music content, audio and symbolic content in the databases of Publishers, rights management agencies, broadcasting archives, so until the Music Meta and the Rights Management practices are not well reconciled, this mapping cannot start effectively.  The unique selling point of our cooperation is that we can give legal access to extract these features from a source that is normally not available to anybody: the agency that collects the original score or recording to identify the rights of a new creation.This is the most comprehensive and exclusive source you can get, and it contains plenty of music that have restricted legal access (but their features could be used!)

One way Polifonia can support this effort is through our ontology network — which has considerably evolved in the past couple of months. The use of our ontologies, even in an experimental stage, will also be useful for Polifonia — as an opportunity to test their robustness, expressivity, and consistency. From your explanation of the project, we can categorise the main requirements into 3 categories:

- Music metadata, as in, artists, compositions, performances, recordings, licenses, broadcasting, etc. —&gt; our Music Meta ontology

- Rights management —&gt; you are right, we do not have particular requirements/ontologies related to this in Polifonia (and I am wondering how complex this would be)

I do not think that adding rights management information is a big deal if the Music Meta ontology better aligns with the databases of the rights management organizations, which in turn hold the data about what you want to describe in Music Meta.  It is also a useful addition, as more general library, catalog, inventory book metadata standards also need information about the rights to access.

So I think that the key issue is how to make the Music Meta ontology work for the purposes of the Slovak Comprehensive Music Database.

There are music ontologies which are Event-centered (a performance), and others a Thing-centered (a music work, a recording, a score); and the way music institutions work, I think that a Thing-centered ontology would be far more usable, as most music data is managed by rights management organisations, which are not event-centred, and usually do not even hold information about Events. But, of course, if the ontology is practical, this distinction disappears at one point.  However, while the music institutions have well-managed PIDs often going back a hundred years for Things, they do not have them for events.  So, to me, answering your question, how hard it would be to align your ontologies with rights management data (and databases, which contain a lot of the data you are looking for!)  would a better organization of Things and making the ontology more useful for Thing-centered databases, as almost all music databases in the world are Thing-centered and do not record much information about the Performance as an Event.

It is important to find anchoring points in PIDs used by music organisations and businesses because they will allow the cross-linking of datasets and databases, and I think that it would be important to define those nodes (classes) that allow linking via internationally recognised PIDs. Again, we need PIDs not to add rights management information (that is a small subset of information) but to tap into a huge treasure trove of rights management databases that can plenty-plenty of data about the music and the persons themselves!

What is the most alien to me is the CreativeProcess part because this differs from how the music industry and rights management thinks about it.  The music industry globally acknowledges three types of creators and three types of rights to the creators: composer (VIAF or ISNI)  and the thing composed ISWC, if set into score ISMN), performer (IPN, and of course the recording or live performance that the performer contributed to) and producer (the entity that recorded the performance, and things produced ISRC).  Data about these creator and creative processes are found in composer, performer and producer databases. Rights management agencies match recorded performances to composers, performers and producers, and in the case of live performances, by composers and Places, and time only.

Being event-centric is for our purposes not a good start,  because nowhere in the world can we find well-maintained event databases, however, the industry have been building, often for more than a hundred years, databases about thing, particularly music works (CISAC has 94.4 million well-documented in their database) and recently about recordings (Spotify’s EchoNest has well over 100 million of them.)  Matching these things to performances in most cases is not possible, so we need a clearer alignment of the critical Things: Musical Work, Sound Recording, Music Score, and persons (Composer, Performer, Producers [often a legal person.]).  I think that it is the US/UK copyright systems that lead to a thing-centered approach to recordings, which are of course recorded performances by adding a copyright to them.  In Europe, we do not have copyrights, and rights are connected to personality rights, and they are Person-centered.  But certainly not Event centered in either big jurisdictions.

I see the most confusion between the concepts of “Recording” and “Work” (which is an abstract concept and can be recorded as a “Recording” or a “Music Score” or equivalent notation like a midi file).  Publishing means making the music work available for use and Releasing means making the recording available for the public.  We have vast collections of recordings where we do not know if they were ever released, or if they were intended for release.  The release is a critical concept to find out who can listen to the recording.  The event of Publishing and the Event of Releasing, or Event of Broadcasting triggers all rights management consequences, even though legally the Published work or the Released recording is protected from Creation, but most information is recorded in the process of Publishing or Releasing.

The Composer(s) of the music created a Musical work, which was either recorded or set into the score, or both.  For a hundred years, to have your music work registered, you must provide either a score or a recording with accompanying lyrics when applicable. mm:Score is related to mm:Recording, but this is not a good relationship; it must relate to the work.The International Standard Music Number (ISMN) is a unique identifier for notated music (scores, parts, vocal scores, choral octavos, miniature scores, pop folios, etc.), whether published in print, online or other media. Each edition or version of a musical work is assigned a separate ISMN.  Currently, our goal is to assign an ISMN (when possible) or an equivalent pre-ISMN IBSN to every score that we find in Slovakia.  These are related to music works (identified by the PID ISWC) and composers (currently, we use both VIAF as a PID and the CISAC composer ID, which is not public, but it is used in every country for identifying the composer rightsholder.)

Via SOZA, we can access the data (a lot of it) of 94.4 million music works globally, and our focus of interest is about 150,000 of them, which are connected somehow to the current territory of Slovakia.  These databases do not only contain rights management information, but plenty of information about the music itself and the creators themselves, and often they can be connected to licensed live performances, or perhaps (though this is a huge work) to licensed broadcast performances.
If you want to add rights management information, then you need to add Copyright (US/UK) and Authors' Right (EU) and the agency that handles it. Also, for the purposes of organizations like Sound and Vision, or the Estonian Folk Archive, or the Slovak Music Information Center, it is getting important to determine if a there is no commercially available recording of a musical work in circulation (therefore an archive copy may be made available for the public, which leads to Recordings soon.)
Sometimes a musical work has no known recording; in most cases (in popular music), it has exactly one, and with popular classical music, often it has hundreds.  With popular music, there may be dozens of unlicensed or bootleg recordings.

The other creative process is Performance, where a musician or a group of musicians interpret a music work and either record it or not.  As the interpretation is often made from a set score, the score is not derived from the performance, but the performance is derived from the score (which is a description of the musical work.)  If the performance is recorded, then the Performers have neighboring rights in Europe (and in the UK and the US, a part of the recorded copyright; copyright does not exist in Europe.) For rights management purposes, you find many performers' information connected to a Performance or Recording. The International Performer Number (IPN) is a unique universal identifier allocated to every registered performer with any rights claim.

The Producer decides whether to release or not the recording.  The producer can be the artist herself, of course. Our biggest problem is the Slovak (and Estonian) music archive is to find out what was the producer’s intent with making the recording. If it was released, it should have an ISRC code as a PID, because it can be legally played in public places.  Releasing is similar to communicating to the public a broadcasting term.  Suppose the recording was released or communicated to the public. In that case, you may find a trace of it or information about it at a label, a distributor, a producer rights management organisation or a broadcaster. If not, then you have to establish if the recording can only be heard by a closed audience (for example, researchers in an archive) or it cannot be heard at all due to personality rights.

In the US/UK there is no separate Producer and Performer right (the right is recognized in both jurisdictions, but assumed to have been bought out by the producer).  In Europe, however, these rigths have their own life, they are both neighboring right(s)  therefore we have large databases about Performers (and their performances) and Producers (and the recordings they produced).

We also have access to a very large number of music scores, and more than half of them are hand-written.  We are working on strategies to digitise them into a machine-readable form, but this is not straightforward, even with printed scores, let alone handwritten ones.  Slovakia was a constituent part of the Hungarian Kingdom till 1918. Part of Czechoslovakia till 1993, and often had little local music score setting know-how and resources (as music publishing was centred in Budapest and Vienna, then Prague.)

Best regards,
Daniel

On 18 May 2023, at 20:34, Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&lt;mailto:daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;&gt; wrote:

You don't often get email from daniel.antal@reprex.nl&lt;mailto:daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;. Learn why this is important&lt;https://aka.ms/LearnAboutSenderIdentification&gt;
Dear Valentina, Jacopo, Roosmarijn,

I actually do not know whom to address in these issues, but I thought that I will start an email to connect our project with Polifonia. I have spent the week in Bratislava to do organizational work on our Open Music Europe output, the Slovak Comprehensive Music Database. Our ambitious goal is to create a linked open database with every Slovak work and its recording, and every composer, and as many performers as possible. (This is my 4th visit in the year, there has been a lot of preparations underway.)

This could be connected in two ways to Polifonia: we could try to use your ontologies, and we could also create very large exploitable datasets.

Currently, we plan to work with the entire work registry of SOZA, every sound recording officially released in the Slovak Republic [about 40,000 since the breakup of Czechoslovakia], and about 40,000 recordings (which are not well documented) of the Slovak Music Information Center -- these have a very mixed legal status --, and the sheet music collection of the Music Fund (a sort of a Composer Union.) We believe that several important Slovak labels will join our initiative, and we will have access to even more recordings. We are also investigating the possibility of working with scores/sheets/midi files. And we will later decide what to do with Czechoslovak recordings (interestingly, IFPI CS is still there and sorting out Czech/Slovak heritage is not easy.)

You have to bear in mind that our project has a rather different angle than yours: we want to make the repertoire audible and want to collect royalties, and we want to measure various cultural policy goals in streaming and broadcasting. This makes the current PON only partly usable, because so far did not find a very good ontology for rights management.  We could, for example, provide access to plenty of music for feature extraction, but our project has very limited goals in this area if at all. Our goal is to improve the documentation and metadata from a rights management perspective, not from a music research perspective, however, as we have access, and the two objectives can go hand in hand, we would have a rather big leeway to pursue both. These institutions have competent IT departments, and for example, many batch feature extraction would be possible in a way that a huge amount of other data could be linked to features.

The Slovak Music Information Center is both a library (I have just presented our plans to about 25 Slovak and Czech music libraries today) and an archive.  Their database is huge and well-designed, but not open. [They have a small subset available on their website in a non-machine readable format, but it shows that this is a very rich database:
https://hc.sk/en/o-slovenskej-hudbe/skladatelia ] The SOZA database is even bigger, but requires some more thinking on how and what can be opened. Our first task will be to add to their own or CISAC/only IDs PIDs and we are looking for keys for connections.

Tomorrow we will try to define a small subset that we will first clear with all rightsholders, where we will see everything: musicological data, works, recordings, master and author's rights, sheets, use volumes, revenues from digital and physical sales, including sheets. We'll use this for a legal and data model, and then we will aim to scale this up during the year to a much larger set; we are currently aiming for about 150,000 works and 200,000 recordings.

The Slovak Music Information Centre uses a similar collection strategy as the Canadian: they collect info on all music that is connected to the territory of modern Slovakia; this means composers and performers born here, or who moved here to a significant amount of time (had concerts in at least three years on certain stages; i.e. their visit was not only a tour).  While we have no genre specification, it is clear that the 20th-21st century classical music is the best documented, followed by 19th and earlier, jazz, and authentic folk.

All in all, I think that we could design our database, which will be a very simple and very large database consisting of only a few datasets that could be a big use case for Polifonia.  However, for this, I think that the best would be if 1-2 Polifonia members could visit Bratislava for a presentation and some local consultations, as we are talking about the entire national system. We have excellent working relations here, but Slovakia is a conservative country, and I think that a personal visit and presentation would be necessary if you have an interest in creating a joint, very large dataset.

I come here for a few days every month in the first phase of our project, because this is our treasure trove, and  we want to demonstrate most of our skills in this country. In the next year, we will try to replicate this in Bulgaria, where we will also start organization, but it will be a far more difficult task as Bulgaria's institutions are much younger and have smaller collections.

Best regards,
Daniel Antal, CFA
co-founder

Hi all,

Thank you for the productive call!

To prepare for our Eurostat microdata application, we need the most recent codebooks and questionnaires for:


  *   EU-LFS
  *   EU-SILC - also specifically 2006 and 2015 - Social and cultural participation (ilc_scp)
  *   AES - also specifically 2007 and 2011 (there may have also been an AES module on culture post-2012 when the ESSnet-Culture recommendations were published - we must check)
  *   HBS
  *   ICT
  *   HETUS

We should tender the microdata application as a research network consisting of EUBA, UVA, SSSA, and UTU (and possibly SINUS if we are recognized in time, otherwise we will tender separately for the SILC and AES data alone).
To prepare specifically for the Slovakia workshop, we also need:


  *   KULT-5-01 and KULT-19 methodological notes (as we already have for KULT-16-01)
  *   ROČ 1-01 and ROČ 2-01 questionnaires
  *   ROČ 2-01 and NSNO 1-01 sampling method
  *   To ask in workshop: response rates

We can use the Eurostat microdata application as a "template" for our Slovakian statistical authority microdata application. This should be ready to hand over to them on Thursday.

Re: the post-workshop with the other CMOs, I will prepare a partner survey on surveys (similarly to the one Magali sent around for D2.1 about airplay quotas, etc.). Basically, we will ask what national-level surveying programmes exist in the target countries, for links to codebooks and questionnaires, and about microdata access procedures. We can introduce the topic during the post-workshop, and I will send out the survey after. I imagine microdata access on a national level will become easier once we have been granted access by Eurostat.

@EUBA, let's plan on lunch and a one-hour meeting to go over any questions on the Slovak surveying program on 19 Sept.

@Daniel and @Joost, separately SINUS will need the codebooks and questionnaires for the CEEMID surveys and UVA anti-piracy survey, respectively. However, this is lower priority.

@Richard and @Daniel, I'll see you at 09:00 in the call with Joost tomorrow.

Please note all templates are here: https://cloud.sinus-institut.de/ws-OpenMusE/templates

Thank you again, and best regards,
James

Hi James,

I only reply to you.  I think that Magali's approach is not something that is a good thing to follow. Most of our partners are not research institutions and I do not think that it is their role to know about policies or survey programs. Official statistics have a clear organisational framework in every country, and they are very transparent.  I think that crowdsourcing research should be done very sparingly and with very good instructions.

Sending emails to national statistical offices is perhaps a better approach.   For the CMOs and MXF, MIH I would only send out tasks with extremely clear instructions, and knowing the capabilities of the person who is going to receive it. I mean, even our academic partners were not able to identify surveys, or simple policy documents.

Best regards,
Daniel

Hi all,



Thank you for the productive call!



To prepare for our Eurostat microdata application, we need the most recent codebooks and questionnaires for:



  *   EU-LFS
  *   EU-SILC - also specifically 2006 and 2015 - Social and cultural participation (ilc_scp)
  *   AES - also specifically 2007 and 2011 (there may have also been an AES module on culture post-2012 when the ESSnet-Culture recommendations were published - we must check)
  *   HBS
  *   ICT
  *   HETUS



We should tender the microdata application as a research network consisting of EUBA, UVA, SSSA, and UTU (and possibly SINUS if we are recognized in time, otherwise we will tender separately for the SILC and AES data alone).

To prepare specifically for the Slovakia workshop, we also need:



  *   KULT-5-01 and KULT-19 methodological notes (as we already have for KULT-16-01)
  *   ROČ 1-01 and ROČ 2-01 questionnaires
  *   ROČ 2-01 and NSNO 1-01 sampling method
  *   To ask in workshop: response rates



We can use the Eurostat microdata application as a "template" for our Slovakian statistical authority microdata application. This should be ready to hand over to them on Thursday.



Re: the post-workshop with the other CMOs, I will prepare a partner survey on surveys (similarly to the one Magali sent around for D2.1 about airplay quotas, etc.). Basically, we will ask what national-level surveying programmes exist in the target countries, for links to codebooks and questionnaires, and about microdata access procedures. We can introduce the topic during the post-workshop, and I will send out the survey after. I imagine microdata access on a national level will become easier once we have been granted access by Eurostat.



@EUBA, let's plan on lunch and a one-hour meeting to go over any questions on the Slovak surveying program on 19 Sept.



@Daniel and @Joost, separately SINUS will need the codebooks and questionnaires for the CEEMID surveys and UVA anti-piracy survey, respectively. However, this is lower priority.



@Richard and @Daniel, I'll see you at 09:00 in the call with Joost tomorrow.



Please note all templates are here: https://cloud.sinus-institut.de/ws-OpenMusE/templates



Thank you again, and best regards,

James

Just to confirm,


  *   Public files (e.g., publicly available sources such as policy documents or open access scientific articles, working versions of our own data collection instruments, etc.) should be put in our repositories on GitHub – in this case, https://github.com/dataobservatory-eu/report-european-music-economy/tree/main/background/
  *   Non-public files (e.g., address lists, interview transcripts, paywall-protected scientific articles, etc.) should be shared internally on SINUS cloud

Note that simply using GitHub as a file repository doesn’t require installing the desktop client or becoming familiar with complex functions. Uploading and downloading are just as easy as with Dropbox, etc.

Let’s avoid using multiple redundant file sharing systems 😊

Hi Maria,

The conference notes
This is very promising.  I think that that your notes require a bit of extra contex:
I copied them here:
Source: https://github.com/dataobservatory-eu/report-european-music-economy/blob/main/background/slovak-policy-documents/conference_notes_20230918.qmd
Rendered: https://github.com/dataobservatory-eu/report-european-music-economy/blob/main/docs/background/slovak-policy-documents/conference_notes_20230918.md

I think that it could be improved a bit, and perhaps written into a blogpost in the following structure?
1 paragraph: what was the conference title, where it was held, who organised it, and why it is relevant for our workshop and our Consortium's work.
2. editing your notes in a way that Arianna, Richard, or others who are not privy to what this was can understand your notes.

We are anyways desperately short of blog posts, and thinking in blog posts forces you to make documents that can be used by people who were not in our Zoom call and do not know what you have been taking notes of.
@Johannes Braunbruck&lt;mailto:johannes.braunbruck@synyo.com&gt;  can help you with editing this furher.

About the literature review for the surveys

For the extra material, I place only one of the documents into the repository.  I think that none of these files are confidential, and they have absolutely nothing to do with the SINUS Cloud, and we do not even need to store them in copy on GitHub. However, they need to be documented, because you cannot even finalise your Eurostat data request without them, so I would like to ask you to add the rest tomorrow morning, so that we can perhaps finalise the data request on Wednesday.

 To recap what we agreed on my visit to Bratisalva to you and Katerina, this is how you can make such material reviewable.  This would have saved countless of hours of work for James, Tomas and I when we desperately tried to find your references during your holiday.

- you add them to the bibliography on Zotero
- download them into a .bib file
- and add a paragraph to this reader to make sure that there is at least 1 sentence written about them (why you selected them) and to see if the reference works properly.

Like this:
https://music.dataobservatory.eu/documents/triple-transition/Reader.html

So, this is how I did it (you can finish yourself the rest):
- I googled EU-SILC_2021.pdf  (this could have been avoided if you place the document into our group Zotero folder or the bibliography)
- I found this document https://circabc.europa.eu/sd/a/de23ebb5-9f97-47ca-a46d-570bdebc6727/Methodological%20guidelines%202021%20operation%20v8.pdf
- I added it to our joint citation collection&lt;https://www.zotero.org/groups/4559070/digital_music_observatory/collections/CUGBQPBT&gt; (not as a file but as a citation)
- I exported the citation from Zotero into BiBlatex  (ExportedItem.bib the default file name)
- I gave it a more memorable identifier @eurostat_eu-silc_2021

It look now like this, and anybody can directly cite it in an economics journal:

@misc{eurostat_eu-silc_2021,
title = {Methodolgoical Guidelines and Description of {EU}-{SILC} Target Variables. 2021 operation (Version 8)},
url = {https://circabc.europa.eu/sd/a/de23ebb5-9f97-47ca-a46d-570bdebc6727/Methodological%20guidelines%202021%20operation%20v8.pdf},
publisher = {Eurostat},
author = {Eurostat},
urldate = {2023-09-18},
date = {2021},
year = {2021},
langid = {english},
note = {{DocSILC}065 (2021 operation)},
keywords = {2021, {EU}-{SILC}, Surveys}
}

I copied this to the bib/surveys.bib in our OPA compliant simpel file repoitory so now everybody in our project can import it or cite it.

Then I added to this Reader:
Surveys

bib/surveys.bib

  *   Methodolgoical Guidelines and Description of EU-SILC Target Variables. 2021 operation (Version 8) [@eurostat_eu-silc_2021]

Just to test out that I have recorded all data of eurostat_eu-silc_2021  correctly and it will work in Word, PDF, epub, and html:


bib/surveys.bib

  *   Methodolgoical Guidelines and Description of EU-SILC Target Variables. 2021 operation (Version 8) (Eurostat 2021&lt;http://localhost:4722/Reader.html#ref-eurostat_eu-silc_2021&gt;)

What I described now is also available in our Contributor Handbook, and we have practiced this in Bratislava. I think that it took me longer to write this email than it would take to put all the survey documentation to its proper place.

As a side note, @James Rhys Edwards&lt;mailto:JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&gt; was referring to a different year of EU-SILC, I do not think that EU-SILC had a 2021 CAP survey, so we need the questionnaires and methodological notes of those years where there is the data that you would like to put into your Eurostat data request.

Do you think that you can try to do that in the morning? I think this is really just 20 minutes of work until you properly copy the document's data that you already looked up today and check if all is working.   It really took me more time to write how to do this, but I do not want to copy the rest of the documents in place, because I think that this is an excellent practice for you and perhaps even Arianna who should anyways be prepared about mixed surveys.

I think that this is a very useful task, because as far as I know, every single economics journal that we may target wants to see citations in this way.

Best regards,
Daniel

Hi all,



Thank you for the productive call!



To prepare for our Eurostat microdata application, we need the most recent codebooks and questionnaires for:



  *   EU-LFS
  *   EU-SILC – also specifically 2006 and 2015 - Social and cultural participation (ilc_scp)
  *   AES – also specifically 2007 and 2011 (there may have also been an AES module on culture post-2012 when the ESSnet-Culture recommendations were published – we must check)
  *   HBS
  *   ICT
  *   HETUS



We should tender the microdata application as a research network consisting of EUBA, UVA, SSSA, and UTU (and possibly SINUS if we are recognized in time, otherwise we will tender separately for the SILC and AES data alone).

To prepare specifically for the Slovakia workshop, we also need:



  *   KULT-5-01 and KULT-19 methodological notes (as we already have for KULT-16-01)
  *   ROČ 1-01 and ROČ 2-01 questionnaires
  *   ROČ 2-01 and NSNO 1-01 sampling method
  *   To ask in workshop: response rates



We can use the Eurostat microdata application as a “template” for our Slovakian statistical authority microdata application. This should be ready to hand over to them on Thursday.



Re: the post-workshop with the other CMOs, I will prepare a partner survey on surveys (similarly to the one Magali sent around for D2.1 about airplay quotas, etc.). Basically, we will ask what national-level surveying programmes exist in the target countries, for links to codebooks and questionnaires, and about microdata access procedures. We can introduce the topic during the post-workshop, and I will send out the survey after. I imagine microdata access on a national level will become easier once we have been granted access by Eurostat.



@EUBA, let’s plan on lunch and a one-hour meeting to go over any questions on the Slovak surveying program on 19 Sept.



@Daniel and @Joost, separately SINUS will need the codebooks and questionnaires for the CEEMID surveys and UVA anti-piracy survey, respectively. However, this is lower priority.



@Richard and @Daniel, I’ll see you at 09:00 in the call with Joost tomorrow.



Please note all templates are here: https://cloud.sinus-institut.de/ws-OpenMusE/templates



Thank you again, and best regards,

James
