Subject: DMP, research data management and data stewarship

Hi James,

I am putting only Tomas and Istvan in CC, because we were supposed to meet about the DMP today, but I still think that there is a fundamental misunderstanding about data, metadata, research data management and the DMP itself, which needs to be sorted out by the coordinator. I tried with Richard many times, I failed, and I informed him yesterday that I am resigning from the T6.3 leadership and the grant amendments should be made accordingly.

Data stewardship is the practice of ensuring that Open Music Europe has data that is accessible for internal and external stakeholders, trustworthy, usable, and secure. We promised a data stewardship for European music sector: to identify the data needs of the industry (with any method, i.e. literature review, interviews, stakeholder consultations, etc.) and find ways to collect the information (Tx.1), collect it in a trustworthy manner (Tx.2) and make it usable (T4.1, T4.2, and T5.1).  The data management plan should only document this work in a machine- and human readable format for other data stewards who identify our project and OMO as a data source.

Every Horizon Europe project should have a “research data management” function, but in our case, this should be central to the project, because our project is about providing data, while most projects are expected to provide the reuse of their data after finishing their task, so this is a secondary function.
Research data management require domain-specific know-how and data know-how, but not data analysis or data engineering know-how. They were placed in WP1, 2, 3 and the “data collection plans” as Richard calls them should be the results of T1.1, T2.1, T3.1; in the original timeline they should be already available to meet the milestones. Currently, they are not even initialised, because the task forces do not have any contributing researchers who have relevant skills to make it.

In this project there should be a central part about “research data management”, which is not clearly described in the project plan created by Richard in the proposal phase, not even in the less prominent format required by HE but not H2020. This should be in WP5 because it is not a secondary project management function.  The research data management is scattered in various parts, mainly the T1.2, T2.2, T3.2, T4.2 data collection and metadata description tasks, but without fully covering research data management, and crucially, without an assigned task leader. The Tx.2 is a technical collection task, it already requires the “data collection plan” to execute them, and the T6.3 is a documentation function only.  To make the data collection in Tx.2 reproducible, the T4.1 should write or modify software code, but these are just supporting functions for a large-scale data collection.

The research data management has an important, standardized documentation format that must be human and machine readable, this is called the “Data Management Plan”.  The DMP describes for data-knowledgeable humans and machines how to access our data. This task requires domain (music specific), data and metadata know-how (ontologies, etc.) Unfortunately, this task went to a contributor who has no music, data, or metadata know-how.  This is very hard to understand, and also hard to understand why this problem is not addressed. SSSA may have the skills somewhere (maybe in the library department, or the IT department) the skills to do research data management in areas where SSSA does quantitative research, but we have never met them, and anyhow, the research data management must be music specific. Unless somebody is a metadata guru, it takes years to learn music data management, and even a metadata guru would take months to learn the music ontologies, because you have to understand music to understand music data.

The new data should be distributed in the OMO, which is T5.1, but it is a data dissemination task, not a data collection task. Not even a research data management task, because providing an observatory is not a requirement in the HE. This is what would go beyond RDM, but our project has no RDM!
Currently, the WP leaders did not assign or do not have personnel to create the “data collection plans”, although at least 4 reseracher-years should have been already spent on these subtasks by now. The “research data management” has no task leader, and its documentation function, the “DMP” is confusingly mixed with non-DMP task, and the PMs are assigned to a contributor who has no skills for music research data management.

Overall, this project will not be able to deliver, because it promises to collect data and exploit them in novel ways, and currently nobody is working on data collection or  (research) data management.  The project has no research data management function, has no skilled resources to document research data management, and the task leaders in WP1-2-3 are missing skills in their task forces to create data collection plans.

Reprex and UTU have PMs to provide the infrastructure of data collection and dissemination, but not to find out what and where should be collected.
Reprex could take over the research data management documentation task (this is the DMP), it is not a very big task, and we can easily provide the human resources to this task, because this is the smallest element of the data management.

However, to collect data, we need a structural change in the Consortium.  Either a research data management function must be consolidated at the expense of T1.1, T2.1, T3.1 (but utilizing T4.2 which is a metadata task) in WP5 as “research data management”) or T1.1, T2.1, T3.1 must get an injection of data know-how immediately.  Reprex does not have the budget or the human resources to do this, but as a small company without complex hiring procedures, and an understanding of music data and metadata, it can hire quickly.  It is really the responsibility of these WP leaders and the Coordinator to think this through: SSSA signed up to T1.1 and T2.1 and even to add resources to WP3 and WP4 without having any music or data or metadata person available, and so far did not even start to hire.  The Coordintator produced a task list that has no research data management and assigned the documentation function to a contributor that has no music or data or metadata know-how.

I think that it is wishful thinking that researchers who are primarily economists or legal scholars, with no experience in music, and no experience in data collection, can provide a data collection plan for music economics or music diversity or music circulation.  The D2.1 document largely missed the topic itself (it is about cultural diversity and not music diversity and not music circulation), and the D1.1 has the basis of this, because it was 90% created by Reprex. The current WP1 and WP2 contributors do not have music and data familiarity, and even if they are going to hire, it will be about 15 months late. It is also questionable if organisations with no background and culture in music and data can quickly absorb and supervise junior staff that should work on music and data related topics.

Reprex did not aim to do significant research, and we are OK if we are not involved in this, however, it seems less and less plausible that this project will deliver anything that is described in the main text of the grant agreement. It may deliver documents that try to address music and data problems, but their quality and usability may be too low to collect data on that basis and “empower stakeholders” with demonstrating how to use it.

Best regards

Daniel Antal, CFA

Aihe: Polifonia - OME cooperation

Dear Leo, Jeba and James,

I spent three working days with another EU music project, Polifonia, that is metadata-only and computer science centered to find out synergies and ways to handle large scales of microdata for our project. I wanted to do this to avoid parallel efforts, and to find synergies; mainly towards the use of knowledge graphs and RDF, which are heavily used, for example, by Spotify, and could greatly increase our metadata handling efficiency and use.

I will write detailed suggestions of works, priorities, even with code examples next week, because I got a lot of useful advice on the [dataset] package and how it could improve the efficiency of maintaining [eurostat], [iotables], [regions] or add new functionality to [spotifyr]

If possible, first I would like to get a quick assessment from Leo about one small thing. Polifonia has a wonderful and well supported RDF tool, SPARQL-Anything&lt;https://sparql-anything.cc/&gt;. I am wondering if we could deploy this as a joint rOpenGov/Polifonia package with a quick and short effort?

This is a java application, which works with many non-RDF resources and pre-processes it much simpler than rdflib to RDF or a knowledge graph.  It could be used both for import and export or exchange our data.

https://github.com/SPARQL-Anything/sparql.anything

It could be deployed in two ways:
- Calling Java from R directly&lt;https://jozef.io/r901-primer-java-from-r-1/#calling-java-from-r-directly&gt;, we get access to the source code, and basically we have to call on only one Java object;
-  Or via packaging the latest release in .jar file and rJava&lt;https://jozef.io/r902-primer-java-from-r-2/&gt;, using the helloJavaWorld&lt;https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/helloJavaWorld/index.html&gt; template.
- They have a similar Python binding&lt;https://pypi.org/project/pysparql-anything/&gt;, which is basically perhaps 1-2 dozens of source code in Python, as we really need to pass on a resource URL to a java object and retrieve the text file it creates.

This would, in my opinion,
- significantly reduce the programming need to the [dataset] package
- create a quick win for our software ecosystem, and connect to a very well maintained community
- put as in the same language with a large music metadata project and allow accessing complex microdata sources with the same pipeline and code, but into our R ecosystem, too
- add to their projects Impact and our deliverables.

I had only worked with rJava as a user, not a developer, but if anybody in Turku has a bit of familiarity with either Java or rJava, to me this looks like 1-2 days job, not counting of course testing, documenting, releasing.

What I could offer is to create the package documentation website, rich tutorials to access relevant statistical and music sources for us, even the template of a quick publication, and of course, a concept paper on how this could improve our other package's functionality. I could do a fair amount of testing, and ask their team to provide us all files for unit testing used in other language binders, and if needed, to take care of the CRAN process.

Best regards,

**Date:** 10/18/2023 13:12:39

<!-- source: OpenMuse_20261009-2156/OpenMuse/messages/202310181312-OpenMusE __ Audit-789.txt -->

Dear Istvan, dear Daniel,

As you know SINUS has started the preparation work on the upcoming Periodic Report for the EC by sending out templates and deadlines for input to all partners. For both REPREX and SINUS an additional factor comes into play as we are the only two organisations within OpenMusE which are over the 430K EUR threshold which makes a financial audit compulsory.

To avoid any nasty surprises by the end of the project SINUS will ask their auditor to make an ‘intermediate’ chek/audit on the SINUS project finances for the first reporting period (01.01.2024 – 31.12.2024) by the end of this year. We strongly suggest that REPREX does the same with their auditor so that we will be aware of any possible necessary adjustments at an early stage when potential errors are still salvageable.

It would be great if you could indicate to us whether you plan on following SINUS’ example to this regard.

Thanks and kind regards,
Richard

<!-- source: OpenMuse_20261009-2156/OpenMuse/messages/202310291626-OpenMusE __ draft minutes of the the 4th PMB meeti-795.txt -->

Hello everyone,

Please find attached the draft (v. 0.9) for the minutes of our last PMB meeting. A giant thank you! goes to Annika who took the lion share of the notes during our discussions and then again went through the session recording once more. Please have a look at the text itself and at the ‘Next Steps’/to-do list. In case you find things misquoted or misspelled which you want to have rectified please (this time) write to James and Isabella up until Monday, 6 November, 23:59. After that the current version 0.9 (incl. possible edits) will become the final version 1.0.

Since there had been some isolated misunderstandings with past PMB minutes I think it’s necessary to point out that these minutes

  *   are a record of what had been said by whom during the meeting, deliberately using neutral language
  *   are not an opportunity to reverse/alter/invalidate/.. decisions that had been made by the PMB during the meeting
  *   are not a forum to add new topics/reasoning/suggestions/.. which had not been part of the meeting discussions itself, i.e.,
  *   are solely meant to represent what a person spoke out in words during the meeting and not what they may or may not have thought
Please keep this in mind when requesting edits to the current text.

Since I am currently on vacation the final version of these minutes will as an exception be prepared by James this time. Looking forward to seeing you all again in December.

Greetings from the edge of a Nicaraguan volcano crater,
Richard

&gt;&gt;     On 30 Oct 2023, at 18:28, Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
&gt;&gt;     wrote:
&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;     Hi Jacopo,
&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;     I wonder if we can have a follow-up call.  I see two topics that
&gt;&gt;     we need to cover, and one of them is urgent because we will not
&gt;&gt;     get any significant data without understanding how we go
&gt;&gt;     forward.  Our databases contain names of composers, performers,
&gt;&gt;     therefore fall under GDPR. Generally, our data is not very rich
&gt;&gt;     without the personal information, because rights management,
&gt;&gt;     music creation and music recommender systems are all very much
&gt;&gt;     person-centric, especially if you do not work with Western
&gt;&gt;     classical music or authentic folk, where the person performing
&gt;&gt;     the work is not so important.
&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;     And we also need to come to a working solution of finding a link
&gt;&gt;     between the key concepts of our databases and yours.I see three
&gt;&gt;     groups of topics, in order of importance, first, we need to find
&gt;&gt;     some equivalence relationships between your ontologies and the
&gt;&gt;     key databases and identifiers of the music industry and music
&gt;&gt;     heritage organisations. Then we have to talk about the attached
&gt;&gt;     personal data, because that will be particularly important for
&gt;&gt;     the NDA.   There is a third group of data that we need to deal
&gt;&gt;     with, but it is less problematic and less urgent.
&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;     _Can we have a call sometime this week?_
&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;     Topic 1: mapping key objects, i.e. music works, sound recordings
&gt;&gt;     (and their releases, playlists), sheets, songboosk, librettors.
&gt;&gt;     In my opinion, an equivalence relation is absolutely necessary to
&gt;&gt;     the main cultural objects of the industry and heritage
&gt;&gt;     organisations; i.e. we must have equivalence relations to works,
&gt;&gt;     recordings, playlists, albums, and published music sheets, lyrics
&gt;&gt;     or librettos. I also believe that an abstract playlist concept
&gt;&gt;     forming either an album release (which is a pre-defined sequence
&gt;&gt;     of song recordings released together) or a playlist in a
&gt;&gt;     broadcast-retransmission-streaming is also extremely important.
&gt;&gt;     In fact, the release concept is confusing because it can mean in
&gt;&gt;     the industry both a single recording and a collection of recordings.
&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;     Topic 2: mapping people and institutions to music objects, which
&gt;&gt;     is the basis of the rights management (people have rights).  We
&gt;&gt;     cannot really identify musical works for example without their
&gt;&gt;     author (composer, lyricist) and title.  But to put names into a
&gt;&gt;     database can be problematic.
&gt;&gt;     Our biggest concern is GDPR in this regard, we wonder how you
&gt;&gt;     treat the GDPR issues of your databases (names of music creators
&gt;&gt;     and their life events.) I’d really like to get permission to use
&gt;&gt;     a few names and show examples, because we will have to be able to
&gt;&gt;     explain how we will use the data.
&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;     Topic 3: Institutions, names, agents. Recordings, works, music
&gt;&gt;     sheets are managed by record labels and publishers, and the muisc
&gt;&gt;     itslef is performed usually by groups of people (band, ensemble,
&gt;&gt;     orchestra, duo, trio).  We need to have a model of people acting
&gt;&gt;     on behalf an institution. In music, these institutions and the
&gt;&gt;     rights they represent change very fast.  For example, one day
&gt;&gt;     Universal represents a song, the other day Schubert music; people
&gt;&gt;     join and quit bands. These are perhaps best attached to music
&gt;&gt;     objects as events.
&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;     Best regards,
&gt;&gt;     Daniel
&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;

&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;&gt;     On 30 Oct 2023, at 18:28, Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
&gt;&gt;&gt;     wrote:
&gt;&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;&gt;     Hi Jacopo,
&gt;&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;&gt;     I wonder if we can have a follow-up call.  I see two topics that
&gt;&gt;&gt;     we need to cover, and one of them is urgent because we will not
&gt;&gt;&gt;     get any significant data without understanding how we go
&gt;&gt;&gt;     forward.  Our databases contain names of composers, performers,
&gt;&gt;&gt;     therefore fall under GDPR. Generally, our data is not very rich
&gt;&gt;&gt;     without the personal information, because rights management,
&gt;&gt;&gt;     music creation and music recommender systems are all very much
&gt;&gt;&gt;     person-centric, especially if you do not work with Western
&gt;&gt;&gt;     classical music or authentic folk, where the person performing
&gt;&gt;&gt;     the work is not so important.
&gt;&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;&gt;     And we also need to come to a working solution of finding a link
&gt;&gt;&gt;     between the key concepts of our databases and yours.I see three
&gt;&gt;&gt;     groups of topics, in order of importance, first, we need to find
&gt;&gt;&gt;     some equivalence relationships between your ontologies and the
&gt;&gt;&gt;     key databases and identifiers of the music industry and music
&gt;&gt;&gt;     heritage organisations. Then we have to talk about the attached
&gt;&gt;&gt;     personal data, because that will be particularly important for
&gt;&gt;&gt;     the NDA.   There is a third group of data that we need to deal
&gt;&gt;&gt;     with, but it is less problematic and less urgent.
&gt;&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;&gt;     _Can we have a call sometime this week?_
&gt;&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;&gt;     Topic 1: mapping key objects, i.e. music works, sound recordings
&gt;&gt;&gt;     (and their releases, playlists), sheets, songboosk, librettors.
&gt;&gt;&gt;     In my opinion, an equivalence relation is absolutely necessary
&gt;&gt;&gt;     to the main cultural objects of the industry and heritage
&gt;&gt;&gt;     organisations; i.e. we must have equivalence relations to works,
&gt;&gt;&gt;     recordings, playlists, albums, and published music sheets,
&gt;&gt;&gt;     lyrics or librettos. I also believe that an abstract playlist
&gt;&gt;&gt;     concept forming either an album release (which is a pre-defined
&gt;&gt;&gt;     sequence of song recordings released together) or a playlist in
&gt;&gt;&gt;     a broadcast-retransmission-streaming is also extremely
&gt;&gt;&gt;     important. In fact, the release concept is confusing because it
&gt;&gt;&gt;     can mean in the industry both a single recording and a
&gt;&gt;&gt;     collection of recordings.
&gt;&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;&gt;     Topic 2: mapping people and institutions to music objects, which
&gt;&gt;&gt;     is the basis of the rights management (people have rights).  We
&gt;&gt;&gt;     cannot really identify musical works for example without their
&gt;&gt;&gt;     author (composer, lyricist) and title.  But to put names into a
&gt;&gt;&gt;     database can be problematic.
&gt;&gt;&gt;     Our biggest concern is GDPR in this regard, we wonder how you
&gt;&gt;&gt;     treat the GDPR issues of your databases (names of music creators
&gt;&gt;&gt;     and their life events.) I’d really like to get permission to use
&gt;&gt;&gt;     a few names and show examples, because we will have to be able
&gt;&gt;&gt;     to explain how we will use the data.
&gt;&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;&gt;     Topic 3: Institutions, names, agents. Recordings, works, music
&gt;&gt;&gt;     sheets are managed by record labels and publishers, and the
&gt;&gt;&gt;     muisc itslef is performed usually by groups of people (band,
&gt;&gt;&gt;     ensemble, orchestra, duo, trio).  We need to have a model of
&gt;&gt;&gt;     people acting on behalf an institution. In music, these
&gt;&gt;&gt;     institutions and the rights they represent change very fast. 
&gt;&gt;&gt;     For example, one day Universal represents a song, the other day
&gt;&gt;&gt;     Schubert music; people join and quit bands. These are perhaps
&gt;&gt;&gt;     best attached to music objects as events.
&gt;&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;&gt;     Best regards,
&gt;&gt;&gt;     Daniel
&gt;&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;&gt;
&gt;&gt;&gt;

&gt;&gt;&gt;&gt;         - *music databases*: this is a more complex issue, because

Hey Daniel,

Sorry for not replying sooner. As you can imagine we had our hands full after the election.
The good news is, that it seems that IKP will have a good working cooperation with our new minister so we can go ahead as planned.

We are working on a contract between you and the ministry of culture, that would give us the permission to give you total acces to our data sources.
Under the condition that you wont share the confidential data with any outside party of course. Other than that the contract will be very liberal and will not hinder our technical or analytical work at all.

We will have the contract in written form shortly. It will be in Slovak. Do you have means to translate it for you? Its like 3-4 pages of mostly legal mumbo jumbo.

Let us know when you will be in Bratislava!

Best regards,

Marcel

From: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
Sent: Thursday, October 12, 2023 1:02 PM
To: Čas Marcel &lt;marcel.cas@culture.gov.sk&gt;
Cc: Rudyjová Michaela &lt;michaela.rudyjova@culture.gov.sk&gt;
Subject: Re: KULT

Hi Marcel and Michaela,


No problem, I am sorry I had to leave so abruptly – I had a meeting about an important strategic document about the investments process in MK SR. The doors of IKP are open to you anytime, so feel free to organize your trips as it suits yourself.

Regarding the KULT surveys:

  *   I agree with starting with them, IF it suits the project – I don’t want to use you

We received public money with a mandate to make an impact with developing usable data products and software tools for public policy.  Some of my Consortium partners are eager to opportunistically spend the money on themselves, I think that spending the money on your needs is 100% aligned with the project goals.  Our mandate is to find data gaps, and use novel data science and statistical methods to fill the data gap by reusing disused open data, or setting up better data collection.


  *   The legality of giving you micro data is kinda wonky and I am trying to find a practical and legal solution. Let me ask you, does the project need the micro data as a project output? Or would the code itself be sufficient as an output? The thing is I cannot legally make the micro data publicly available – only aggregates. But I don’t consider you writing a code for us on our publicly unavailable datasets a breach of this law. If the data does not leave IKP and you, it should not be a problem. I will consult this with our lawyers.

In Europe, the Open Data Directive, which is transposed to Slovak law, allows access for public sector information for reuse at no cost, or marginal cost of provision.  Even Eurostat gives access to researchers who meet data protection rules to microdata.  However, we do not want to publish microdata at all.  I think that what we would do is exactly what we want to do with the Slovak statistical office.

The datasets will be your publicly-held datasets. However, I need to access them to write a code that can re-process them to a more usable microdata file and then to process statistical information from it.  For us, this is a worthy goal provided that the statistically processed data will be public.  (I also believe that it would be illegal to stop making them public based on the Open Data Directive.)

In a practical term, the code will eventually be run on your computer and by your colleague in RStudio. However, to write that code I need to access the data and it would be very practical to move into your office for weeks until everything is perfect. It would be good if I could get a subsample of the data to write the code that fixes it.

Working with microdata is only really problematic if the microdata identifies private persons.  I think that at least some of the KULT surveys only survey legal persons, so GDPR is not applicable to the microdata. However, any concerns can be mitigated if we simply remove the identifiers that would help identifying the responsend, say, if Hudobné centrum is named as a respondent in the file, we will give it a random identifier, for example KULT-RESPONDENT-7865.  I can also write any statement that I will not publish the data.



  *   We are talking roughly about 20 Kult questionnaires in excel (.csv format – sometimes giving us “not IT nerds” problems). Each KULT type, for example “theather” has a separate excel file for each year – roughly from 2014-2021, so 8 excel files for each of the 20 KULT types/questionnaires. Each excel file has tens of  columns (lets say about 50) with indicators and hundreds (f.e. theatres), sometimes thousands (f.e. libraries) rows with cultural institutions and their data.

In my opinion, the only possible concern with this data is the name-identifier of the respondent.  If you are concerned about this, perhaps I could spend a working day in IKP and we could select parts of at least some of the files that are of no concern. For example, visitor numbers without any reference to the size and name of the institutions become sust an abstract time series.  But again, if the respondents are not private persons, this is less of a concern, much of this data should be in their public annual report. And if they are state-public entities, I assume that most of their responses should be public, too.



  *   You can see the data at IKP anytime you want :D Actually sending you the data… I have to figure out the best way. Maybe I will get you to sign a statement that you cannot share the data with anyone else, but IKP. Or something of that sort.

Well, please check our MoU and let's sign a confidentiality agreement. SOSR would require me to work with their micordata in their premises, but it is because they have GDPR protected or business secrecy data, too, and they would monitor me that I do not try to identify the respondents (they would not give me names, but for example, in a small village, technically I could identify a person by gender, age, and occupation.)

To me, in the first round, the most interesting are the three music related surveys.  The ensembles may have private entities, but in my opinion the other two only have legal person and mainly public legal persons data.

In my opinion, this is what you would get:
- An analysis of the quality of the KULT microdata: how sampling, data recording, surveying, and data storage could be improved to avoid future data problems -- private to you, but perhaps good to discuss with SOSR, and other institutions responsible for KULT for quality improvements;
- A report and a code (that can be read, as I showed, either as a report, or just code, or both, annotated) on every problem and how it was fixed, private to you;
- The fixed dataset with every correction in log file (reproducible and reviewable, to ensure that our code works well);
- Summary statistical tables and data visualisations: you must commit to make this public and place it among your website to the EU's open repositories.  This is in my opinion is legal obligation, not a  right, which follows from the Open Data Directive and spending EU money on reprocessing bad data into usable format.  But I do not think that this would be a problem at all.

Best regards,
Daniel



  *
  *   Yeah I agree, that would be the best way forward.

Best regards,

Marcel

-          Do we need to sign any agreement, or the MoU is sufficent for me to get the raw data files that you need to stich together to time series – longitudional format?

-          How many files are we talking about in total? When could I get a first view of them?

---------- Forwarded message ---------


Hi Daniel,



so I checked the contract and I dont think it is very suitable for your work planned with the Ministry. There are two main problems:



- these types of contracts (agreements other than basic employment agreements according to the Labour Code) cannot be concluded when creating databases, PC programs, source codes as they are protected by the Copyright Act and there should be a license agreement instead (or a basic employment agreement);

- the contract should be limited to a 12 month maximum period - extensions are not possible.



Details and reasoning behind it can be found in my comments in the document.



If there is no other way possible for the Ministry to give you what you need, the red parts in 1.1. should be taken out (or it should be changed to something very, very vague, so the words as database, source codes are not used) and the timeframe for the contract should be a 1 year maximum.



I am sorry for not delivering a more positive assessment. If the Ministry manages to change it to be in accordance with the law, please send it to me for a review.



Best,



Richard

From: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&lt;mailto:daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;&gt;
Sent: Thursday, October 12, 2023 1:02 PM
To: Čas Marcel &lt;marcel.cas@culture.gov.sk&lt;mailto:marcel.cas@culture.gov.sk&gt;&gt;
Cc: Rudyjová Michaela &lt;michaela.rudyjova@culture.gov.sk&lt;mailto:michaela.rudyjova@culture.gov.sk&gt;&gt;
Subject: Re: KULT

Hi Marcel and Michaela,


No problem, I am sorry I had to leave so abruptly – I had a meeting about an important strategic document about the investments process in MK SR. The doors of IKP are open to you anytime, so feel free to organize your trips as it suits yourself.

Regarding the KULT surveys:

  *   I agree with starting with them, IF it suits the project – I don’t want to use you

We received public money with a mandate to make an impact with developing usable data products and software tools for public policy.  Some of my Consortium partners are eager to opportunistically spend the money on themselves, I think that spending the money on your needs is 100% aligned with the project goals.  Our mandate is to find data gaps, and use novel data science and statistical methods to fill the data gap by reusing disused open data, or setting up better data collection.


  *   The legality of giving you micro data is kinda wonky and I am trying to find a practical and legal solution. Let me ask you, does the project need the micro data as a project output? Or would the code itself be sufficient as an output? The thing is I cannot legally make the micro data publicly available – only aggregates. But I don’t consider you writing a code for us on our publicly unavailable datasets a breach of this law. If the data does not leave IKP and you, it should not be a problem. I will consult this with our lawyers.

In Europe, the Open Data Directive, which is transposed to Slovak law, allows access for public sector information for reuse at no cost, or marginal cost of provision.  Even Eurostat gives access to researchers who meet data protection rules to microdata.  However, we do not want to publish microdata at all.  I think that what we would do is exactly what we want to do with the Slovak statistical office.

The datasets will be your publicly-held datasets. However, I need to access them to write a code that can re-process them to a more usable microdata file and then to process statistical information from it.  For us, this is a worthy goal provided that the statistically processed data will be public.  (I also believe that it would be illegal to stop making them public based on the Open Data Directive.)

In a practical term, the code will eventually be run on your computer and by your colleague in RStudio. However, to write that code I need to access the data and it would be very practical to move into your office for weeks until everything is perfect. It would be good if I could get a subsample of the data to write the code that fixes it.

Working with microdata is only really problematic if the microdata identifies private persons.  I think that at least some of the KULT surveys only survey legal persons, so GDPR is not applicable to the microdata. However, any concerns can be mitigated if we simply remove the identifiers that would help identifying the responsend, say, if Hudobné centrum is named as a respondent in the file, we will give it a random identifier, for example KULT-RESPONDENT-7865.  I can also write any statement that I will not publish the data.



  *   We are talking roughly about 20 Kult questionnaires in excel (.csv format – sometimes giving us “not IT nerds” problems). Each KULT type, for example “theather” has a separate excel file for each year – roughly from 2014-2021, so 8 excel files for each of the 20 KULT types/questionnaires. Each excel file has tens of  columns (lets say about 50) with indicators and hundreds (f.e. theatres), sometimes thousands (f.e. libraries) rows with cultural institutions and their data.

In my opinion, the only possible concern with this data is the name-identifier of the respondent.  If you are concerned about this, perhaps I could spend a working day in IKP and we could select parts of at least some of the files that are of no concern. For example, visitor numbers without any reference to the size and name of the institutions become sust an abstract time series.  But again, if the respondents are not private persons, this is less of a concern, much of this data should be in their public annual report. And if they are state-public entities, I assume that most of their responses should be public, too.



  *   You can see the data at IKP anytime you want :D Actually sending you the data… I have to figure out the best way. Maybe I will get you to sign a statement that you cannot share the data with anyone else, but IKP. Or something of that sort.

Well, please check our MoU and let's sign a confidentiality agreement. SOSR would require me to work with their micordata in their premises, but it is because they have GDPR protected or business secrecy data, too, and they would monitor me that I do not try to identify the respondents (they would not give me names, but for example, in a small village, technically I could identify a person by gender, age, and occupation.)

To me, in the first round, the most interesting are the three music related surveys.  The ensembles may have private entities, but in my opinion the other two only have legal person and mainly public legal persons data.

In my opinion, this is what you would get:
- An analysis of the quality of the KULT microdata: how sampling, data recording, surveying, and data storage could be improved to avoid future data problems -- private to you, but perhaps good to discuss with SOSR, and other institutions responsible for KULT for quality improvements;
- A report and a code (that can be read, as I showed, either as a report, or just code, or both, annotated) on every problem and how it was fixed, private to you;
- The fixed dataset with every correction in log file (reproducible and reviewable, to ensure that our code works well);
- Summary statistical tables and data visualisations: you must commit to make this public and place it among your website to the EU's open repositories.  This is in my opinion is legal obligation, not a  right, which follows from the Open Data Directive and spending EU money on reprocessing bad data into usable format.  But I do not think that this would be a problem at all.

Best regards,
Daniel



  *
  *   Yeah I agree, that would be the best way forward.

Best regards,

Marcel

From: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
Sent: Thursday, November 23, 2023 2:40 PM
To: Čas Marcel &lt;marcel.cas@culture.gov.sk&gt;; Rudyjová Michaela &lt;michaela.rudyjova@culture.gov.sk&gt;
Subject: Functional and data requirements / beyond KULT

Dear Marcel and Michalea,

We use a methodology, eXtreme Design with some UX additions to describe data problems in a simple, natural language to our users and their expected, ideal outcome.  For example,
Before: Michaela currently manually opens each KULT xlxs file, and adjust the columns to the format of blablabla.
After: We would like the new application to open all KULT files, read them in, and put them into a tidy data format where blablabal

https://docs.google.com/document/d/185IeCTRnjVv4lY3kYJQKJ1kD93V3ubfFwtNH3wWv_ak/edit?usp=sharing

I would like to spend about an hour reviewing these things in situ, on site, so that I have an idea what data problems you face and how I can help.

Before/After
- It would be good if you could imagine a few scenarios when you would like to automate data access, data wrangling, formatting, linking, and validation
- We are collecting our metadata and functional data requirements for the next year's developments, and whatever you specify now will likely be supported.

The before statements are important because we know which are the processes whose data we need to sample, and which are the processes that we will automate and improve. The after statements can be dreamed up by you or I will invent improvements.

Personas
I invented fictional names and ages, but they should reflect with fictional names your actual colleagues and workflows. The age and background should mildly reflect reality, because that gives an indication on the documentation and UX need.  So we only use personas instead of Michaela or Marcel because these files will be shared in a wider development team and we do not want you to be identified with your personal problems.

Statements
These are coming from the XD method, and they relate to metadata ontologies more than functional requirements, however, in both WPs we will work with both metadata and data.

The statement parts of the stories describe hypothetical but crystal clear statements that you want to be able to make in your rights management work  or your research practice.

- The ISRC of "Let It Be" ISRCXY1234 can be matched with the music work of John Lennon - Paul McCartney: Let It Be with ISWC19203943.  -&gt; this means that we solved the problem if our solution can be tested against such statements and it succeeds.  Our computer system is successful if it successfully matches a work in the CIS-Net (described with title, author, and ISWC) with a recording described by title, ISRC.
- The variable QA2_12 in the Eurobarometer series refers to TheSOZ concept "Occupation" / SDMX concept ("Occupation") and its data can be joined with the variable in AES X67 which equally refers to these concepts.
- The variable QA2_12 has a sufficiently similar question label to Afrobarometer Wave 5 67 and pending approval from the Principal Investigator should be seen as a harmonisation target.


While these statements relate to metadata (they have ontological consequences) they also relate to functional software requirements, i.e. retroharmonize must support relabelling and concept harmonisation.

Best regards,
Daniel

&gt; Aihe: WP4 meeting agenda point suggestions and WP3 requirements
&gt;
&gt; Dear Leo,
&gt;
&gt; For our meeting on Friday I suggest at least the following agenda.
&gt;
&gt; 1.   Background / foreground separation
&gt; - What is exactly the background (i.e. what is the software created before
&gt; the WP4 started to work?)
&gt; - How do we treat maintenance of code, which is not a Horizon Europe
&gt; objective  but necessary for the code that we will reuse for new software
&gt; functionality.
&gt; 2.  Preparing the work plan
&gt; - User requirements (internal stakeholder, external stakeholder, and from
&gt; data science literature)
&gt; - Translating the user requirements to subtasks and issues
&gt; -  which will be the initial element of the D4.1 software ecosystem?
&gt; HearDis!?
&gt; 3.  Initial work
&gt; - code to be written and presented by 31 January
&gt; - quality control: alignment with the user requirements, testing in
&gt; production, CRAN release;
&gt; - cut off date for software to be considered by 31 January ;
&gt; - publication plans and data science/statistical peer review;
&gt; - new software development already in the pipeline.
&gt; 4. Presenting future plans
&gt; - how do we communicate elements of D4.1 that are not yet in place on 31
&gt; January 2024? [f.e. working paper on Zenodo with a bridging report to be
&gt; submitted to the Commission]
&gt; - alignment with the dissemination plan
&gt; - alignment with the exploitation plan
&gt; - alignment with the DMP.
&gt;
&gt; The rough document that I made is the result of intensive meetings in
&gt; Bratislava with our external and internal stakeholders and it is only about
&gt; survey data harmonisation.
&gt;
&gt; We want to go back to all stakeholders, especially the statistical
&gt; authority, in the 2nd week of January with results, I think that this is
&gt; the only user feedback possible for our "software ecosystem" first elements
&gt; by 31 January.  Of course, other feedback, such as the accepted CRAN
&gt; release for new functions can be taken into consideration, too.
&gt;
&gt; Whatever is needed to meet the requirement of the statistical office,
&gt; Reprex can even produce those elements alone in WP4.1 if your team cannot
&gt; contribute significantly.  But in that case we will also have to bring up
&gt; some resource planning for the future.  I can move 1 PM easily but not that
&gt; many. Our expectation is that you have 2 full time programmers available
&gt; for these tasks and your active contribution.  The WP4.1 is a taskstream 1
&gt; task and you cannot spread the PMs over 3 years -- the code is essential to
&gt; be production ready for Taskstream 2 and 3 tasks, so most of the
&gt; performance should be now, particularly in M9-M15. Reprex alone cannot fill
&gt; the gap of 2-3 full time equivalents.
&gt;

Hi!

Ok great - I have now tried to read all the email from you, Daniel. As my computer crashed this week and there were some extra delays. I would like to mention that the amount of emails I get is preventing me to read longer emails on a short notice. I prefer meetings to resolve open issues, combined with short documents outlining the concrete tasks and timelines by each party.

Personnel:
- Pyry is not working for OpenMUSE project any more, expect finalizing the eurostat package and being a close collaborator and may cross-contribute here and there when natural. Hence we shall not plan or allocate tasks for him. I thought I had mentioned this but I hope it is clear now.
- Jeba has been specifically recruited for this project. His background is in IT, and he is the best applicant we could recruit for the time being. We will do what we can do with him.
- I will supervise the process, and also checking what other resources/personnel to find to support the development.

Plans:
As far as I can see, the following is what we can at least work on right now. We can discuss how to modify and match these on Monday.

1) finalizing the substantial upgrade on eurostat (they changed their API and the pkg had to be completely rewritten to keep it functional; Pyry is doing, Jeba supports)

2) contributing to datasets package (Jeba can work on this but would help if you can interact with him as this package is based on your vision)

3) sparql Java bindings: if possible, this can be packaged; we are looking into this. We need to decide how much time we spend trying to get it working.

4) other package: iotables, regions etc. we can help if you have needs.

5) interoperability between packages; natural part of the ecosystem development, we just need to talk on a regular basis and map the needs clearly so that they can be implemented

6) Shiny app: ready to implement after we know what task it should solve exactly; we can discuss this

7) Automated reports: very feasible outcome from the package work. If I understand correctly you already have a clear outline but we can help and contribute as relevant.

8) Landing page: If I understand correctly you already have a clear outline but we can help and contribute as relevant.

8) Subsequent publications, we can think about this afterwards; we could start by helping with the ones you have already listed as they all make sense (eurostat, datasets, sparql etc)

When put together well and communicated clearly via a landing page these should pretty much address the required task and deliverable for January as far as I can see.

Other tasks we can discuss as well.

We could consider maintaining a short list of agreed technical tasks, together with priorities. I had previously prepared such for our own use but it might be easier to have a shared one to improve coordination.

See you on Monday!

Leo

Lähettäjä: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
Lähetetty: torstai 9. marraskuuta 2023 18.01.54

Aihe: Re: Polifonia - OME cooperation

Hi Leo,

I am answering with James in CC because I think that we will have to revisit these issues next Monday.

Re: connecting the eurostat package works to Open Music Europe I published a first personified requirement to connect the dataset package to eurostat, which could give a head start to connect Pyry's work to this project:
source: https://github.com/dataobservatory-eu/dataset-development/tree/main/stories
html: https://music.dataobservatory.eu/documents/open_music_europe/dataset-development/stories/eurostat-user1.html
 and I uploaded this working/concept paper to Zenodo&lt;https://zenodo.org/records/10091666&gt;.

I think that connecting Eurostat to Open Music Europe is very straightforward, we just have to ensure that with the new package the relevant data can be put into the OMO.  And to start developing the ecosystem, at least the eurostat, iotables and dataset packages should work functionally well together by January. To me this is very feasible if Pyry can assign most of his time on this. The little requirement I wrote is about the latter, but we can define how to contribute with Eurostat data to the project easily.

Re: developing dataset
If you remember, I had posted the first conceptual release on rOpenSci&lt;https://github.com/ropensci/software-review/issues/553&gt; so that we can recruit co-developers, and I released a very preliminary version of the package on CRAN before the kick-off of our project.

About working with Jeba, I am not sure how he can be involved, but we can discuss this with James next week.  I would like to bring this package into production by January, because by May we have to release a huge pile of data, partly from Eurostat, but mainly not from Eurostat.

To me, these are the requirements for a contributor:
- Has experience in writing R code to a level that passes CRAN review -- developing the software
- Has experience in technical R documentation with packagedown, and CRAN standards -- releasoin the work
- Experienced with publishing in the R Journal or similar data science journals and on Rbloggers -- dissemination work
- Experienced with data modeling or knowledge modeling, metadata languages -- conceptual contributions to the package [currently I get this a cross-favors with the Polifonia project, because they want to use our data from Computer Science assistant professors who are very experienced with metadata languages]

I can imagine that Jeba by the end of the project will be able to take over maintainer responsibilities for this package or other packages, but right now, I do not know how to involve him in the development work, I would require your guidance in this regard.

On rOpenSci, we had one person who showed interest in contributing, Dr Anna Krystally&lt;https://annakrystalli.me/&gt;, who is a research data engineer, and an editor at rOpenSci, and a contributor to the rdflib package and an author to a somewhat similar but far less functional dataspice package (which creates datasets that are not complying with SDMX but simpler schema.org&lt;http://schema.org&gt; standards.) I think somebody like her on a few months on the project could really make a difference, and could also connect and disseminate our packages well in the far wider rOpenSci universe, giving a boost generally to all rOpenGov packages.

Re: developing rSPARQL-Anything
To me, this would be a favor to the Polifonia project so that they keep supporting our project, as they have done so in the last two month, with hands on metadata knowledge to actually get towards receiving granular music data, which is a number one priority of our project. The reason why I suggested that Pyry/Jeba start with this  is that there is a template how to do it, it does not require any know-how of music, advanced metadata, https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/helloJavaWorld/vignettes/helloJavaWorld.pdf

My hands are full now, because my main task is the 5.1 which is only in smaller part an R programming task, and the Tx.2 tasks, which will require a production-ready ecosystem from us. I think that I can bring the dataset to a 0.3.0 version even without UTU assistance but I also have to make sure that the T2.2, T2.3, T1.2 tasks are not delayed, and my big deliverable, D5.1 comes up in May.

Best regards,
Daniel

Aihe: Re: Polifonia - OME cooperation

 Hi Leo,
We have a deliverable coming up in January, and subsequent deliverables up till May (first data collection tasks, then the observatory task), my suggestion of task division would be this.

-          We have a first draft of requirements of the software ecosystem by the end of November, using some sort of simple requirements matching with our non-programming WPs; we will first rely on the UX requirements template from James, and pick a suitable template that our internal consortium stakeholders can work with.  Please take a look at the template we work with Polifonia and WP2 about ontology development: https://docs.google.com/document/d/185IeCTRnjVv4lY3kYJQKJ1kD93V3ubfFwtNH3wWv_ak/edit?usp=sharing  I think that something similar to this could work.

-          Our working plan schedules scaled data collection for January-March 2023 already; the OMO deliverable is due in May 2023. The OMO will be empty if we did not create a larger set of useful and releasable datasets.

- A new landing page: first I think we should have a mission statement on how we connect these packages before making the page public, and then add a bit of feedback from our internal consortium users, and other R developers.

-          We have some progress made on the following elements of the software ecosystems basic R infrastructure:

o   A new release (only repackaging) rSPARQL-Anything sent to CRAN by end of November, and start the back and forth review process; if you agree with it, you can get started immediately as this may be a very small task.

o   A new major release of [dataset] by the end of December, please see the longer formal description I sent yesterday; hopefully this can be rolled out to [eurostat] as well maybe already in January and in that case we can claim new results, functionality and extension of of our work

o   A new vignette or working paper on adopting our new functionalities to the Eurostat package; same description;

o   A working paper or article that defines the requirements of the retroharmonize package; we already have this ready and unchanged since last year. https://github.com/dataobservatory-eu/retroharmonize-publication&lt;https://github.com/dataobservatory-eu/retroharmonize-publication&gt;; and a minor release of documentation improvements, small bug fixes after testing it with real data (James should provide us access to data from EU-SILC/AES or other surveys that the package had not been tested with.)
Regarding the division of tasks between UTU and Reprex, I’d like to suggest that we reflect the division of tasks in the Grant Agreement, so WP4 under your supervision is more focused on data programming in R; and WP5 under my supervision is more focused on metadata and knowledge.
This means that Reprex will hire somebody who cannot write code in R, but works well with metadata languages, particularly OWL, RFD and one/two serialisation formats of RDF.  I will gladly supervise and give guidance, and write some code in my own packages, but I’d like to keep it to high-level work; however, I also encourage Jeba to get a bit involved in this front, as the planned use of [dataset] is really using more and better metadata to make R data packages work better.
There is this old library catalogue package that is not released --- I would like to take a look at least, even if we do not plan to do anything with it now.   The work that Reprex is planning to do with metadata, and partly what we hope to do with [dataset] intersects with library catalogues a bit, because we want to make sure that libraries, statistical services and data providers are correctly cataloging a dataset in their possession. That is generally the same process as cataloguing, but of course, cataloguing a book or a music sheet publication is still working with a different object and different working traditions, data notation traditions, etc.
Beware that the [dataset] package is on CRAN, but it is merely a concept with a lot of text. I assume that it has to be reprogrammed, which is not  a big deal as there is not much to program.  The document I shared yesterday is aimed towards  this.  The reason why I think Pyry should be engaged at this point because it would be a first step to harmonise the  [dataset] package and the new [eurostat] package. See how I suggest to go about this, but I think it is really feasible as the dataset package essentially works with the attributes of the tibble or data.table that holds the data from Eurostat, and switching to a dataset-extended attribute set should not, must not alter the way eurostat functions work other than retrieving and keeping more metadata in the attributes fields. https://music.dataobservatory.eu/documents/open_music_europe/dataset-development/dataset-development.html
For the survey harmonisation, I think that it is a bit distinct from the other data collection tasks and it should be more aligned with the work of James. I can imagine that the person who is supporting the modernisation of the retroharmonize package and the survey harmonisation workflow is a completely different person as this work is rather different from the dataset/statcodelists/eurostat/iotables/regions group of R packages that deal with statistically processed data.  The retroharmonize package and also spotifyr work with microdata; but right now, I think we should only test what retroharmonize already can do and how it could be improved.
Best regards,
Daniel

Hi Leo,

Sorry for the late reply.  I have a very important conference on 6-7 November, and it is still unclear to me if on the 6th November I am available. If you allow a bit of uncertainty that I have to cancel then the 6 November 3 PM  / 4 PM can work, I'll do my best to keep that time slot free (95% that no change will occur).  I created a shorter document on how I see the future of our package ecosystem, which is not the same as the software ecosystem as we also promised user-facing Shiny Apps.

I am almost finished with a more conceptual working paper for the dataset package itself, but I think to start off this document that I am sending is sufficient, and hopefully not too technical for James.

My suggested priorities are these: start working on some metadata packages so that we can start getting new data; in the meantime, do literature and conceptual review for survey harmonisation, then implement changes in packages like retroharmonize.  The metadata work has a big advantage, the way I imagine and explain in this paper, it works on the attributes level of R objects, i.e. it is not intrusive, and does not change the way the existing package functions return the R objects themselves.  This means that we can roll out the new functionality with low risk and relatively soon on all our existing packages.

I tried to write this primer to be more or less useful for James, too, for reconciliation with WP3, the next paper will be very much data/computer science centric.

Best regards,
Daniel

Aihe: Polifonia - OME cooperation

Dear Leo, Jeba and James,

I spent three working days with another EU music project, Polifonia, that is metadata-only and computer science centered to find out synergies and ways to handle large scales of microdata for our project. I wanted to do this to avoid parallel efforts, and to find synergies; mainly towards the use of knowledge graphs and RDF, which are heavily used, for example, by Spotify, and could greatly increase our metadata handling efficiency and use.

I will write detailed suggestions of works, priorities, even with code examples next week, because I got a lot of useful advice on the [dataset] package and how it could improve the efficiency of maintaining [eurostat], [iotables], [regions] or add new functionality to [spotifyr]

If possible, first I would like to get a quick assessment from Leo about one small thing. Polifonia has a wonderful and well supported RDF tool, SPARQL-Anything&lt;https://sparql-anything.cc/&gt;. I am wondering if we could deploy this as a joint rOpenGov/Polifonia package with a quick and short effort?

This is a java application, which works with many non-RDF resources and pre-processes it much simpler than rdflib to RDF or a knowledge graph.  It could be used both for import and export or exchange our data.

https://github.com/SPARQL-Anything/sparql.anything

It could be deployed in two ways:
- Calling Java from R directly&lt;https://jozef.io/r901-primer-java-from-r-1/#calling-java-from-r-directly&gt;, we get access to the source code, and basically we have to call on only one Java object;
-  Or via packaging the latest release in .jar file and rJava&lt;https://jozef.io/r902-primer-java-from-r-2/&gt;, using the helloJavaWorld&lt;https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/helloJavaWorld/index.html&gt; template.
- They have a similar Python binding&lt;https://pypi.org/project/pysparql-anything/&gt;, which is basically perhaps 1-2 dozens of source code in Python, as we really need to pass on a resource URL to a java object and retrieve the text file it creates.

This would, in my opinion,
- significantly reduce the programming need to the [dataset] package
- create a quick win for our software ecosystem, and connect to a very well maintained community
- put as in the same language with a large music metadata project and allow accessing complex microdata sources with the same pipeline and code, but into our R ecosystem, too
- add to their projects Impact and our deliverables.

I had only worked with rJava as a user, not a developer, but if anybody in Turku has a bit of familiarity with either Java or rJava, to me this looks like 1-2 days job, not counting of course testing, documenting, releasing.

What I could offer is to create the package documentation website, rich tutorials to access relevant statistical and music sources for us, even the template of a quick publication, and of course, a concept paper on how this could improve our other package's functionality. I could do a fair amount of testing, and ask their team to provide us all files for unit testing used in other language binders, and if needed, to take care of the CRAN process.

Best regards,
Daniel Antal, CFA

Dear James,

Please find my answers. The circle of information as below reflect the research frame of 2019 yet the basic approaches hardly changed during the years in order to ensure comparability.


  *   F2F CAPI
  *   According to the agreement, the basic population investigated as a minimum was the Hungarian population aged 15-69, at the same time, the commitment referred to the ESSNet Culture recommendations and undertook to follow the best practice. ESSNet's recommendation was to examine the 15-75 age group as a minimum, but preferably the age group older than six years.
  *   We therefore supplemented the primary base population with the 10-14 year old age group on the one hand, and the 70+ year old age group on the other hand. The sociodemographic characteristics of the basic population were defined on the basis of the data of the 2011 Census for easier comparability with the previous surveys, and taking into account the data of the later microcensus would have caused a very small, unnoticeable deviation from this. So the sampling frame is the population aged 10+ living in Hungarian households. Since the basic unit of analysis is the individual, we accordingly took a personal sample (as in previous years).
  *   The method used was the disproportionately stratified random sample, in which the 10-14-year-old and 70+-year-old age groups were present in different (lower) proportions than in the basic population.
  *   The settlements were selected randomly. Within the settlement, households were selected by random walking. Within a household, the interviewees were selected according to quota criteria. The 10-17-year-olds came from households where we also asked someone from among the adults. (Sampling aimed at random selection of minors would have increased the costs of the research to an unrealistic extent.) The selection of the minor respondents was made with the consent of the parents. We asked a maximum of one adult and one minor in a household.
  *   The sample consisted of three parts: 1) base sample aged 15-69: N=~1000 people; 2) boosted sample of 10-14 year olds: N=~50 people; 3) boosted sample of 70+ year olds: N=~50 people.
  *   In the sample, marginal quotas are applied taking into account the following aspects: region, type of settlement, gender and age. In determining the quotas, we used the data of the latest Population Census.

I do hope that above information would support your job.

Best regards,

Tamás

I hope that you have been well, and I apologize for the long delay in replying to your indicative cost quote. As always, it took the European Commission a bit of time to evaluate the proposal. Fortunately, however, we were chosen to be invited to the grant agreement process. Currently, we’re reworking the proposal text into an agreement.

So, first off: thank you for your fast response to our initial inquiry, which was very helpful in putting our proposal on a solid enough foundation to be chosen!

Pursuant the grant agreement process, we’d like to ask a question about surveying mode. While the proposal was well-evaluated, the reviewers expressed concern about the fieldwork cost. We recognize that face-to-face surveying remains the “gold standard” for high-quality data; however, quite a bit has been learned during the SERISS (https://seriss.eu/) and CRONOS projects and the COVID-19 pandemic about effective non-f2f sampling and fieldwork, mode effects and how to compensate for them, etc. As you may have read, the European Social Survey has even announced a forthcoming change in data collection mode from face-to-face interviews to online and paper self-completion surveys (https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/singlenew.html?a=/about/news/essnews0130.html).

Given the rapidly progressing state of the art, we wonder what options Kantar Hoffmann might be able to offer with regard to a mixed-mode, or even entirely self-completion-based, survey. A probability rather than quota sample would still be strongly preferred. We are happy to keep conversing by email, or alternatively, to set up a call once Daniel is back from holiday later this month.

Again, many thanks, and best regards,
James

Without any documentation? Does he really know how iotables should work?

I would like to review the documentation of Pyry's work: what requirements was he following, what did he change conceptually, and I want to see if it is helpful for the other R packages and for the ecosystem that we promised to build.  I really do not see how I can contribute to the WP4 if I am completely out of the loop.

The entire concept of the [dataset] package was necessary because Eurostat and the European Open Data Portal harmonised all EU open data services, including Eurostat's data release. So, Eurostat created the StatDCAT-AP mapping, which maps SDMX into DCAT-AP.  DCAT is the global W3C standard, while DCAT-AP is the EU's open data definition, and how it must be applied in Europe. Furthermore, our OMO and generally all data management plans must follow this new standard.  I would really like to see exactly what was Pyry's model to make the changes so that the rest of the packages can be brought in line.

If he did change the eurostat package to work with DCAT-AP/DCAT 2, then great, because we can now read in European standard data source, not only Eurostat, and in this case, we have no need for the dataset package, the rSPARQL-Anything, because Eurostat changed the API metadata to RDF and you claim that he brought the eurostat package in line with the new API.


Best regards,
Daniel

Lähetetty: torstai 9. marraskuuta 2023 18.01.54
Vastaanottaja: Leo Lahti
Kopio: James Rhys Edwards
Aihe: Re: Polifonia - OME cooperation

Hi Leo,

I am answering with James in CC because I think that we will have to revisit these issues next Monday.

Re: connecting the eurostat package works to Open Music Europe I published a first personified requirement to connect the dataset package to eurostat, which could give a head start to connect Pyry's work to this project:
source: https://github.com/dataobservatory-eu/dataset-development/tree/main/stories
html: https://music.dataobservatory.eu/documents/open_music_europe/dataset-development/stories/eurostat-user1.html
 and I uploaded this working/concept paper to Zenodo&lt;https://zenodo.org/records/10091666&gt;.

I think that connecting Eurostat to Open Music Europe is very straightforward, we just have to ensure that with the new package the relevant data can be put into the OMO.  And to start developing the ecosystem, at least the eurostat, iotables and dataset packages should work functionally well together by January. To me this is very feasible if Pyry can assign most of his time on this. The little requirement I wrote is about the latter, but we can define how to contribute with Eurostat data to the project easily.

Re: developing dataset
If you remember, I had posted the first conceptual release on rOpenSci&lt;https://github.com/ropensci/software-review/issues/553&gt; so that we can recruit co-developers, and I released a very preliminary version of the package on CRAN before the kick-off of our project.

About working with Jeba, I am not sure how he can be involved, but we can discuss this with James next week.  I would like to bring this package into production by January, because by May we have to release a huge pile of data, partly from Eurostat, but mainly not from Eurostat.

To me, these are the requirements for a contributor:
- Has experience in writing R code to a level that passes CRAN review -- developing the software
- Has experience in technical R documentation with packagedown, and CRAN standards -- releasoin the work
- Experienced with publishing in the R Journal or similar data science journals and on Rbloggers -- dissemination work
- Experienced with data modeling or knowledge modeling, metadata languages -- conceptual contributions to the package [currently I get this a cross-favors with the Polifonia project, because they want to use our data from Computer Science assistant professors who are very experienced with metadata languages]

I can imagine that Jeba by the end of the project will be able to take over maintainer responsibilities for this package or other packages, but right now, I do not know how to involve him in the development work, I would require your guidance in this regard.

On rOpenSci, we had one person who showed interest in contributing, Dr Anna Krystally&lt;https://annakrystalli.me/&gt;, who is a research data engineer, and an editor at rOpenSci, and a contributor to the rdflib package and an author to a somewhat similar but far less functional dataspice package (which creates datasets that are not complying with SDMX but simpler schema.org&lt;http://schema.org&gt;&lt;http://schema.org&gt;&lt;http://schema.org&gt;&lt;http://schema.org&gt; standards.) I think somebody like her on a few months on the project could really make a difference, and could also connect and disseminate our packages well in the far wider rOpenSci universe, giving a boost generally to all rOpenGov packages.

Re: developing rSPARQL-Anything
To me, this would be a favor to the Polifonia project so that they keep supporting our project, as they have done so in the last two month, with hands on metadata knowledge to actually get towards receiving granular music data, which is a number one priority of our project. The reason why I suggested that Pyry/Jeba start with this  is that there is a template how to do it, it does not require any know-how of music, advanced metadata, https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/helloJavaWorld/vignettes/helloJavaWorld.pdf

My hands are full now, because my main task is the 5.1 which is only in smaller part an R programming task, and the Tx.2 tasks, which will require a production-ready ecosystem from us. I think that I can bring the dataset to a 0.3.0 version even without UTU assistance but I also have to make sure that the T2.2, T2.3, T1.2 tasks are not delayed, and my big deliverable, D5.1 comes up in May.

Best regards,
Daniel

Lähetetty: maanantai 6. marraskuuta 2023 17.37.39
Vastaanottaja: Leo Lahti
Kopio: James Rhys Edwards; Akewak Jeba
Aihe: Re: Polifonia - OME cooperation

 Hi Leo,
We have a deliverable coming up in January, and subsequent deliverables up till May (first data collection tasks, then the observatory task), my suggestion of task division would be this.

-          We have a first draft of requirements of the software ecosystem by the end of November, using some sort of simple requirements matching with our non-programming WPs; we will first rely on the UX requirements template from James, and pick a suitable template that our internal consortium stakeholders can work with.  Please take a look at the template we work with Polifonia and WP2 about ontology development: https://docs.google.com/document/d/185IeCTRnjVv4lY3kYJQKJ1kD93V3ubfFwtNH3wWv_ak/edit?usp=sharing  I think that something similar to this could work.

-          Our working plan schedules scaled data collection for January-March 2023 already; the OMO deliverable is due in May 2023. The OMO will be empty if we did not create a larger set of useful and releasable datasets.

- A new landing page: first I think we should have a mission statement on how we connect these packages before making the page public, and then add a bit of feedback from our internal consortium users, and other R developers.

-          We have some progress made on the following elements of the software ecosystems basic R infrastructure:

o   A new release (only repackaging) rSPARQL-Anything sent to CRAN by end of November, and start the back and forth review process; if you agree with it, you can get started immediately as this may be a very small task.

o   A new major release of [dataset] by the end of December, please see the longer formal description I sent yesterday; hopefully this can be rolled out to [eurostat] as well maybe already in January and in that case we can claim new results, functionality and extension of of our work

o   A new vignette or working paper on adopting our new functionalities to the Eurostat package; same description;

o   A working paper or article that defines the requirements of the retroharmonize package; we already have this ready and unchanged since last year. https://github.com/dataobservatory-eu/retroharmonize-publication&lt;https://github.com/dataobservatory-eu/retroharmonize-publication&gt;; and a minor release of documentation improvements, small bug fixes after testing it with real data (James should provide us access to data from EU-SILC/AES or other surveys that the package had not been tested with.)
Regarding the division of tasks between UTU and Reprex, I’d like to suggest that we reflect the division of tasks in the Grant Agreement, so WP4 under your supervision is more focused on data programming in R; and WP5 under my supervision is more focused on metadata and knowledge.
This means that Reprex will hire somebody who cannot write code in R, but works well with metadata languages, particularly OWL, RFD and one/two serialisation formats of RDF.  I will gladly supervise and give guidance, and write some code in my own packages, but I’d like to keep it to high-level work; however, I also encourage Jeba to get a bit involved in this front, as the planned use of [dataset] is really using more and better metadata to make R data packages work better.
There is this old library catalogue package that is not released --- I would like to take a look at least, even if we do not plan to do anything with it now.   The work that Reprex is planning to do with metadata, and partly what we hope to do with [dataset] intersects with library catalogues a bit, because we want to make sure that libraries, statistical services and data providers are correctly cataloging a dataset in their possession. That is generally the same process as cataloguing, but of course, cataloguing a book or a music sheet publication is still working with a different object and different working traditions, data notation traditions, etc.
Beware that the [dataset] package is on CRAN, but it is merely a concept with a lot of text. I assume that it has to be reprogrammed, which is not  a big deal as there is not much to program.  The document I shared yesterday is aimed towards  this.  The reason why I think Pyry should be engaged at this point because it would be a first step to harmonise the  [dataset] package and the new [eurostat] package. See how I suggest to go about this, but I think it is really feasible as the dataset package essentially works with the attributes of the tibble or data.table that holds the data from Eurostat, and switching to a dataset-extended attribute set should not, must not alter the way eurostat functions work other than retrieving and keeping more metadata in the attributes fields. https://music.dataobservatory.eu/documents/open_music_europe/dataset-development/dataset-development.html
For the survey harmonisation, I think that it is a bit distinct from the other data collection tasks and it should be more aligned with the work of James. I can imagine that the person who is supporting the modernisation of the retroharmonize package and the survey harmonisation workflow is a completely different person as this work is rather different from the dataset/statcodelists/eurostat/iotables/regions group of R packages that deal with statistically processed data.  The retroharmonize package and also spotifyr work with microdata; but right now, I think we should only test what retroharmonize already can do and how it could be improved.
Best regards,
Daniel

Kopio: James Rhys Edwards; Akewak Jeba; Pyry Kantanen
Aihe: Re: Polifonia - OME cooperation

Hi Leo,

Sorry for the late reply.  I have a very important conference on 6-7 November, and it is still unclear to me if on the 6th November I am available. If you allow a bit of uncertainty that I have to cancel then the 6 November 3 PM  / 4 PM can work, I'll do my best to keep that time slot free (95% that no change will occur).  I created a shorter document on how I see the future of our package ecosystem, which is not the same as the software ecosystem as we also promised user-facing Shiny Apps.

I am almost finished with a more conceptual working paper for the dataset package itself, but I think to start off this document that I am sending is sufficient, and hopefully not too technical for James.

My suggested priorities are these: start working on some metadata packages so that we can start getting new data; in the meantime, do literature and conceptual review for survey harmonisation, then implement changes in packages like retroharmonize.  The metadata work has a big advantage, the way I imagine and explain in this paper, it works on the attributes level of R objects, i.e. it is not intrusive, and does not change the way the existing package functions return the R objects themselves.  This means that we can roll out the new functionality with low risk and relatively soon on all our existing packages.

I tried to write this primer to be more or less useful for James, too, for reconciliation with WP3, the next paper will be very much data/computer science centric.

Best regards,
Daniel
