Call for chapters for an edited volume to be submitted to Springer's Music Business Research Series



Music Ecosystems: Challenges and Opportunities



Editors

Guy Morrow (University of Melbourne)

Carsten Winter (Hanover University of Music, Drama Media)



Following the (15th) _International Music Business Research Days_ conference (Music Ecosystems Research: Challenges and Opportunities) produced by the _International Music Business Research Association_ and held from June 5-7, 2024 at the Hanover University of Music, Drama and Media, we invite you to further elucidate the formation and special features of "music ecosystems" by submitting a chapter proposal for this contributed volume.



We are looking for contributions that will help to better understand and explain music contexts as "ecosystems". The term "ecosystem", which has now become a key strategic and political term, was introduced into strategicdiscussions to emphasize the fact that the environment of more and more organizations was becoming more dynamic, complex, interdependent and borderless; that such organizations were beginning to resemble "ecosystems", i.e. biological systems in nature (see for e.g.

in particular Davidson, Harmer &amp; Marshall 2014 and, for the origin and logic of ecological thinking, the literature review by de Bernard, Comunian &amp; Gross 2021). We only understand these newly (more dynamic, complex, interdependent and borderless) social relationships/environments if we take these characteristics and normative implications that go with them into account. Some even think that we cannot/should not do this with classic economic concepts (e.g.

Scharmer &amp; Kaufer 2013), which focus mostly on the economic efficiency of relationships, markets, contracts, advertising, etc. or for example with classic concepts concerning culture for similar reasons.



These new social ecosystem dynamics, with their complexity, interdependence and borderless nature, were developed by everyone who contributed to them, from _Napster_, _MySpace_, _YouTube_ to _TikTok_.

Today, almost everyone who does something with music digitally for themselves and others contributes to production and distribution within these more dynamic, complex, interdependent and borderless music ecosystems. In this contributed volume, the term "ecosystem" also refers to the growing data complexity that has arisen in the wake of the arrival of new actors such as Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and algorithms (Clancy 2023). There is a need for new holistic and normative theories in this context: holistic because concepts that, for example, distinguish a private from a public music sector are becoming problematic due to the growing interdependencies between them; normative because this development shows that legitimizing strategic considerations either with a view to economic or artistic goals alone is becoming problematic. Indeed, they are also expected to be more comprehensively oriented towards global sustainability goals, as the European Union (EU) program _Music Moves Europe_ shows very well. Music can also increasingly rarely be meaningfully attributed to either the private or the public sector, since classical music is becoming more and more commercial and popular music in its variousforms is also publicly funded, or must be, because in some instances fewer and fewer private actors are doing so. It is becoming more complicated and it is therefore important for us to understand what is connected to what or whom and why in the music sector today, and what this means for distinguishable connections at different levels, regionally, nationally, internationally and geostrategically. For example, as part of its _Music Moves Europe _program, the EU wants to find out exactly what a music ecosystem is and what distinguishes the "European music ecosystem" globally from other comparable "music ecosystems" economically, socially, artistically, structurally, etc. It is assumed that such a comparison should best take a conceptual look at all relationships in an ecosystem:

not just media or economic or social or cultural relationships, but all the relationships that make ecosystems more valuable for those involved, that are important for the work of the future, and that make them attractive, competitive, sustainable, resilient, productive, creative or innovative.



This poses a completely new conceptual and normative challenge for research into the music business and music culture. It can no longer only explore contractual relationships, transactions (economics), intrinsic value(art and culture), power (politics), networks or more personal relationships. It is long overdue that the use of the term "music ecosystem" becomes more scientific, empirical, conceptual and analytical. This includes examining how different ways of using the term differ; since it has become a key term or metaphor, the term ecosystem has also been used to articulate interests or to develop and legitimize new commercial and private business models. Recently, two new ways of using the term have become more common in music discourse, which have little to do with the previously established uses, which indicates increasing dynamism, complexity, interdependence and the borderless nature of music sectors. For example, it is now becoming more common for representatives of the established music industries to understand their industrial structures in the sector as forming part of an "ecosystem".

This use has precursors in the Chicago School of Sociology and makes it possible for the status quo to promote the preservation of their structures in the same way that the preservation of otherwise extinct animals or plants is promoted (e.g. Federal Association of the Music Industry).



In addition to this (conservative) use, we are increasingly encountering a private-commercial technical use of the concept "ecosystem". When it comes to big tech and big content companies, ecosystems are closed, data-based, independent and autonomous private contexts that operate as private markets in which customers belong to those who own the ecosystem infrastructure and that orchestrate the actors and relationships (see, for example, the McKinsey strategists and authors Atluri &amp; Dietz 2023 and, with a stronger focus on the data, see in particular Subramaniam 2022. Also see Giblin and Doctorow, 2022).



Research into newer and more complex music ecosystems is possible from many disciplinary and interdisciplinary perspectives with a view to a wide variety of objects and processes: What do these developments mean for old and new actors, for old structures and institutions? What new structures and institutions are emerging or being developed? What new relevant contexts and processes are there in music ecosystems? How do they form and reform, with new ones emerging in different contexts? Who will be the new and important players in the music ecosystems of the future and why? Who is changing how and why they operate, with what arguments? Do the dynamics, complexity, interdependence and borderlessness need to be regulated? What role does politics and political goals such as those of the EU play in the context of, for example, the _Music Moves Europe_ program? What distinguishes music ecosystems globally, nationally or as music city ecosystems?



This call is aimed at researchers from all disciplines, as well as players from music culture and the music industries.



- Deadline for submission of abstracts (300-400 words) and bionotes (100

words): 15 October 2024

- Notification of acceptance: 20 October 2024

- Book proposal submission: 30 October 2024

- Book contracted: November 2024

- First book chapter draft: 30 April 2025

- Feedback to the authors: 30 May 2025

- Book manuscript submission: September 2025



Initial expressions of interest, enquiries and/or abstracts should be submitted to editors: Guy Morrow (guy.morrow@unimelb.edu.au&lt;mailto:guy.morrow@unimelb.edu.au&gt;) and Carsten Winter (carsten.winter@hmtm-hannover.de&lt;mailto:carsten.winter@hmtm-hannover.de&gt;)



References

De Bernard, M., Cominian, R., &amp; Gross, J. (2021). Cultural and creative

ecosystems: a review of theories and methods, towards a new research agenda. _Cultural Trends_. Routledge

(http://doi.org/10.1080/095486963.2021.2004073)



Clancy, M. (Ed.) (2023). _Artificial Intelligence and Music Ecosystem_.

Routledge.

Giblin, R., &amp; Doctorow, C. (2022). _Chokepoint capitalism: How big tech and_



_big content captured creative labor markets and how we'll win them back_.



Scribe Publications.

From: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
Sent: 11 October 2024 13:45
To: James Rhys Edwards &lt;JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&gt;
Subject: Wikipedian in Residence

Hi James,

So I was thinking the following.

1. Hudobné centrum and Matej are absolutely crucial to make WP2 and WP5 succeed, as nobody else gives and disseminates high quality data.  So I think it is an absolute necessity that they are in the consortium and comfortable. If this makes Igor comfortable, we should swallow this 10-12.000 euros, because all our plans fall through.

2. I would be willing to swallow most or almost all of the cost, perhaps I will ask Tomas to pitch in, but we will resolve this.

3. So the question is how.

We have a Hungarian subcontracting budget, and I think that we will not spend it the way I thought.  The cooperation with all Hungarian partners is extremely fraught by censorship and self-censorship. So while we have 12,500 euros (if I remember correctly, plus indirect costs?) as a service line, to make sure that we have something, I am making no less than four replications.  This will anyway never pay off from 12500 and I do not know which will succeed.

So what I would like to do is to place Matej on this as a Wikipedian without reference to Slovakia. He is well-liked and respected in the international Wikipedia as a chairperson of a national chapter, so he can make some contribution to any Hungarian or Latvian or Romanian replication case that we are pursuing.

The other thing that I can do is to place him on payroll, to contribute to the Reprex PMs, and then take something out to the service cost line.

What I want to say that how this Slovak dissemination and its Hungarian? Latvian? Ukrainian? Romanian? replication will work is not something that I can plan.  I already spend more on it than could be justified from my overheads, because it must happen.   Matej is a reliable person, and to pay out 12,000 for a year of help is something that we should do.

Another useful route could be if Rosina is still in the consortium that we switch back to a minimal Bulgarian replication.  We have spoken with the Bulgarian Wikipedia, they would be willing to do something small. In this case, Rosina could pitch in with 1-2 months of pay for Matej.

I generally do not feel good about taking on individually all the extra cost, because this is saving at least two entire work packages, and we are talking about a very small sum.  But also a partner pitching in 2000 euros is not a material issue. What I would need more is this:

- maximum flexibility how we will replicate, because we are in the hands of external partners,
- keep Matej because his loyalty and commitment is key to success.

To make Rosina or SOZA pay 2000 would be a way of acknowledging their ownership of the problem, but if that happens in a different way, that is also good. It is not about the money, but it is rather difficult that Reprex has to support Hudobné centrum and to care for all the replication partners -- something that is due to Musicautor's default on this WP.

All in all, I would be willing to take on this extra cost, if we find a way how to do it within or exiting (promised) new budget with the HU service line replication cost and our PMs, in a way that is the easiest to explain for you as a Coordinator to the EU. Reprex will not ask for any extra money, but to acknowledge the ownership of being in this together, a small token commitment in money or other consideration from Musicautor or SOZA would be appreciated.

Daniel

From: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
Sent: 15 October 2024 11:40

Subject: Hudobne centrum + ALOADED + OpenMuse

Dear Igor, James, Tomas,

We had talked through with James, Tomas, and the ALOADED team to address your concerns about joining our consortium and participating in fully the scientific, data, and music visibility work.

Today we had a meeting with the Lavtian Folk Archive and ALOADED, so that we are addressing contractually the same issues that Hudobné centrum has in terms of music metadata and music distribution. @Tomas Miks&lt;mailto:tomas.miks@soza.sk&gt; suggested that their lawyers pitch in to assist all of us.

- We want to make it clear that it is impossible that the 25,000 euro fake streaming clause can apply to Hudobné centrum.
- With both the Hudobné centrum and LFA, we are anyways happy to create a contract that avoids royalty payments altogether, with spending all of your royalty share in a documented, high-quality and transparent marketing of Slovak-Latvian music.
- If you do not earn royalties, any royalty cheating clause will not apply to you. But even if you do, we can put many safeguards that this will not apply, and your contract can be terminated even before this issue would be raised, which we also find a practically impossible scenario from a fake streaming point of view.

What I would like to suggest is that @Love Ojensa&lt;mailto:love@aloaded.com&gt; shares with us with the new ALOADED standard terms, and @Tomas Miks&lt;mailto:tomas.miks@soza.sk&gt; 's colleagues and make take it from there to make sure that you feel safe to sign the contract.

Regarding the Wikipedia issue, I will write a separate email. With @Stefan Kragh&lt;mailto:stefan@aloaded.com&gt; we wil meet again on Friday to work out some data issues.

Best regards,
Daniel

From: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
Sent: 16 October 2024 12:21

Subject: Re: Wikipedian in Residence

Hi James,

I think that we should talk, I have availability both tomorrow or on Friday.  Tomorrow would be better because we have a long chat with Stef from Aloaded and I could already utilise our agreement.

Working with these replications on a shoestring budget is hell difficult.  I do not know if we will ever have a contract with A38 or somebody else, we could not even conclude the Hudobné centrum contract over almost a year.   This means that my work is quadruple while all that I can offer is this 12k that was promised to A38 but is not contracted yet.

A38 immediately sent us some very low quality data, but they lost interest because this sum is a drop in the ocean of their budget, even in their IT department budget. So I had been pursuing parallel the following leads:

- trying to work with A38
- trying to replace them with the Bartok Archive of Hungary
- trying to work with a Romanian library
- trying to replace them with the Hungarian Folk Archive -- they would have been a stronger partner than all, but political roadblocks prevented me.
- trying to work with the University of Tartu reserachers (Estonian and Finnougrin folk archives.)
- trying to work with ZAIKS-Music Export Poland
- trying a replication with Alona in Ukraine
- trying to replace them with the Latvian Folk Archive -- this seems to be now the most promising.

We also agreed to work with the British Library (aggregator for Europeana Sound) and they are super helpful, but all these efforts failed to get even to producing a small dataset that could be placed on Europeana as a demo.

Unless there is any further funds available, I have the money promised to A38 that I could give to Matej.  Matej is instrumental at least to the Slovak work, and has very good contacts with the Bulgarian, Latvian and some other Wikipedias, who may help me in these regards.  But this is only filling one hole that we do not lose Slovakia as the primary country, at this point I do not see how we will do a replication. I am chasing a lot of leads, and accumulating a large number unaccounted for management hours.

I want to present at IAMIC a SLovak and partially replicated Hungarian, Latvian, Bulgarian, Polish or whatever solution, because I cannot keep spending on this task a lot next year.  I had a replication budget of 12k, but it seems that this 12k is needed to save the initial output in Slovakia.

Best regards,
Daniel

So I think it is an absolute necessity that they are in the consortium and comfortable. If this makes Igor comfortable, we should swallow this 10-12.000 euros, because all our plans fall through.

2. I would be willing to swallow most or almost all of the cost, perhaps I will ask Tomas to pitch in, but we will resolve this.

3. So the question is how.

We have a Hungarian subcontracting budget, and I think that we will not spend it the way I thought.  The cooperation with all Hungarian partners is extremely fraught by censorship and self-censorship. So while we have 12,500 euros (if I remember correctly, plus indirect costs?) as a service line, to make sure that we have something, I am making no less than four replications.  This will anyway never pay off from 12500 and I do not know which will succeed.

So what I would like to do is to place Matej on this as a Wikipedian without reference to Slovakia. He is well-liked and respected in the international Wikipedia as a chairperson of a national chapter, so he can make some contribution to any Hungarian or Latvian or Romanian replication case that we are pursuing.

The other thing that I can do is to place him on payroll, to contribute to the Reprex PMs, and then take something out to the service cost line.

What I want to say that how this Slovak dissemination and its Hungarian? Latvian? Ukrainian? Romanian? replication will work is not something that I can plan.  I already spend more on it than could be justified from my overheads, because it must happen.   Matej is a reliable person, and to pay out 12,000 for a year of help is something that we should do.

Another useful route could be if Rosina is still in the consortium that we switch back to a minimal Bulgarian replication.  We have spoken with the Bulgarian Wikipedia, they would be willing to do something small. In this case, Rosina could pitch in with 1-2 months of pay for Matej.

I generally do not feel good about taking on individually all the extra cost, because this is saving at least two entire work packages, and we are talking about a very small sum.  But also a partner pitching in 2000 euros is not a material issue. What I would need more is this:

- maximum flexibility how we will replicate, because we are in the hands of external partners,
- keep Matej because his loyalty and commitment is key to success.

To make Rosina or SOZA pay 2000 would be a way of acknowledging their ownership of the problem, but if that happens in a different way, that is also good. It is not about the money, but it is rather difficult that Reprex has to support Hudobné centrum and to care for all the replication partners -- something that is due to Musicautor's default on this WP.

All in all, I would be willing to take on this extra cost, if we find a way how to do it within or exiting (promised) new budget with the HU service line replication cost and our PMs, in a way that is the easiest to explain for you as a Coordinator to the EU. Reprex will not ask for any extra money, but to acknowledge the ownership of being in this together, a small token commitment in money or other consideration from Musicautor or SOZA would be appreciated.

Call for chapters for an edited volume to be submitted to Springer’s Music Business Research Series



Music Ecosystems: Challenges and Opportunities



Editors

Guy Morrow (University of Melbourne)

Carsten Winter (Hanover University of Music, Drama Media)



Following the (15th) _International Music Business Research Days_ conference (Music Ecosystems Research: Challenges and Opportunities) produced by the _International Music Business Research Association_ and held from June 5-7, 2024 at the Hanover University of Music, Drama and Media, we invite you to further elucidate the formation and special features of "music ecosystems" by submitting a chapter proposal for this contributed volume.



We are looking for contributions that will help to better understand and explain music contexts as "ecosystems". The term "ecosystem", which has now become a key strategic and political term, was introduced into strategicdiscussions to emphasize the fact that the environment of more and more organizations was becoming more dynamic, complex, interdependent and borderless; that such organizations were beginning to resemble "ecosystems", i.e. biological systems in nature (see for e.g.

in particular Davidson, Harmer &amp; Marshall 2014 and, for the origin and logic of ecological thinking, the literature review by de Bernard, Comunian &amp; Gross 2021). We only understand these newly (more dynamic, complex, interdependent and borderless) social relationships/environments if we take these characteristics and normative implications that go with them into account. Some even think that we cannot/should not do this with classic economic concepts (e.g.

Scharmer &amp; Kaufer 2013), which focus mostly on the economic efficiency of relationships, markets, contracts, advertising, etc. or for example with classic concepts concerning culture for similar reasons.



These new social ecosystem dynamics, with their complexity, interdependence and borderless nature, were developed by everyone who contributed to them, from _Napster_, _MySpace_, _YouTube_ to _TikTok_.

Today, almost everyone who does something with music digitally for themselves and others contributes to production and distribution within these more dynamic, complex, interdependent and borderless music ecosystems. In this contributed volume, the term "ecosystem" also refers to the growing data complexity that has arisen in the wake of the arrival of new actors such as Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and algorithms (Clancy 2023). There is a need for new holistic and normative theories in this context: holistic because concepts that, for example, distinguish a private from a public music sector are becoming problematic due to the growing interdependencies between them; normative because this development shows that legitimizing strategic considerations either with a view to economic or artistic goals alone is becoming problematic. Indeed, they are also expected to be more comprehensively oriented towards global sustainability goals, as the European Union (EU) program _Music Moves Europe_ shows very well. Music can also increasingly rarely be meaningfully attributed to either the private or the public sector, since classical music is becoming more and more commercial and popular music in its variousforms is also publicly funded, or must be, because in some instances fewer and fewer private actors are doing so. It is becoming more complicated and it is therefore important for us to understand what is connected to what or whom and why in the music sector today, and what this means for distinguishable connections at different levels, regionally, nationally, internationally and geostrategically. For example, as part of its _Music Moves Europe _program, the EU wants to find out exactly what a music ecosystem is and what distinguishes the “European music ecosystem” globally from other comparable “music ecosystems” economically, socially, artistically, structurally, etc. It is assumed that such a comparison should best take a conceptual look at all relationships in an ecosystem:

not just media or economic or social or cultural relationships, but all the relationships that make ecosystems more valuable for those involved, that are important for the work of the future, and that make them attractive, competitive, sustainable, resilient, productive, creative or innovative.



This poses a completely new conceptual and normative challenge for research into the music business and music culture. It can no longer only explore contractual relationships, transactions (economics), intrinsic value(art and culture), power (politics), networks or more personal relationships. It is long overdue that the use of the term "music ecosystem" becomes more scientific, empirical, conceptual and analytical. This includes examining how different ways of using the term differ; since it has become a key term or metaphor, the term ecosystem has also been used to articulate interests or to develop and legitimize new commercial and private business models. Recently, two new ways of using the term have become more common in music discourse, which have little to do with the previously established uses, which indicates increasing dynamism, complexity, interdependence and the borderless nature of music sectors. For example, it is now becoming more common for representatives of the established music industries to understand their industrial structures in the sector as forming part of an "ecosystem".

This use has precursors in the Chicago School of Sociology and makes it possible for the status quo to promote the preservation of their structures in the same way that the preservation of otherwise extinct animals or plants is promoted (e.g. Federal Association of the Music Industry).



In addition to this (conservative) use, we are increasingly encountering a private-commercial technical use of the concept "ecosystem". When it comes to big tech and big content companies, ecosystems are closed, data-based, independent and autonomous private contexts that operate as private markets in which customers belong to those who own the ecosystem infrastructure and that orchestrate the actors and relationships (see, for example, the McKinsey strategists and authors Atluri &amp; Dietz 2023 and, with a stronger focus on the data, see in particular Subramaniam 2022. Also see Giblin and Doctorow, 2022).



Research into newer and more complex music ecosystems is possible from many disciplinary and interdisciplinary perspectives with a view to a wide variety of objects and processes: What do these developments mean for old and new actors, for old structures and institutions? What new structures and institutions are emerging or being developed? What new relevant contexts and processes are there in music ecosystems? How do they form and reform, with new ones emerging in different contexts? Who will be the new and important players in the music ecosystems of the future and why? Who is changing how and why they operate, with what arguments? Do the dynamics, complexity, interdependence and borderlessness need to be regulated? What role does politics and political goals such as those of the EU play in the context of, for example, the _Music Moves Europe_ program? What distinguishes music ecosystems globally, nationally or as music city ecosystems?



This call is aimed at researchers from all disciplines, as well as players from music culture and the music industries.



- Deadline for submission of abstracts (300-400 words) and bionotes (100

words): 15 October 2024

- Notification of acceptance: 20 October 2024

- Book proposal submission: 30 October 2024

- Book contracted: November 2024

- First book chapter draft: 30 April 2025

- Feedback to the authors: 30 May 2025

- Book manuscript submission: September 2025



Initial expressions of interest, enquiries and/or abstracts should be submitted to editors: Guy Morrow (guy.morrow@unimelb.edu.au&lt;mailto:guy.morrow@unimelb.edu.au&gt;) and Carsten Winter (carsten.winter@hmtm-hannover.de&lt;mailto:carsten.winter@hmtm-hannover.de&gt;)

(http://doi.org/10.1080/095486963.2021.2004073)

Call for chapters for an edited volume to be submitted to Springer’s Music Business Research Series



Music Ecosystems: Challenges and Opportunities



Editors

Guy Morrow (University of Melbourne)

Carsten Winter (Hanover University of Music, Drama Media)



Following the (15th) _International Music Business Research Days_ conference (Music Ecosystems Research: Challenges and Opportunities) produced by the _International Music Business Research Association_ and held from June 5-7, 2024 at the Hanover University of Music, Drama and Media, we invite you to further elucidate the formation and special features of "music ecosystems" by submitting a chapter proposal for this contributed volume.



We are looking for contributions that will help to better understand and explain music contexts as "ecosystems". The term "ecosystem", which has now become a key strategic and political term, was introduced into strategicdiscussions to emphasize the fact that the environment of more and more organizations was becoming more dynamic, complex, interdependent and borderless; that such organizations were beginning to resemble "ecosystems", i.e. biological systems in nature (see for e.g.

in particular Davidson, Harmer &amp; Marshall 2014 and, for the origin and logic of ecological thinking, the literature review by de Bernard, Comunian &amp; Gross 2021). We only understand these newly (more dynamic, complex, interdependent and borderless) social relationships/environments if we take these characteristics and normative implications that go with them into account. Some even think that we cannot/should not do this with classic economic concepts (e.g.

Scharmer &amp; Kaufer 2013), which focus mostly on the economic efficiency of relationships, markets, contracts, advertising, etc. or for example with classic concepts concerning culture for similar reasons.



These new social ecosystem dynamics, with their complexity, interdependence and borderless nature, were developed by everyone who contributed to them, from _Napster_, _MySpace_, _YouTube_ to _TikTok_.

Today, almost everyone who does something with music digitally for themselves and others contributes to production and distribution within these more dynamic, complex, interdependent and borderless music ecosystems. In this contributed volume, the term "ecosystem" also refers to the growing data complexity that has arisen in the wake of the arrival of new actors such as Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and algorithms (Clancy 2023). There is a need for new holistic and normative theories in this context: holistic because concepts that, for example, distinguish a private from a public music sector are becoming problematic due to the growing interdependencies between them; normative because this development shows that legitimizing strategic considerations either with a view to economic or artistic goals alone is becoming problematic. Indeed, they are also expected to be more comprehensively oriented towards global sustainability goals, as the European Union (EU) program _Music Moves Europe_ shows very well. Music can also increasingly rarely be meaningfully attributed to either the private or the public sector, since classical music is becoming more and more commercial and popular music in its variousforms is also publicly funded, or must be, because in some instances fewer and fewer private actors are doing so. It is becoming more complicated and it is therefore important for us to understand what is connected to what or whom and why in the music sector today, and what this means for distinguishable connections at different levels, regionally, nationally, internationally and geostrategically. For example, as part of its _Music Moves Europe _program, the EU wants to find out exactly what a music ecosystem is and what distinguishes the “European music ecosystem” globally from other comparable “music ecosystems” economically, socially, artistically, structurally, etc. It is assumed that such a comparison should best take a conceptual look at all relationships in an ecosystem:

not just media or economic or social or cultural relationships, but all the relationships that make ecosystems more valuable for those involved, that are important for the work of the future, and that make them attractive, competitive, sustainable, resilient, productive, creative or innovative.



This poses a completely new conceptual and normative challenge for research into the music business and music culture. It can no longer only explore contractual relationships, transactions (economics), intrinsic value(art and culture), power (politics), networks or more personal relationships. It is long overdue that the use of the term "music ecosystem" becomes more scientific, empirical, conceptual and analytical. This includes examining how different ways of using the term differ; since it has become a key term or metaphor, the term ecosystem has also been used to articulate interests or to develop and legitimize new commercial and private business models. Recently, two new ways of using the term have become more common in music discourse, which have little to do with the previously established uses, which indicates increasing dynamism, complexity, interdependence and the borderless nature of music sectors. For example, it is now becoming more common for representatives of the established music industries to understand their industrial structures in the sector as forming part of an "ecosystem".

This use has precursors in the Chicago School of Sociology and makes it possible for the status quo to promote the preservation of their structures in the same way that the preservation of otherwise extinct animals or plants is promoted (e.g. Federal Association of the Music Industry).



In addition to this (conservative) use, we are increasingly encountering a private-commercial technical use of the concept "ecosystem". When it comes to big tech and big content companies, ecosystems are closed, data-based, independent and autonomous private contexts that operate as private markets in which customers belong to those who own the ecosystem infrastructure and that orchestrate the actors and relationships (see, for example, the McKinsey strategists and authors Atluri &amp; Dietz 2023 and, with a stronger focus on the data, see in particular Subramaniam 2022. Also see Giblin and Doctorow, 2022).



Research into newer and more complex music ecosystems is possible from many disciplinary and interdisciplinary perspectives with a view to a wide variety of objects and processes: What do these developments mean for old and new actors, for old structures and institutions? What new structures and institutions are emerging or being developed? What new relevant contexts and processes are there in music ecosystems? How do they form and reform, with new ones emerging in different contexts? Who will be the new and important players in the music ecosystems of the future and why? Who is changing how and why they operate, with what arguments? Do the dynamics, complexity, interdependence and borderlessness need to be regulated? What role does politics and political goals such as those of the EU play in the context of, for example, the _Music Moves Europe_ program? What distinguishes music ecosystems globally, nationally or as music city ecosystems?



This call is aimed at researchers from all disciplines, as well as players from music culture and the music industries.



- Deadline for submission of abstracts (300-400 words) and bionotes (100

words): 15 October 2024

- Notification of acceptance: 20 October 2024

- Book proposal submission: 30 October 2024

- Book contracted: November 2024

- First book chapter draft: 30 April 2025

- Feedback to the authors: 30 May 2025

- Book manuscript submission: September 2025

Hi all,

I am continuing work on the "indicator" deliverable and believe that a visualisation of the "whole musical economy" would be helpful for our readers. Also for any visualisations eventually hosted on our websites.

As described in D1.1, the musical economy comprises a mix of activities measured in ESS (e.g., via NACE and ISCO code categories) and unmeasured in ESS.

The "whole musical economy" could be defined as A+B+C+D, where:

A. Measured fully-musical activities
B. Musical activities within mixed code categories defined as "cultural" by ESS
C. Musical activities within mixed code categories defined as "partly-cultural" or "non-cultural" by ESS
D. Unmeasured musical activities

Examples:

A = luthiers (NACE code 32.2 “Manufacture of musical instruments”)
B = musicians employed in orchestras (incl. in NACE 90.01 “Performing arts”)
C = musicologists employed at universities (incl. in NACE 85.42 “Tertiary education”)
D = musicians whose work is informal / unreported

Here's the ghetto graphic I came up with. I will ask our graphics person to have a look on Monday, but if you could take a quick peek and let me know if I am missing anything, I'd appreciate it!

Thank you and best regards,
James

Dear Daniel,

Thank you for your comprehensive response, I greatly appreciate it. I agree and will rethink this based on ISCO/ESCO.

Connecting to ESCO would be especially valuable as the ESCO team has mapped "occupations" to "skills"&lt;https://esco.ec.europa.eu/en/about-esco/data-science-and-esco/esco-skill-occupation-matrix-tables-linking-occupation-and-skill-groups&gt;, and plans to the same with "transversal skills and competences", "knowledge", and "qualifications" — triangulating between these classifications would allow a much more precise identification of who/what is and isn't part of the "musical economy".

I think it would also be more respondent-friendly in surveying. For instance, instead of asking "what is your occupation", we could ask "which of these activities do you do for income?", and then use the Skill-Occupation Matrix Tables to calculate the probability of the respondent being in certain occupations. This could partially solve the challenge of patchwork careers in the industry. Just a rough example.

From: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
Sent: 18 October 2024 13:54

Cc: Joost Poort &lt;j.p.poort@uva.nl&gt;; Arianna Martinelli &lt;Arianna.Martinelli@santannapisa.it&gt;; Leo Lahti &lt;leo.lahti@utu.fi&gt;; Isabella Tautscher &lt;Isabella.Tautscher@sinus-institut.de&gt;; Marc Calmbach &lt;Marc.Calmbach@sinus-institut.de&gt;
Subject: Re: OpenMusE -- visualising the "whole musical economy"

Dear James,

I participated in a panel discussion about this topic in Brussels a year ago, and we had follow up calls with the experts of the Commission.  I think that your approach points in the right direction, but needs to be refined. (A lot of this work was actually carried out with Artisjus and SOZA earlier.)

The NACE "economic activity" codes and their national variations (only the first 4 digits are set on the UN/EU level, the 5th digit is a national competence) refers to enterprises, not public institutions and informal economy enterprises.  So this is not what you need. The NACE classification is not very relevant for us. The reason why we suggested to the local partners, including the statistical authority (which was very much welcome by our policy officer) to create a so-called satellite business register is exactly because we know, they know, everybody knows that the NACE-based official business register is not fulfilling the purpose. SOZA knows who receives music royalties and that does not cover the enterprises who registered as their main economic activity music publishing. However, we know where the royalties go.

Unfortunately because the NACE activity classification does not know the term "music", this approach will not work without examining the economic or scientific output of the workers of the organisation. A "publisher" will be a music publisher if it is publishing music sheets or musical works.  A university will have musicological output if it has researchers who publish or teach in accepted journals or accredited courses of musicology.

Another  drawback of NACE is that it only applies to enterprises, while many of the activities you mention take place outside of enterprises.

What you need is the ISCO/ESCO/ national classification of the occupations. You mention "luthiers", "musicians", "musicologists", but these are not economic activities but occupations of people.  The European Commision and our policy officer would very much welcome it if we would provide a correct classification of economic occupations, and they even developed an ESCO ontology that could be connected to our DMO ontology.

To give an example of the "musicologist", that person is likely to be in a job of a "scientific researcher"  at a university, and probably a "librarian"  at a music library, and an "archivist" in a music archive, and a "music editor"  in a label, and a "music journalist" in a magazine.  To find public institutions that employ a "musicologist", only the occupation helps (which is a bit broader term than the job description.) For example, you can state that a university has a musicologist on the payroll if they have "scientific researchers" who have in their bibliography papers that were published in journals that meet the scientific literature classification criteria for "musicology" or "ethnomusicology", etc. Or they have an accredited course, for example, a BA in musicology or MA in musicology or a PhD in musicology.

In Slovakia, we are working on a bottom-up approach that allows the identification of music releated activities regardless of the NACE code of enterprises (because there are no music NACE codes anyway), and also including informal enterprises and public institutions that do not have a NACE code by definition.

Best regards,
Daniel

Dear Igor, James, Tomas,

We had talked through with James, Tomas, and the ALOADED team to address your concerns about joining our consortium and participating in fully the scientific, data, and music visibility work.

Today we had a meeting with the Lavtian Folk Archive and ALOADED, so that we are addressing contractually the same issues that Hudobné centrum has in terms of music metadata and music distribution. @Tomas Miks&lt;mailto:tomas.miks@soza.sk&gt; suggested that their lawyers pitch in to assist all of us.

- We want to make it clear that it is impossible that the 25,000 euro fake streaming clause can apply to Hudobné centrum.
- With both the Hudobné centrum and LFA, we are anyways happy to create a contract that avoids royalty payments altogether, with spending all of your royalty share in a documented, high-quality and transparent marketing of Slovak-Latvian music.
- If you do not earn royalties, any royalty cheating clause will not apply to you. But even if you do, we can put many safeguards that this will not apply, and your contract can be terminated even before this issue would be raised, which we also find a practically impossible scenario from a fake streaming point of view.

What I would like to suggest is that @Love Ojensa&lt;mailto:love@aloaded.com&gt; shares with us with the new ALOADED standard terms, and @Tomas Miks&lt;mailto:tomas.miks@soza.sk&gt; 's colleagues and make take it from there to make sure that you feel safe to sign the contract.

Regarding the Wikipedia issue, I will write a separate email. With @Stefan Kragh&lt;mailto:stefan@aloaded.com&gt; we wil meet again on Friday to work out some data issues.

Best regards,
Daniel

Dear Measuring CCS team,



First off, I hope you are well. Belated congratulations on the completion of your project.



I am writing on behalf of the Horizon Europe project Open Music Europe or OpenMusE (https://www.openmuse.eu/), which I coordinate. Our objective is to support EU music ecosystems in becoming more competitive, fairer, and more sustainable. To this end, we map data availabilities and gaps, bridge high-priority data gaps, and develop tools to support data-driven policymaking.



We have read with great interest the Measuring CCS Final Report, and have noticed references to prior reports, e.g.:



  *   Report on Inventory of Sources
  *   28 Country Reports
  *   Analysis Report – A New Framework for Cultural and Creative Sector Statistics



Based on the Final Report, material contained in these prior reports may duplicate work in which we are currently engaged: e.g., updating the review of national cultural access and participation surveys present in the ESSnet-Culture 2012 report, etc.



However, we have not been able to find these reports online. Would it be possible to access these reports? Doing so may save our project team a great deal of redundant work, and thus greatly improve the efficiency of our EU funding usage.



Our Project Officer @VYZIKA Melpomeni&lt;mailto:Melpomeni.VYZIKA@ec.europa.eu&gt; is in CC for reference.



Thank you for your consideration, and best regards,



James Edwards, PhD

Senior Researcher, SINUS Markt- und Sozialforschung GmbH (https://www.sinus-institut.de/)

Project Coordinator, Open Music Europe (https://www.openmuse.eu/)

Hi Daniel,

Apologies for pushing this meeting, I am slightly under pressure as we must submit a *tentative* questionnaire (or at least a list of topics covered) to the SSSA institutional review board at least a couple of months before launch. Although SINUS is administering the audience survey, and as a private entity we don't need review board clearance, it will be beneficial for publications to have gone through the process.

I agree — let's use this call to discuss the use of the survey. From the Bergfest, I also understood we should focus on public performance. However, we didn't have time to go into details.

If we can run through the current draft as we discuss, it would be beneficial, as this would give us at least a rough idea of how much new material should be developed.

Thank you all and best regards,
James

Dear James,



we prepared a rough English translation of the latest CAP questionnaire used in 2018.



The research that time was prepared by the TNS Hoffman Hungary and Daniel’s business, the field work was done by the TNS. We have some exploitation rights over the questionnaire but we cannot reuse it as is together with the insrtuctions, etc. So please use it as a sample. The transaltion was made with deepL, and this stage we have not checked the accuracy yet.



Please take a peek at it whether you can use it, and if it is needed we van have a short call on it as well.



There are questions which should be considered with regard to the following info:



  *   for our purpose we had to have questions on audiovisual content;
  *   there were some questions on CDs, DVDs, smathphones, tablets, PC-s, HDDs, smartTV-s, ect – posession and usage (mostly for copying) of these goods – these are related to private copy remuneration which was the focus of the research at the time
  *   there were questions about how listening to music on youtube could be substituted– the study which analysed the data of the survey had a chapter on the so called value gap effect of youtube which was a mostly not licensed or underlicensed sercice that time. As this has changed since then these parts should be reconsidered according to a reconsiedered modeling of the pilote study.



Kind regards,



Eszter

### Re: Review of data shared and procedures {#email-749}

**From:** Anna Zilkova &lt;anna.zilkova@hc.sk&gt;  
**To:** Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;, AnnA Mester &lt;anna.mester@reprex.nl&gt;, Demčák Richard &lt;Richard.Demcak@soza.sk&gt;, Jankovič Marián &lt;marian.jankovic@soza.sk&gt;, Matej Grochal &lt;matej.grochal@wikimedia.sk&gt;  
**Date:** 11/07/2024 16:14:33

<!-- source: OpenMuse_20261009-2156/OpenMuse/messages/202411071614-Re_ Review of data shared and procedures-37.txt -->


Anna Žilková
Hudobné centrum / Music Centre Slovakia
vedúca Oddelenia dokumentácie a informatiky /
Head of Documentation and Information Department
tel./phone +421220470310, +421911980328
www.hc.sk



Dňa 7. 11. 2024 o 12:36 Daniel Antal napísal(a):
&gt; Dear Colleagues,
&gt;
&gt; With Anna Mester we will finalise a presentation and a table for the 
&gt; following procedures.  We will make a presentation in the meeting, but 
&gt; the main ideas are here.
&gt;
&gt; Thursday, November 7 · 3:30 – 4:30pm
&gt; Time zone: Europe/Prague
&gt; Google Meet joining info
&gt; Video call link: _https://meet.google.com/azg-smsm-edx_
&gt;
&gt; We would like to formalise the following procedures.
&gt;
&gt; _Verify or assign a global identifier for the author
&gt; _- Verify or assign a global identifier for the author, first VIAF, 
&gt; but we also ask for quotes from ISNI agencies.
&gt; - Review of the data needs.
&gt; - Differences between people who opted in and those who did not 
&gt; opt-out. It should be considered that this procedure may be suitable 
&gt; for those people who have not opted out.
&gt;
&gt; _Verify or assign a global identifier for performer groups
&gt; _- This is only possible if the founder(s) of the group, such as a 
&gt; quartet, a band, an ensemble are identified or willing to identify 
&gt; themselves.
&gt;
&gt;
&gt; For SOZA: This is the first step in matching ISWCs and ISRCs, and it 
&gt; is a tool to improve identity checks before distribution. The argument 
&gt; can be made that this is possibly an improvement of rights management 
&gt; procedures, especially for authors who have at least one work in a 
&gt; public library. That public library, for example, the Bratislava 
&gt; Municipal Library, could add the person's name to the VIAF authority.
&gt;
&gt; For Wikimedia:  I think that we should only link the discovered or new 
&gt; VIAF entries to people who a) already have an existing page OR b) have 
&gt; signed our consent form and whose works reach the notability criteria 
&gt; of Wikipedia Slovakia.
&gt;
&gt; _Europeana_
&gt; List the author's publicly viewable and listenable works as part of 
&gt; European cultural heritage and improve its findability with Europe's 
&gt; search engine support, library, museum, and archive coordination 
&gt; system Europeana.
&gt;
&gt; - First discussion of the data needs.
&gt; - We need a title, author, and a URL where the work can be seen or 
&gt; listened to without a password.
&gt; - We can create such an HTML page for those who do not have it.
&gt; - This should be a service for those who opt-in and for Hudobné Centrum.
&gt; - In my opinion, this is the part where Wikidata and Wikipedia should 
&gt; be involved.
&gt;
&gt;
&gt; _Release on Spotify and other DSPs_
&gt; We are finalising a procedure with ALOADED to release or re-release 
&gt; music and connect biographical information via Wikipedia and Wikidata. 
&gt; In this procedure, assigning an ISNI to each credited person is also 
&gt; possible. We are piloting this service with the Latvian Folk Archive, 
&gt; but we would also like to do this with Hudobné centrum. With the 
&gt; combination of the VIAF, ISNI and Wikidata identification, we are very 
&gt; positive that we can increase your catalogue's visibility and payouts. 
&gt; Still, our main aim is to provide an integrated service where Hudobné 
&gt; centrum would be able to publish music, ensure that it is found on all 
&gt; global platforms, on Europeana,  and via the hc.sk &lt;http://hc.sk&gt; 
&gt; website you can identify all rentable or commercially available 
&gt; sheets, records, and also legal platforms where you can listen to the 
&gt; works.
&gt;
&gt; SOZA and ALODED promised via Tomas Miks legal help to clarify that the 
&gt; fake algorithm provisions will never apply to Hudobné centrum.
&gt;
&gt; *We would also be happy to find a smaller label that would try this out.*
&gt;
&gt; Best regards,

Anna Žilková

tel./phone +421220470310, +421911980328

Dňa 7. 11. 2024 o 12:36 Daniel Antal napísal(a):
&gt; Dear Colleagues,
&gt;
&gt; With Anna Mester we will finalise a presentation and a table for the 
&gt; following procedures.  We will make a presentation in the meeting, but 
&gt; the main ideas are here.
&gt;
&gt; Thursday, November 7 · 3:30 – 4:30pm
&gt; Time zone: Europe/Prague
&gt; Google Meet joining info
&gt; Video call link: _https://meet.google.com/azg-smsm-edx_
&gt;
&gt; We would like to formalise the following procedures.
&gt;
&gt; _Verify or assign a global identifier for the author
&gt; _- Verify or assign a global identifier for the author, first VIAF, 
&gt; but we also ask for quotes from ISNI agencies.
&gt; - Review of the data needs.
&gt; - Differences between people who opted in and those who did not 
&gt; opt-out. It should be considered that this procedure may be suitable 
&gt; for those people who have not opted out.
&gt;
&gt; _Verify or assign a global identifier for performer groups
&gt; _- This is only possible if the founder(s) of the group, such as a 
&gt; quartet, a band, an ensemble are identified or willing to identify 
&gt; themselves.
&gt;
&gt;
&gt; For SOZA: This is the first step in matching ISWCs and ISRCs, and it 
&gt; is a tool to improve identity checks before distribution. The argument 
&gt; can be made that this is possibly an improvement of rights management 
&gt; procedures, especially for authors who have at least one work in a 
&gt; public library. That public library, for example, the Bratislava 
&gt; Municipal Library, could add the person's name to the VIAF authority.
&gt;
&gt; For Wikimedia:  I think that we should only link the discovered or new 
&gt; VIAF entries to people who a) already have an existing page OR b) have 
&gt; signed our consent form and whose works reach the notability criteria 
&gt; of Wikipedia Slovakia.
&gt;
&gt; _Europeana_
&gt; List the author's publicly viewable and listenable works as part of 
&gt; European cultural heritage and improve its findability with Europe's 
&gt; search engine support, library, museum, and archive coordination 
&gt; system Europeana.
&gt;
&gt; - First discussion of the data needs.
&gt; - We need a title, author, and a URL where the work can be seen or 
&gt; listened to without a password.
&gt; - We can create such an HTML page for those who do not have it.
&gt; - This should be a service for those who opt-in and for Hudobné Centrum.
&gt; - In my opinion, this is the part where Wikidata and Wikipedia should 
&gt; be involved.
&gt;
&gt;
&gt; _Release on Spotify and other DSPs_
&gt; We are finalising a procedure with ALOADED to release or re-release 
&gt; music and connect biographical information via Wikipedia and Wikidata. 
&gt; In this procedure, assigning an ISNI to each credited person is also 
&gt; possible. We are piloting this service with the Latvian Folk Archive, 
&gt; but we would also like to do this with Hudobné centrum. With the 
&gt; combination of the VIAF, ISNI and Wikidata identification, we are very 
&gt; positive that we can increase your catalogue's visibility and payouts. 
&gt; Still, our main aim is to provide an integrated service where Hudobné 
&gt; centrum would be able to publish music, ensure that it is found on all 
&gt; global platforms, on Europeana,  and via the hc.sk &lt;http://hc.sk&gt; 
&gt; website you can identify all rentable or commercially available 
&gt; sheets, records, and also legal platforms where you can listen to the 
&gt; works.
&gt;
&gt; SOZA and ALODED promised via Tomas Miks legal help to clarify that the 
&gt; fake algorithm provisions will never apply to Hudobné centrum.
&gt;
&gt; *We would also be happy to find a smaller label that would try this out.*
&gt;
&gt; Best regards,
&gt; *Daniel Antal, CFA*
&gt; *co-founder*
&gt; +31615058460
&gt; linkedin &lt;https://www.linkedin.com/in/antaldaniel/&gt; • reprex bv 
&gt; &lt;http://reprex.nl/&gt; •eviota &lt;https://eviota.nl/&gt;

Subject: RE: request for indicative price



Dear James,



Please find my answers. The circle of information as below reflect the research frame of 2019 yet the basic approaches hardly changed during the years in order to ensure comparability.



  1.  F2F CAPI
  2.  According to the agreement, the basic population investigated as a minimum was the Hungarian population aged 15-69, at the same time, the commitment referred to the ESSNet Culture recommendations and undertook to follow the best practice. ESSNet's recommendation was to examine the 15-75 age group as a minimum, but preferably the age group older than six years.
  3.  We therefore supplemented the primary base population with the 10-14 year old age group on the one hand, and the 70+ year old age group on the other hand. The sociodemographic characteristics of the basic population were defined on the basis of the data of the 2011 Census for easier comparability with the previous surveys, and taking into account the data of the later microcensus would have caused a very small, unnoticeable deviation from this. So the sampling frame is the population aged 10+ living in Hungarian households. Since the basic unit of analysis is the individual, we accordingly took a personal sample (as in previous years).
  4.  The method used was the disproportionately stratified random sample, in which the 10-14-year-old and 70+-year-old age groups were present in different (lower) proportions than in the basic population.
  5.  The settlements were selected randomly. Within the settlement, households were selected by random walking. Within a household, the interviewees were selected according to quota criteria. The 10-17-year-olds came from households where we also asked someone from among the adults. (Sampling aimed at random selection of minors would have increased the costs of the research to an unrealistic extent.) The selection of the minor respondents was made with the consent of the parents. We asked a maximum of one adult and one minor in a household.
  6.  The sample consisted of three parts: 1) base sample aged 15-69: N=~1000 people; 2) boosted sample of 10-14 year olds: N=~50 people; 3) boosted sample of 70+ year olds: N=~50 people.
  7.  In the sample, marginal quotas are applied taking into account the following aspects: region, type of settlement, gender and age. In determining the quotas, we used the data of the latest Population Census.



I do hope that above information would support your job.



Best regards,



Tamás

Dear Mr. Tamás,



I hope that you have been well, and I apologize for the long delay in replying to your indicative cost quote. As always, it took the European Commission a bit of time to evaluate the proposal. Fortunately, however, we were chosen to be invited to the grant agreement process. Currently, we’re reworking the proposal text into an agreement.



So, first off: thank you for your fast response to our initial inquiry, which was very helpful in putting our proposal on a solid enough foundation to be chosen!



Pursuant the grant agreement process, we’d like to ask a question about surveying mode. While the proposal was well-evaluated, the reviewers expressed concern about the fieldwork cost. We recognize that face-to-face surveying remains the “gold standard” for high-quality data; however, quite a bit has been learned during the SERISS (https://seriss.eu/) and CRONOS projects and the COVID-19 pandemic about effective non-f2f sampling and fieldwork, mode effects and how to compensate for them, etc. As you may have read, the European Social Survey has even announced a forthcoming change in data collection mode from face-to-face interviews to online and paper self-completion surveys (https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/singlenew.html?a=/about/news/essnews0130.html).



Given the rapidly progressing state of the art, we wonder what options Kantar Hoffmann might be able to offer with regard to a mixed-mode, or even entirely self-completion-based, survey. A probability rather than quota sample would still be strongly preferred. We are happy to keep conversing by email, or alternatively, to set up a call once Daniel is back from holiday later this month.



Again, many thanks, and best regards,

James

We would like to replicate the surveys we have conducted in 2015, 2017,2018,2019 with you with mainly the same questionnaire and sampling for comparability, because our work was seen as a best practice by the European Commission and relevant bodies in post-Brexit UK.

We are applying for an EU research and innovation grant with leading experts in this field, the Information Law Research Center of the University of Amsterdam, the University of Turku Data Science Group, the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies, Sinus and my company, and Artisjus and its sister societies. Subject: RE: request for indicative price



Dear James,



Please find my answers. The circle of information as below reflect the research frame of 2019 yet the basic approaches hardly changed during the years in order to ensure comparability.



  1.  F2F CAPI
  2.  According to the agreement, the basic population investigated as a minimum was the Hungarian population aged 15-69, at the same time, the commitment referred to the ESSNet Culture recommendations and undertook to follow the best practice. ESSNet's recommendation was to examine the 15-75 age group as a minimum, but preferably the age group older than six years.
  3.  We therefore supplemented the primary base population with the 10-14 year old age group on the one hand, and the 70+ year old age group on the other hand. The sociodemographic characteristics of the basic population were defined on the basis of the data of the 2011 Census for easier comparability with the previous surveys, and taking into account the data of the later microcensus would have caused a very small, unnoticeable deviation from this. So the sampling frame is the population aged 10+ living in Hungarian households. Since the basic unit of analysis is the individual, we accordingly took a personal sample (as in previous years).
  4.  The method used was the disproportionately stratified random sample, in which the 10-14-year-old and 70+-year-old age groups were present in different (lower) proportions than in the basic population.
  5.  The settlements were selected randomly. Within the settlement, households were selected by random walking. Within a household, the interviewees were selected according to quota criteria. The 10-17-year-olds came from households where we also asked someone from among the adults. (Sampling aimed at random selection of minors would have increased the costs of the research to an unrealistic extent.) The selection of the minor respondents was made with the consent of the parents. We asked a maximum of one adult and one minor in a household.
  6.  The sample consisted of three parts: 1) base sample aged 15-69: N=~1000 people; 2) boosted sample of 10-14 year olds: N=~50 people; 3) boosted sample of 70+ year olds: N=~50 people.
  7.  In the sample, marginal quotas are applied taking into account the following aspects: region, type of settlement, gender and age. In determining the quotas, we used the data of the latest Population Census.



I do hope that above information would support your job.



Best regards,



Tamás

Dear Mr. Tamás,



I hope that you have been well, and I apologize for the long delay in replying to your indicative cost quote. As always, it took the European Commission a bit of time to evaluate the proposal. Fortunately, however, we were chosen to be invited to the grant agreement process. Currently, we’re reworking the proposal text into an agreement.



So, first off: thank you for your fast response to our initial inquiry, which was very helpful in putting our proposal on a solid enough foundation to be chosen!



Pursuant the grant agreement process, we’d like to ask a question about surveying mode. While the proposal was well-evaluated, the reviewers expressed concern about the fieldwork cost. We recognize that face-to-face surveying remains the “gold standard” for high-quality data; however, quite a bit has been learned during the SERISS (https://seriss.eu/) and CRONOS projects and the COVID-19 pandemic about effective non-f2f sampling and fieldwork, mode effects and how to compensate for them, etc. As you may have read, the European Social Survey has even announced a forthcoming change in data collection mode from face-to-face interviews to online and paper self-completion surveys (https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/singlenew.html?a=/about/news/essnews0130.html).



Given the rapidly progressing state of the art, we wonder what options Kantar Hoffmann might be able to offer with regard to a mixed-mode, or even entirely self-completion-based, survey. A probability rather than quota sample would still be strongly preferred. We are happy to keep conversing by email, or alternatively, to set up a call once Daniel is back from holiday later this month.



Again, many thanks, and best regards,

James

Dear Tamás,

I hope that this email finds you well.  I would like to ask an indicative quote from you for a survey to be carried out in January/February 2024.

We would like to replicate the surveys we have conducted in 2015, 2017,2018,2019 with you with mainly the same questionnaire and sampling for comparability, because our work was seen as a best practice by the European Commission and relevant bodies in post-Brexit UK.

We are applying for an EU research and innovation grant with leading experts in this field, the Information Law Research Center of the University of Amsterdam, the University of Turku Data Science Group, the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies, Sinus and my company, and Artisjus and its sister societies.  We would like to show to the European Commission, Eurostat, and the scientific community that our work is not only the best example in this field but it is replicable.

We would like to have indicative budgets from you for the following countries, either separately, or together (if there is a cost saving):

-          Hungary (for replication)  CAPI + online (limited questionnaire, to compare the differences of answers in CAPI and online mode)

-          Bulgaria  CAPI

-          Germany  CAPI

-          Italy CAPI

You can assume that the questionnaire, the sample design and all parameters are the same, though we believe that some questionnaire blocks will have to be changed, as we are merging a similar research done in 12 other countries with a slightly different questionnaire and our research project.   The sample size is n=1000, with overweighting younger groups (similarly to our prior work) and using the same selection of participants.

For the online mode, I think that our questionnaire is too long, but we would use the most important question blocks for comparing the properties of the two modes.  So I think that we can count for a half-length questionnaire in the online mode.

I understand that giving prices for 2024 is very indicative, but we need to make a budget this week (latest next Tuesday) for a Horizon Europe grant proposal.  Because of the size and complexity of the grant, there will be some room to make changes, if we get the grant, in January 2023, still one year ahead of the fieldwork.  So the quote does not have to be very precise, which would not be possible at such a short notice.

Sincerely yours,

Subject: RE: request for indicative price



Dear James,



Please find my answers. The circle of information as below reflect the research frame of 2019 yet the basic approaches hardly changed during the years in order to ensure comparability.



  1.  F2F CAPI
  2.  According to the agreement, the basic population investigated as a minimum was the Hungarian population aged 15-69, at the same time, the commitment referred to the ESSNet Culture recommendations and undertook to follow the best practice. ESSNet's recommendation was to examine the 15-75 age group as a minimum, but preferably the age group older than six years.
  3.  We therefore supplemented the primary base population with the 10-14 year old age group on the one hand, and the 70+ year old age group on the other hand. The sociodemographic characteristics of the basic population were defined on the basis of the data of the 2011 Census for easier comparability with the previous surveys, and taking into account the data of the later microcensus would have caused a very small, unnoticeable deviation from this. So the sampling frame is the population aged 10+ living in Hungarian households. Since the basic unit of analysis is the individual, we accordingly took a personal sample (as in previous years).
  4.  The method used was the disproportionately stratified random sample, in which the 10-14-year-old and 70+-year-old age groups were present in different (lower) proportions than in the basic population.
  5.  The settlements were selected randomly. Within the settlement, households were selected by random walking. Within a household, the interviewees were selected according to quota criteria. The 10-17-year-olds came from households where we also asked someone from among the adults. (Sampling aimed at random selection of minors would have increased the costs of the research to an unrealistic extent.) The selection of the minor respondents was made with the consent of the parents. We asked a maximum of one adult and one minor in a household.
  6.  The sample consisted of three parts: 1) base sample aged 15-69: N=~1000 people; 2) boosted sample of 10-14 year olds: N=~50 people; 3) boosted sample of 70+ year olds: N=~50 people.
  7.  In the sample, marginal quotas are applied taking into account the following aspects: region, type of settlement, gender and age. In determining the quotas, we used the data of the latest Population Census.



I do hope that above information would support your job.



Best regards,



Tamás

Dear Mr. Tamás,



I hope that you have been well, and I apologize for the long delay in replying to your indicative cost quote. As always, it took the European Commission a bit of time to evaluate the proposal. Fortunately, however, we were chosen to be invited to the grant agreement process. Currently, we’re reworking the proposal text into an agreement.



So, first off: thank you for your fast response to our initial inquiry, which was very helpful in putting our proposal on a solid enough foundation to be chosen!



Pursuant the grant agreement process, we’d like to ask a question about surveying mode. While the proposal was well-evaluated, the reviewers expressed concern about the fieldwork cost. We recognize that face-to-face surveying remains the “gold standard” for high-quality data; however, quite a bit has been learned during the SERISS (https://seriss.eu/) and CRONOS projects and the COVID-19 pandemic about effective non-f2f sampling and fieldwork, mode effects and how to compensate for them, etc. As you may have read, the European Social Survey has even announced a forthcoming change in data collection mode from face-to-face interviews to online and paper self-completion surveys (https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/singlenew.html?a=/about/news/essnews0130.html).



Given the rapidly progressing state of the art, we wonder what options Kantar Hoffmann might be able to offer with regard to a mixed-mode, or even entirely self-completion-based, survey. A probability rather than quota sample would still be strongly preferred. We are happy to keep conversing by email, or alternatively, to set up a call once Daniel is back from holiday later this month.



Again, many thanks, and best regards,

James

Am 28.11.2024 um 11:09 schrieb James Rhys Edwards &lt;JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&lt;mailto:JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&gt;&gt;:

Hi all,

I hope you're all well!

I'm writing to connect on the topic of background music / in-store music / public performances of recorded music, which SOZA indicated at the Bergfest as a priority for the forthcoming surveying.

SINUS will include a few questions on this topic in the general population survey we will conduct in January. However, there are some questions that this type of survey can't answer: e.g., the economic added value of background music (hypothetical questions like "how much more would you pay for a cup of coffee in a shop with great music" do not work in practice).

The HEARDIS research — which will be conducted in-store — could be a much better vector to get at these questions.

If we could get representatives from both partners into either the WP3 meeting on Friday at 9am or into a separate a call next week, that would be fantastic. We'd like to:

  *   Get a more precise view of exactly what SOZA needs / wants to learn about background music

  *   Run through the SINUS survey questions on background music

  *   Check in re: the progress of the HEARDIS research design and your fieldwork plans

  *   Plan out who will do what in the coming months
My schedule next week is flexible so far, with the exception of Weds afternoon.

Thank you and best regards,
James

Hi Anna,

Please start working on adding these questions to a new part of the questionbank.

https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Rg_AAajImNJmnLCjcnUkEVi9rZWKWNSMmOQyoAnuCfc/edit?usp=sharing

1. For each new question, create a row in the spreadsheet with the Hungarian label.
2. Add a variable name following the first examples.  No problem if the var name is not great, I will change them as needed. Always add (CAP) to the variable short label. Create a snake_case_version as an alias.
3. Add the question text as description

We will discuss the rest, but try to understand the representation base type and three representation forms, and try to match these up with the questions.
- numeric if the question only wants a number.
- yes-no-selector with decline option if the answer is yes/have/approve no/don't have/disapprove or decline to answer
- a broader binary base type if only two answer options are possible excluding do not know and decline to answer.
- category base type if the answer options come from a controlled vocabulary but without hierarchy, or direction.
- scale base type if the answer categories represent some ordinal scale, like totally agree, agree, neither agree nor disagree, disagree, totally disagree, or small, medium, large.

For now just please transcribe all question texts, question numbers, give them a temporary short label and var name, and try to mark the simpler representation types.

With time questions, if the time is not explicitly asked like on 1989-10-23, but on categories like yesterday, last week, etc. then treat the time as time appellation with a scale or category.

For each answer option we will need concepts as items. That will take some time, but let us take stock of our questions, organise them to groups, and ask James for feedback before we research thesauri and start looking up concepts.

Best regards ,
Daniel
