Call for chapters for an edited volume to be submitted to Springer’s Music Business Research Series



Music Ecosystems: Challenges and Opportunities



Editors

Guy Morrow (University of Melbourne)

Carsten Winter (Hanover University of Music, Drama Media)



Following the (15th) _International Music Business Research Days_ conference (Music Ecosystems Research: Challenges and Opportunities) produced by the _International Music Business Research Association_ and held from June 5-7, 2024 at the Hanover University of Music, Drama and Media, we invite you to further elucidate the formation and special features of "music ecosystems" by submitting a chapter proposal for this contributed volume.



We are looking for contributions that will help to better understand and explain music contexts as "ecosystems". The term "ecosystem", which has now become a key strategic and political term, was introduced into strategicdiscussions to emphasize the fact that the environment of more and more organizations was becoming more dynamic, complex, interdependent and borderless; that such organizations were beginning to resemble "ecosystems", i.e. biological systems in nature (see for e.g.

in particular Davidson, Harmer &amp; Marshall 2014 and, for the origin and logic of ecological thinking, the literature review by de Bernard, Comunian &amp; Gross 2021). We only understand these newly (more dynamic, complex, interdependent and borderless) social relationships/environments if we take these characteristics and normative implications that go with them into account. Some even think that we cannot/should not do this with classic economic concepts (e.g.

Scharmer &amp; Kaufer 2013), which focus mostly on the economic efficiency of relationships, markets, contracts, advertising, etc. or for example with classic concepts concerning culture for similar reasons.



These new social ecosystem dynamics, with their complexity, interdependence and borderless nature, were developed by everyone who contributed to them, from _Napster_, _MySpace_, _YouTube_ to _TikTok_.

Today, almost everyone who does something with music digitally for themselves and others contributes to production and distribution within these more dynamic, complex, interdependent and borderless music ecosystems. In this contributed volume, the term "ecosystem" also refers to the growing data complexity that has arisen in the wake of the arrival of new actors such as Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and algorithms (Clancy 2023). There is a need for new holistic and normative theories in this context: holistic because concepts that, for example, distinguish a private from a public music sector are becoming problematic due to the growing interdependencies between them; normative because this development shows that legitimizing strategic considerations either with a view to economic or artistic goals alone is becoming problematic. Indeed, they are also expected to be more comprehensively oriented towards global sustainability goals, as the European Union (EU) program _Music Moves Europe_ shows very well. Music can also increasingly rarely be meaningfully attributed to either the private or the public sector, since classical music is becoming more and more commercial and popular music in its variousforms is also publicly funded, or must be, because in some instances fewer and fewer private actors are doing so. It is becoming more complicated and it is therefore important for us to understand what is connected to what or whom and why in the music sector today, and what this means for distinguishable connections at different levels, regionally, nationally, internationally and geostrategically. For example, as part of its _Music Moves Europe _program, the EU wants to find out exactly what a music ecosystem is and what distinguishes the “European music ecosystem” globally from other comparable “music ecosystems” economically, socially, artistically, structurally, etc. It is assumed that such a comparison should best take a conceptual look at all relationships in an ecosystem:

not just media or economic or social or cultural relationships, but all the relationships that make ecosystems more valuable for those involved, that are important for the work of the future, and that make them attractive, competitive, sustainable, resilient, productive, creative or innovative.



This poses a completely new conceptual and normative challenge for research into the music business and music culture. It can no longer only explore contractual relationships, transactions (economics), intrinsic value(art and culture), power (politics), networks or more personal relationships. It is long overdue that the use of the term "music ecosystem" becomes more scientific, empirical, conceptual and analytical. This includes examining how different ways of using the term differ; since it has become a key term or metaphor, the term ecosystem has also been used to articulate interests or to develop and legitimize new commercial and private business models. Recently, two new ways of using the term have become more common in music discourse, which have little to do with the previously established uses, which indicates increasing dynamism, complexity, interdependence and the borderless nature of music sectors. For example, it is now becoming more common for representatives of the established music industries to understand their industrial structures in the sector as forming part of an "ecosystem".

This use has precursors in the Chicago School of Sociology and makes it possible for the status quo to promote the preservation of their structures in the same way that the preservation of otherwise extinct animals or plants is promoted (e.g. Federal Association of the Music Industry).



In addition to this (conservative) use, we are increasingly encountering a private-commercial technical use of the concept "ecosystem". When it comes to big tech and big content companies, ecosystems are closed, data-based, independent and autonomous private contexts that operate as private markets in which customers belong to those who own the ecosystem infrastructure and that orchestrate the actors and relationships (see, for example, the McKinsey strategists and authors Atluri &amp; Dietz 2023 and, with a stronger focus on the data, see in particular Subramaniam 2022. Also see Giblin and Doctorow, 2022).



Research into newer and more complex music ecosystems is possible from many disciplinary and interdisciplinary perspectives with a view to a wide variety of objects and processes: What do these developments mean for old and new actors, for old structures and institutions? What new structures and institutions are emerging or being developed? What new relevant contexts and processes are there in music ecosystems? How do they form and reform, with new ones emerging in different contexts? Who will be the new and important players in the music ecosystems of the future and why? Who is changing how and why they operate, with what arguments? Do the dynamics, complexity, interdependence and borderlessness need to be regulated? What role does politics and political goals such as those of the EU play in the context of, for example, the _Music Moves Europe_ program? What distinguishes music ecosystems globally, nationally or as music city ecosystems?



This call is aimed at researchers from all disciplines, as well as players from music culture and the music industries.

words): 15 October 2024

3. Add the question text as description

We will discuss the rest, but try to understand the representation base type and three representation forms, and try to match these up with the questions.
- numeric if the question only wants a number.
- yes-no-selector with decline option if the answer is yes/have/approve no/don't have/disapprove or decline to answer
- a broader binary base type if only two answer options are possible excluding do not know and decline to answer.
- category base type if the answer options come from a controlled vocabulary but without hierarchy, or direction.
- scale base type if the answer categories represent some ordinal scale, like totally agree, agree, neither agree nor disagree, disagree, totally disagree, or small, medium, large.

For now just please transcribe all question texts, question numbers, give them a temporary short label and var name, and try to mark the simpler representation types.

With time questions, if the time is not explicitly asked like on 1989-10-23, but on categories like yesterday, last week, etc. then treat the time as time appellation with a scale or category.

For each answer option we will need concepts as items. That will take some time, but let us take stock of our questions, organise them to groups, and ask James for feedback before we research thesauri and start looking up concepts.

Best regards ,
Daniel

Subject: Re: Processing, conceptualising and categorizing a questionnaire

Hi James,

So this is my suggestion for the work, bearing in mind that we also need a scientific publication at one point.

Questionbank

1. We create a questionbank with all EU languages, based on a small number of select questions from the EU 2013 CAP survey – because the GESIS archive has them in all EU languages.  Anna will guide your intern on how to fill out these in a Google spreadsheet.
2. You will curate concepts from relevant thesauri; I would suggest Wikidata, SDMX, EuroVoc. In the very few instances where no SDMX vocabulary applies, find any sociological vocabuarly that you find fit. There will be a few questions like that, but they have the highest novelty value. Most of them relate to the well-harmonised concepts of urbanisation, education level, age, etc.
3. You and I agree on the interpretation of DDI regarding a very small number of concepts (i.e. study, study no, question, question text, variable representation type, etc.) so that we can claim that we created a questionbank tool that is DDI compliant and technically capable to work on the entire EU level.
4. I write an extension package for retroharmonize and provide a reproducible workflow.

This can be spilled off into 1 or 2 publications, and if the Turku postdoc wants to be involved, he can, too.  One would be an interpretation of DDI for questionbanks, and one potentially a R Journal publication for making an R library to do the work.  The EU dimension of our work is the questionbank, not the rather limited surveys, so I think we must put in a few days of work to have some questions in all EU official languages.  What could be a great plus, and overlaps with our new project, is to perhaps add a few minority language items, too.


Aside from this, we need to come up with a model for the live music. For this, I would have a two-level approach, as the SSSA postdoc is not yet proven.

Live music valuation

1. The postdoc a.s.a.p comes up with an economically literate review of your live music census in the context of music economics.
2. If this work is competently done, I can make the postdoc a co-author to publish in English or a general valuation model developed together with Eszter Kabai, as a third author, and we can work our general model aligned with whatever aspect your postdoc finds on live music in particular. You can motivate the postdoc with almost immediate publication opportunities, but only if he or she proves to be an asset and not a liability to the work.
3. Our general valuation model has very clear variable descriptions, and these will be matched against administrative and questionnaire survey items.
4. Anna will guide your intern regarding the questionnaire elements related to these questions. We already know which will be certainly used, and for those, your intern can start to create English, German, Italian translations.
So this means that you, your intern, Anna, and the new postdoc can start working in parallel.  I think that a very high percentage of our existing surveys can be reused, we just must be mindful that in many cases the base language is not Hungarian but English.

Eviota

Your live music census uses the same methodology that our Eviota software does, which is now also having an opportunity to an academic book chapter. Regarding the academic KPIs, this is a really successful coincidence, because I believe that this can lead to 2-3 academic publications, given that we use the very same software tool and methodology for economic impact analysis and  environmental impact analysis.

I would very much suggest a minimal re-run of your census, because I think that to make it work with Evitoa it will be probably less work to re-run it then to ex post recode your collected data, though who knows: your data must conform to NACE and CPA codes.

For a re-run, in Slovakia, I would aim for Kosice as Bratislava is too big for that.  One way to do this could be to define a Slovak sample in CAP that is over-sampling Kosice, or adds a mixed mode extra Kosice component. In Hungary, I would suggest Debrecen, Pécs, or Szeged, which are mid-sized towns with some music activities, as Budapest would not be feasible.  Or, but this is an issue of its own, to think of a Budapest XI. district or Budapest V. district analysis. It would be very logical to do a run on a location where HearDis is working, too.

On environmental analysis, it would be very important to get access to bookkeeping data of SOZA, ALOADED, MIH and some of their partners, HEARDIS, etc. Maybe Slnko records in Slovakia, who will be working with us.

Best regards,
Daniel

Dear James,



Please find my answers. The circle of information as below reflect the research frame of 2019 yet the basic approaches hardly changed during the years in order to ensure comparability.



  *   F2F CAPI
  *   According to the agreement, the basic population investigated as a minimum was the Hungarian population aged 15-69, at the same time, the commitment referred to the ESSNet Culture recommendations and undertook to follow the best practice. ESSNet's recommendation was to examine the 15-75 age group as a minimum, but preferably the age group older than six years.
  *   We therefore supplemented the primary base population with the 10-14 year old age group on the one hand, and the 70+ year old age group on the other hand. The sociodemographic characteristics of the basic population were defined on the basis of the data of the 2011 Census for easier comparability with the previous surveys, and taking into account the data of the later microcensus would have caused a very small, unnoticeable deviation from this. So the sampling frame is the population aged 10+ living in Hungarian households. Since the basic unit of analysis is the individual, we accordingly took a personal sample (as in previous years).
  *   The method used was the disproportionately stratified random sample, in which the 10-14-year-old and 70+-year-old age groups were present in different (lower) proportions than in the basic population.
  *   The settlements were selected randomly. Within the settlement, households were selected by random walking. Within a household, the interviewees were selected according to quota criteria. The 10-17-year-olds came from households where we also asked someone from among the adults. (Sampling aimed at random selection of minors would have increased the costs of the research to an unrealistic extent.) The selection of the minor respondents was made with the consent of the parents. We asked a maximum of one adult and one minor in a household.
  *   The sample consisted of three parts: 1) base sample aged 15-69: N=~1000 people; 2) boosted sample of 10-14 year olds: N=~50 people; 3) boosted sample of 70+ year olds: N=~50 people.
  *   In the sample, marginal quotas are applied taking into account the following aspects: region, type of settlement, gender and age. In determining the quotas, we used the data of the latest Population Census.



I do hope that above information would support your job.



Best regards,



Tamás

Given the rapidly progressing state of the art, we wonder what options Kantar Hoffmann might be able to offer with regard to a mixed-mode, or even entirely self-completion-based, survey. Hi James,

So this is my suggestion for the work, bearing in mind that we also need a scientific publication at one point.

Questionbank

1. We create a questionbank with all EU languages, based on a small number of select questions from the EU 2013 CAP survey – because the GESIS archive has them in all EU languages.  Anna will guide your intern on how to fill out these in a Google spreadsheet.
2. You will curate concepts from relevant thesauri; I would suggest Wikidata, SDMX, EuroVoc. In the very few instances where no SDMX vocabulary applies, find any sociological vocabuarly that you find fit. There will be a few questions like that, but they have the highest novelty value. Most of them relate to the well-harmonised concepts of urbanisation, education level, age, etc.
3. You and I agree on the interpretation of DDI regarding a very small number of concepts (i.e. study, study no, question, question text, variable representation type, etc.) so that we can claim that we created a questionbank tool that is DDI compliant and technically capable to work on the entire EU level.
4. I write an extension package for retroharmonize and provide a reproducible workflow.

This can be spilled off into 1 or 2 publications, and if the Turku postdoc wants to be involved, he can, too.  One would be an interpretation of DDI for questionbanks, and one potentially a R Journal publication for making an R library to do the work.  The EU dimension of our work is the questionbank, not the rather limited surveys, so I think we must put in a few days of work to have some questions in all EU official languages.  What could be a great plus, and overlaps with our new project, is to perhaps add a few minority language items, too.


Aside from this, we need to come up with a model for the live music. For this, I would have a two-level approach, as the SSSA postdoc is not yet proven.

Live music valuation

1. The postdoc a.s.a.p comes up with an economically literate review of your live music census in the context of music economics.
2. If this work is competently done, I can make the postdoc a co-author to publish in English or a general valuation model developed together with Eszter Kabai, as a third author, and we can work our general model aligned with whatever aspect your postdoc finds on live music in particular. You can motivate the postdoc with almost immediate publication opportunities, but only if he or she proves to be an asset and not a liability to the work.
3. Our general valuation model has very clear variable descriptions, and these will be matched against administrative and questionnaire survey items.
4. Anna will guide your intern regarding the questionnaire elements related to these questions. We already know which will be certainly used, and for those, your intern can start to create English, German, Italian translations.
So this means that you, your intern, Anna, and the new postdoc can start working in parallel.  I think that a very high percentage of our existing surveys can be reused, we just must be mindful that in many cases the base language is not Hungarian but English.

Eviota

Your live music census uses the same methodology that our Eviota software does, which is now also having an opportunity to an academic book chapter. Regarding the academic KPIs, this is a really successful coincidence, because I believe that this can lead to 2-3 academic publications, given that we use the very same software tool and methodology for economic impact analysis and  environmental impact analysis.

I would very much suggest a minimal re-run of your census, because I think that to make it work with Evitoa it will be probably less work to re-run it then to ex post recode your collected data, though who knows: your data must conform to NACE and CPA codes.

For a re-run, in Slovakia, I would aim for Kosice as Bratislava is too big for that.  One way to do this could be to define a Slovak sample in CAP that is over-sampling Kosice, or adds a mixed mode extra Kosice component. In Hungary, I would suggest Debrecen, Pécs, or Szeged, which are mid-sized towns with some music activities, as Budapest would not be feasible.  Or, but this is an issue of its own, to think of a Budapest XI. district or Budapest V. district analysis. It would be very logical to do a run on a location where HearDis is working, too.

On environmental analysis, it would be very important to get access to bookkeeping data of SOZA, ALOADED, MIH and some of their partners, HEARDIS, etc. Maybe Slnko records in Slovakia, who will be working with us.

Best regards,
Daniel

So, we should be discussing the following aspects of the work:


- generally the DDI model that we put into Wikibase (this could be a scientific publication of its own), i.e, how we define "question", "question text",  "study", "study id",  "variable representation type"etc in our system. This should also work for you to be able to create a questionnaire and process with our without our R package the received data.

- looking up existing and established translation (mainly in GESIS); and deciding when new translation is needed.

- organising the translation of labels to new languages

- connecting concrete variable representation (like type of community in Eurobarometer 97.4) to other uses of the same variable; particularly important for harmonised CAP

- adding concepts from thesauri, but by senior experts, not interns. The intern can help in translating the findings into URIs and adding them to Wikibase, but an INTERN must not decide on various aspects of GDP, or royalty income, etc.


We have a lot more than what we put into the system ready to upload, but we want to make sure that the current structure is certainly useful, because restructuring the database is many days of work ex post.


Best regards,

Daniel

Subject: Processing, conceptualising and categorizing a questionnaire

Hi Anna,

Please start working on adding these questions to a new part of the questionbank.

https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Rg_AAajImNJmnLCjcnUkEVi9rZWKWNSMmOQyoAnuCfc/edit?usp=sharing

1. For each new question, create a row in the spreadsheet with the Hungarian label.
2. Add a variable name following the first examples.  No problem if the var name is not great, I will change them as needed. Always add (CAP) to the variable short label. Create a snake_case_version as an alias.
3. Add the question text as description

We will discuss the rest, but try to understand the representation base type and three representation forms, and try to match these up with the questions.
- numeric if the question only wants a number.
- yes-no-selector with decline option if the answer is yes/have/approve no/don't have/disapprove or decline to answer
- a broader binary base type if only two answer options are possible excluding do not know and decline to answer.
- category base type if the answer options come from a controlled vocabulary but without hierarchy, or direction.
- scale base type if the answer categories represent some ordinal scale, like totally agree, agree, neither agree nor disagree, disagree, totally disagree, or small, medium, large.

For now just please transcribe all question texts, question numbers, give them a temporary short label and var name, and try to mark the simpler representation types.

With time questions, if the time is not explicitly asked like on 1989-10-23, but on categories like yesterday, last week, etc. then treat the time as time appellation with a scale or category.

For each answer option we will need concepts as items. That will take some time, but let us take stock of our questions, organise them to groups, and ask James for feedback before we research thesauri and start looking up concepts.

Best regards ,
Daniel

@Arianna Martinelli&lt;mailto:Arianna.Martinelli@santannapisa.it&gt;, please ask Olga to read our deliverable D1.1 before our onboarding call on Thursday (attached). It would also be beneficial if she did a preliminary query on economic valuation models for live music.

  *

James

Subject: RE: request for indicative price



Dear James,



Please find my answers. The circle of information as below reflect the research frame of 2019 yet the basic approaches hardly changed during the years in order to ensure comparability.



  *   F2F CAPI
  *   According to the agreement, the basic population investigated as a minimum was the Hungarian population aged 15-69, at the same time, the commitment referred to the ESSNet Culture recommendations and undertook to follow the best practice. ESSNet's recommendation was to examine the 15-75 age group as a minimum, but preferably the age group older than six years.
  *   We therefore supplemented the primary base population with the 10-14 year old age group on the one hand, and the 70+ year old age group on the other hand. The sociodemographic characteristics of the basic population were defined on the basis of the data of the 2011 Census for easier comparability with the previous surveys, and taking into account the data of the later microcensus would have caused a very small, unnoticeable deviation from this. So the sampling frame is the population aged 10+ living in Hungarian households. Since the basic unit of analysis is the individual, we accordingly took a personal sample (as in previous years).
  *   The method used was the disproportionately stratified random sample, in which the 10-14-year-old and 70+-year-old age groups were present in different (lower) proportions than in the basic population.
  *   The settlements were selected randomly. Within the settlement, households were selected by random walking. Within a household, the interviewees were selected according to quota criteria. The 10-17-year-olds came from households where we also asked someone from among the adults. (Sampling aimed at random selection of minors would have increased the costs of the research to an unrealistic extent.) The selection of the minor respondents was made with the consent of the parents. We asked a maximum of one adult and one minor in a household.
  *   The sample consisted of three parts: 1) base sample aged 15-69: N=~1000 people; 2) boosted sample of 10-14 year olds: N=~50 people; 3) boosted sample of 70+ year olds: N=~50 people.
  *   In the sample, marginal quotas are applied taking into account the following aspects: region, type of settlement, gender and age. In determining the quotas, we used the data of the latest Population Census.



I do hope that above information would support your job.



Best regards,



Tamás

Pursuant the grant agreement process, we’d like to ask a question about surveying mode. While the proposal was well-evaluated, the reviewers expressed concern about the fieldwork cost. We recognize that face-to-face surveying remains the “gold standard” for high-quality data; however, quite a bit has been learned during the SERISS (https://seriss.eu/) and CRONOS projects and the COVID-19 pandemic about effective non-f2f sampling and fieldwork, mode effects and how to compensate for them, etc. As you may have read, the European Social Survey has even announced a forthcoming change in data collection mode from face-to-face interviews to online and paper self-completion surveys (https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/singlenew.html?a=/about/news/essnews0130.html).



Given the rapidly progressing state of the art, we wonder what options Kantar Hoffmann might be able to offer with regard to a mixed-mode, or even entirely self-completion-based, survey. We are happy to keep conversing by email, or alternatively, to set up a call once Daniel is back from holiday later this month.



Again, many thanks, and best regards,

James

Dear Tamás,

I hope that this email finds you well.  I would like to ask an indicative quote from you for a survey to be carried out in January/February 2024.

We would like to replicate the surveys we have conducted in 2015, 2017,2018,2019 with you with mainly the same questionnaire and sampling for comparability, because our work was seen as a best practice by the European Commission and relevant bodies in post-Brexit UK.

We are applying for an EU research and innovation grant with leading experts in this field, the Information Law Research Center of the University of Amsterdam, the University of Turku Data Science Group, the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies, Sinus and my company, and Artisjus and its sister societies.  We would like to show to the European Commission, Eurostat, and the scientific community that our work is not only the best example in this field but it is replicable.

We would like to have indicative budgets from you for the following countries, either separately, or together (if there is a cost saving):

-          Hungary (for replication)  CAPI + online (limited questionnaire, to compare the differences of answers in CAPI and online mode)

Subject: RE: request for indicative price



Dear James,



Please find my answers. The circle of information as below reflect the research frame of 2019 yet the basic approaches hardly changed during the years in order to ensure comparability.



  *   F2F CAPI
  *   According to the agreement, the basic population investigated as a minimum was the Hungarian population aged 15-69, at the same time, the commitment referred to the ESSNet Culture recommendations and undertook to follow the best practice. ESSNet's recommendation was to examine the 15-75 age group as a minimum, but preferably the age group older than six years.
  *   We therefore supplemented the primary base population with the 10-14 year old age group on the one hand, and the 70+ year old age group on the other hand. The sociodemographic characteristics of the basic population were defined on the basis of the data of the 2011 Census for easier comparability with the previous surveys, and taking into account the data of the later microcensus would have caused a very small, unnoticeable deviation from this. So the sampling frame is the population aged 10+ living in Hungarian households. Since the basic unit of analysis is the individual, we accordingly took a personal sample (as in previous years).
  *   The method used was the disproportionately stratified random sample, in which the 10-14-year-old and 70+-year-old age groups were present in different (lower) proportions than in the basic population.
  *   The settlements were selected randomly. Within the settlement, households were selected by random walking. Within a household, the interviewees were selected according to quota criteria. The 10-17-year-olds came from households where we also asked someone from among the adults. (Sampling aimed at random selection of minors would have increased the costs of the research to an unrealistic extent.) The selection of the minor respondents was made with the consent of the parents. We asked a maximum of one adult and one minor in a household.
  *   The sample consisted of three parts: 1) base sample aged 15-69: N=~1000 people; 2) boosted sample of 10-14 year olds: N=~50 people; 3) boosted sample of 70+ year olds: N=~50 people.
  *   In the sample, marginal quotas are applied taking into account the following aspects: region, type of settlement, gender and age. In determining the quotas, we used the data of the latest Population Census.



I do hope that above information would support your job.



Best regards,



Tamás

Dear Mr. Tamás,



I hope that you have been well, and I apologize for the long delay in replying to your indicative cost quote. As always, it took the European Commission a bit of time to evaluate the proposal. Fortunately, however, we were chosen to be invited to the grant agreement process. Currently, we’re reworking the proposal text into an agreement.



So, first off: thank you for your fast response to our initial inquiry, which was very helpful in putting our proposal on a solid enough foundation to be chosen!



Pursuant the grant agreement process, we’d like to ask a question about surveying mode. While the proposal was well-evaluated, the reviewers expressed concern about the fieldwork cost. We recognize that face-to-face surveying remains the “gold standard” for high-quality data; however, quite a bit has been learned during the SERISS (https://seriss.eu/) and CRONOS projects and the COVID-19 pandemic about effective non-f2f sampling and fieldwork, mode effects and how to compensate for them, etc. As you may have read, the European Social Survey has even announced a forthcoming change in data collection mode from face-to-face interviews to online and paper self-completion surveys (https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/singlenew.html?a=/about/news/essnews0130.html).



Given the rapidly progressing state of the art, we wonder what options Kantar Hoffmann might be able to offer with regard to a mixed-mode, or even entirely self-completion-based, survey. A probability rather than quota sample would still be strongly preferred. We are happy to keep conversing by email, or alternatively, to set up a call once Daniel is back from holiday later this month.



Again, many thanks, and best regards,

James

Dear Tamás,

I hope that this email finds you well.  I would like to ask an indicative quote from you for a survey to be carried out in January/February 2024.

We would like to replicate the surveys we have conducted in 2015, 2017,2018,2019 with you with mainly the same questionnaire and sampling for comparability, because our work was seen as a best practice by the European Commission and relevant bodies in post-Brexit UK.

We are applying for an EU research and innovation grant with leading experts in this field, the Information Law Research Center of the University of Amsterdam, the University of Turku Data Science Group, the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies, Sinus and my company, and Artisjus and its sister societies.  We would like to show to the European Commission, Eurostat, and the scientific community that our work is not only the best example in this field but it is replicable.

We would like to have indicative budgets from you for the following countries, either separately, or together (if there is a cost saving):

-          Hungary (for replication)  CAPI + online (limited questionnaire, to compare the differences of answers in CAPI and online mode)

-          Bulgaria  CAPI

-          Germany  CAPI

-          Italy CAPI

You can assume that the questionnaire, the sample design and all parameters are the same, though we believe that some questionnaire blocks will have to be changed, as we are merging a similar research done in 12 other countries with a slightly different questionnaire and our research project. For the online mode, I think that our questionnaire is too long, but we would use the most important question blocks for comparing the properties of the two modes.  So I think that we can count for a half-length questionnaire in the online mode.

Subject: RE: request for indicative price



Dear James,



Please find my answers. The circle of information as below reflect the research frame of 2019 yet the basic approaches hardly changed during the years in order to ensure comparability.



* F2F CAPI
* According to the agreement, the basic population investigated as a minimum was the Hungarian population aged 15-69, at the same time, the commitment referred to the ESSNet Culture recommendations and undertook to follow the best practice. ESSNet's recommendation was to examine the 15-75 age group as a minimum, but preferably the age group older than six years.
* We therefore supplemented the primary base population with the 10-14 year old age group on the one hand, and the 70+ year old age group on the other hand. The sociodemographic characteristics of the basic population were defined on the basis of the data of the 2011 Census for easier comparability with the previous surveys, and taking into account the data of the later microcensus would have caused a very small, unnoticeable deviation from this. So the sampling frame is the population aged 10+ living in Hungarian households. Since the basic unit of analysis is the individual, we accordingly took a personal sample (as in previous years).
* The method used was the disproportionately stratified random sample, in which the 10-14-year-old and 70+-year-old age groups were present in different (lower) proportions than in the basic population.
* The settlements were selected randomly. Within the settlement, households were selected by random walking. Within a household, the interviewees were selected according to quota criteria. The 10-17-year-olds came from households where we also asked someone from among the adults. (Sampling aimed at random selection of minors would have increased the costs of the research to an unrealistic extent.) The selection of the minor respondents was made with the consent of the parents. We asked a maximum of one adult and one minor in a household.
* The sample consisted of three parts: 1) base sample aged 15-69: N=~1000 people; 2) boosted sample of 10-14 year olds: N=~50 people; 3) boosted sample of 70+ year olds: N=~50 people.
* In the sample, marginal quotas are applied taking into account the following aspects: region, type of settlement, gender and age. In determining the quotas, we used the data of the latest Population Census.



I do hope that above information would support your job.



Best regards,



Tamás

Pursuant the grant agreement process, we’d like to ask a question about surveying mode. While the proposal was well-evaluated, the reviewers expressed concern about the fieldwork cost. We recognize that face-to-face surveying remains the “gold standard” for high-quality data; however, quite a bit has been learned during the SERISS (https://seriss.eu/) and CRONOS projects and the COVID-19 pandemic about effective non-f2f sampling and fieldwork, mode effects and how to compensate for them, etc. As you may have read, the European Social Survey has even announced a forthcoming change in data collection mode from face-to-face interviews to online and paper self-completion surveys (https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/singlenew.html?a=/about/news/essnews0130.html).



Given the rapidly progressing state of the art, we wonder what options Kantar Hoffmann might be able to offer with regard to a mixed-mode, or even entirely self-completion-based, survey. ### Re: request for indicative price {#email-789}

**From:** James Rhys Edwards &lt;JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&gt;  
**To:** Isabella Tautscher &lt;Isabella.Tautscher@sinus-institut.de&gt;, Falus Tamás &lt;tamas.falus@kantar-hoffmann.hu&gt;  
**Cc:** Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;, Roszjár Attila &lt;attila.roszjar@kantar-hoffmann.hu&gt;  
**Date:** 11/27/2024 15:02:59

<!-- source: OpenMuse_20261009-2156/OpenMuse/messages/202411271502-Re_ request for indicative price-698.txt -->

Hi Tamas and Attila,

Here is the 'formal' briefing! Please let us know if you have any questions.

Best regards,
James

==

Dear Kantar-Hoffmann team,
I am writing with an inquiry on survey research on behalf of the Horizon Europe project Open Music Europe (www.openmuse.eu&lt;http://www.openmuse.eu&gt;). Our aim is to better assess the economic and non-economic contributions of music to European society.To this end, we will conduct a nationally representative music audience survey within Germany, Hungary, Italy, and Slovakia. The parameters are as follows:

  *
Fieldwork timeframe — two possibilities:
     *   Mid- to late January 2025, OR
     *   Rolling sample, January to March 2025 – open to discussion
  *   Target countries: Germany, Hungary, Italy, Slovakia
  *   Probability sample – sampling frame / method to-be-discussed with fieldwork provider
  *   Age: 15 or 16 and above, depending on cost – to-be-discussed with fieldwork partner
  *   Mode: CAPI or mixed-mode (CAPI, CATI, and/or CAWI) – to-be-discussed with fieldwork provider – mode need not be identical in all countries
  *   Sample size: min. N=1000 per country
  *   Length: max 30 min
  *   Boosts:
     *   Attended a live music concert / event, past 3 months: N=250 per country. Incidence rate in 2013 was approx. 11% (EU average).
     *   Earned any income from any musical activities, past 12 months: N=100 per country on best-effort basis. Incidence rate is unknown, but expected to be low.

We would like two cost quotes:

  *   WITH questionnaire programming and hosting. Outputs = quality controlled dataset in CSV / SAV formats and technical report detailing the sampling frame / method, fieldwork procedures, data quality control procedures, etc.
  *    FIELDWORK ONLY (we would program and host the questionnaire). Output = technical report detailing the sampling frame / method, fieldwork procedures, etc.

As our project is funded by the European Commission, we must justify best service for cost, and thus request you send along some material on your experience conducting multi-country CAPI or mixed-mode studies.
Is this the kind of project that might interest you? If so, we would greatly appreciate the chance to discuss by phone or email.
Thank you, and best regards,

Subject: RE: request for indicative price



Dear James,



Please find my answers. The circle of information as below reflect the research frame of 2019 yet the basic approaches hardly changed during the years in order to ensure comparability.



  1.  F2F CAPI
  2.  According to the agreement, the basic population investigated as a minimum was the Hungarian population aged 15-69, at the same time, the commitment referred to the ESSNet Culture recommendations and undertook to follow the best practice. ESSNet's recommendation was to examine the 15-75 age group as a minimum, but preferably the age group older than six years.
  3.  We therefore supplemented the primary base population with the 10-14 year old age group on the one hand, and the 70+ year old age group on the other hand. The sociodemographic characteristics of the basic population were defined on the basis of the data of the 2011 Census for easier comparability with the previous surveys, and taking into account the data of the later microcensus would have caused a very small, unnoticeable deviation from this. So the sampling frame is the population aged 10+ living in Hungarian households. Since the basic unit of analysis is the individual, we accordingly took a personal sample (as in previous years).
  4.  The method used was the disproportionately stratified random sample, in which the 10-14-year-old and 70+-year-old age groups were present in different (lower) proportions than in the basic population.
  5.  The settlements were selected randomly. Within the settlement, households were selected by random walking. Within a household, the interviewees were selected according to quota criteria. The 10-17-year-olds came from households where we also asked someone from among the adults. (Sampling aimed at random selection of minors would have increased the costs of the research to an unrealistic extent.) The selection of the minor respondents was made with the consent of the parents. We asked a maximum of one adult and one minor in a household.
  6.  The sample consisted of three parts: 1) base sample aged 15-69: N=~1000 people; 2) boosted sample of 10-14 year olds: N=~50 people; 3) boosted sample of 70+ year olds: N=~50 people.
  7.  In the sample, marginal quotas are applied taking into account the following aspects: region, type of settlement, gender and age. In determining the quotas, we used the data of the latest Population Census.



I do hope that above information would support your job.



Best regards,



Tamás

Dear Mr. Tamás,



I hope that you have been well, and I apologize for the long delay in replying to your indicative cost quote. As always, it took the European Commission a bit of time to evaluate the proposal. Fortunately, however, we were chosen to be invited to the grant agreement process. Currently, we’re reworking the proposal text into an agreement.



So, first off: thank you for your fast response to our initial inquiry, which was very helpful in putting our proposal on a solid enough foundation to be chosen!



Pursuant the grant agreement process, we’d like to ask a question about surveying mode. While the proposal was well-evaluated, the reviewers expressed concern about the fieldwork cost. We recognize that face-to-face surveying remains the “gold standard” for high-quality data; however, quite a bit has been learned during the SERISS (https://seriss.eu/) and CRONOS projects and the COVID-19 pandemic about effective non-f2f sampling and fieldwork, mode effects and how to compensate for them, etc. As you may have read, the European Social Survey has even announced a forthcoming change in data collection mode from face-to-face interviews to online and paper self-completion surveys (https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/singlenew.html?a=/about/news/essnews0130.html).



Given the rapidly progressing state of the art, we wonder what options Kantar Hoffmann might be able to offer with regard to a mixed-mode, or even entirely self-completion-based, survey. A probability rather than quota sample would still be strongly preferred. We are happy to keep conversing by email, or alternatively, to set up a call once Daniel is back from holiday later this month.



Again, many thanks, and best regards,

James

  1.  basic sample size: N=1000 / country; representative sample of people aged 15-69
  2.  boosted sample: N=100 / country; aged 10-14; overweighting younger groups (similarly to our prior work) and using the same selection of participants.

  4.  services of Kantar Hoffmann: questionnaire, translation, scripting, pilot, fieldwork in 4 countries, fieldwork supervision in 4 countries, fieldwork quality control, data cleaning, data supply according to the agreed data frame (no analysis and reporting included)

     *   Germany: EUR 64,900 (+VAT if applicable); it includes full supervision from Hungary by Kantar Hoffmann
     *   Italy: EUR 59,900 (+VAT if applicable); it includes full supervision from Hungary by Kantar Hoffmann

  1.  basic sample size: N=1000; representative sample of people aged 15-69
  2.  boosted sample: N=100; aged 10-14; overweighting younger groups
  3.  Questionnaire: max. 25 min. long questionnaire, we would use the most important question blocks for comparing the properties of the two modes
  4.  services of Kantar Hoffmann: questionnaire, scripting, pilot, fieldwork, data cleaning, data supply according to the agreed data frame (no analysis and reporting included)
  5.  Indicative budget for 2024 (only Hungary): EUR 8190 (+VAT if applicable)





Please note that we are not in the position to guarantee fixed prices for 2024 even if the research frame did not change at all. So the total budget I gave is indicative indeed.



if you have other questions or suggestions I am at your disposal.



Best regards,



Tamás

Dear Tamás,

I hope that this email finds you well.  I would like to ask an indicative quote from you for a survey to be carried out in January/February 2024.

We would like to replicate the surveys we have conducted in 2015, 2017,2018,2019 with you with mainly the same questionnaire and sampling for comparability, because our work was seen as a best practice by the European Commission and relevant bodies in post-Brexit UK.

We are applying for an EU research and innovation grant with leading experts in this field, the Information Law Research Center of the University of Amsterdam, the University of Turku Data Science Group, the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies, Sinus and my company, and Artisjus and its sister societies.  We would like to show to the European Commission, Eurostat, and the scientific community that our work is not only the best example in this field but it is replicable.

We would like to have indicative budgets from you for the following countries, either separately, or together (if there is a cost saving):

-          Hungary (for replication)  CAPI + online (limited questionnaire, to compare the differences of answers in CAPI and online mode)

-          Bulgaria  CAPI

-          Germany  CAPI

-          Italy CAPI

You can assume that the questionnaire, the sample design and all parameters are the same, though we believe that some questionnaire blocks will have to be changed, as we are merging a similar research done in 12 other countries with a slightly different questionnaire and our research project.   The sample size is n=1000, with overweighting younger groups (similarly to our prior work) and using the same selection of participants.

For the online mode, I think that our questionnaire is too long, but we would use the most important question blocks for comparing the properties of the two modes.  So I think that we can count for a half-length questionnaire in the online mode.

I'm writing to connect on the topic of background music / in-store music / public performances of recorded music, which SOZA indicated at the Bergfest as a priority for the forthcoming surveying.

SINUS will include a few questions on this topic in the general population survey we will conduct in January. However, there are some questions that this type of survey can't answer: e.g., the economic added value of background music (hypothetical questions like "how much more would you pay for a cup of coffee in a shop with great music" do not work in practice).

The HEARDIS research — which will be conducted in-store — could be a much better vector to get at these questions.

Hello Fabio,


  1.  I initialised a new repository for your code only, and I put the auto-generated documentation so that Joost can also review your work, and Anna can help with some documentation and testing. It is here: https://music.dataobservatory.eu/documents/aloaded/  [ The source code is hidden and you can see it, but not even Joost or Anna. This makes it secure that no ALOADED data will be revealed; the documentation will be visible for Joost, Anna, and ALOADED colleagues.]
  2.  The variable documentation is here, it is handled by Anna and you, and it can be read by people who do not write code: https://github.com/dataobservatory-eu/datacatalogue.  It is a public repository, there are no secrets here.
Your code (with my supervision and help) need to placed in an R package.  Why? Because this way it can be transported to an ALOADED or SOZA computer, and the code can be run there, far from your computer.

How we ensure that it will run on any computer?
- You make explicit any package reference you use (see the R files, not for Joost and Anna), it is simple, for example @importFrom dplyr mutate makes clear that the mutate function must be installed for the ALOADED computer from the dpyr package so that they can run it.
- In the test/ library, we write automated tests to ensure that as you develop your data pipeline, it runs correctly on all platforms (our unit tests are running on Windows, Mac, Linux machines.)

To make the work reviewable and understandable for ALOADED and SOZA colleagues, and for Joost:
-  Each new function that you write (a series of scripts, for example, to establish the average price per territory for a DSP), should be a separate file in the R folder. If you document it correctly, it will have a documentation like this: get_aloaded_price_data&lt;https://music.dataobservatory.eu/documents/aloaded/reference/get_aloaded_price_data.html&gt;  [this is only for those who run R]
- Each output, for example, a price comparison, or the regression that Joost asked, should be in a 'vignette' (markdown plus a notebook of your code) like this:
Price.html&lt;https://music.dataobservatory.eu/documents/aloaded/articles/Price.html&gt;

If you get used to this environment, we will be ready to run this code probably already in January on a large scale in both SOZA and ALOADED.

I set this repo up with testing, creating the price filtering, and the chart in about 90 minutes. In my opinion, you can do what Joost asked in a couple of hours, and the extra documentation burden will pay off even in 1-2 months, because there are no scripts written in early December that you remember perfectly well in February.

Best regards,
Daniel

Generally, in order to comply with FAIR and OPA, you should follow the structure of our repositories like this one (the README has invisible comments, only visible in Quarto on how to do it.)

Like I said on Thursday, these variables are based on DDEX, which is a standard based on the ISO standards, not only ISRC and ISWC, but several data exchange standards. So the variables that you could not figure out will be described in DDEX.  What I will ask from Anna on Monday is to place into the bibliography and our open citation database all DDEX standards (their website is not very user friendly) so that you can look up the missing variables.  When we are lost, we will ask Stef's data engineer. You can find the link to two of the DDEX standards in the bib file and connected Zotero online citation database, Anna will add the rest.

Please @Fábio Generoso Vieira&lt;mailto:f.v.vieira@uva.nl&gt; @AnnA Mester&lt;mailto:anna.mester@reprex.nl&gt; both fork this repository and further metadata references and definitions here: https://github.com/dataobservatory-eu/datacatalogue/

Best regards,
Daniel

Dear Fabio,

Thank you very much for your very neat work.  I could not replicate your error, but I have some suspicions.  Here are a few very small remarks, they will help you later.

Whenever you add a new function to a package that relies on a function from another package, for example dplyr::select(), you have to do to things:

- at the first time use of the dplyr package, usethis::use_package("dplyr"),
- at the use of the select function, in the @importFrom field, dplyr select

You do not have to this with packages only used for the vignettes, in this case, for rvest.  However, it may still cause problems. There is a recommended practice for this:

- at the first time use of the dplyr package, usethis::use_package("rvest", type="Suggests"),
in which case the DESCRIPTION file will contain the information that while the package functions works without rvest, but you cannot do everything shown here without rvest.

So, please open the DESCRIPTION file of the aloaded package and

- add your name next to mine
- see how the DESCRIPTION is structured
- if any other package that you used in the vignettes is missing, f.e. tidyr, run
usethis::use_package("tidyr", type="Suggests"), which will update the DESCRIPTION file.

Whenever you make a change to a package, give it a new version number. So currently with my latest edits, I renamed the version from 0.1.0001.   Either with devtools::build() or the build/ install buttons make sure that you install on your computer the latest version of the package.

In my opinion, it will work in your computer. However, if not, then start a clean session, with a clean environment. If it does not work properly, send a new error issue after with the output of the sessionInfo() command.

The most important use of the sessionInfo() is to show if you are using the 0.1.0001. If R still uses your previous version (which does not have your new function!) then obviously it will not work.

Now, regarding your new vignette, I think that it is a very neat work, and this is not necessary for such trivial tasks.  You should write a vignette Rmd or a Quarto qmd file for things that need to be discussed with ALOADED, Joost, me, or somebody else.  But if it is only me, then only if it is a complex problem.

So, we will need such a file to show your results with the data, or how you put it together, but how you download the Spotify launch dates is not necessary. However, it was a very neat work, and I really appreciate that you took the time to do it.

Regarding the way you work with rvest, I think that we can have a separate R consultation on how to do it more efficiently.  Generally, if you are already a bit familiar with its use, this extractor makes it very easy to locate which document child you want to scrape&gt; https://rvest.tidyverse.org/articles/harvesting-the-web.html

However, there are more efficient ways, for example, if a page has only one table, then you can programatically find the only table and select it.  But I think this is worth learning only if we will have to rely more often on rvest.

I do not know what caused the problem with you, but I think some versioning. If this problem persists, than just change the chunk that makes it stop to eval=FALSE and I will take a look. Which brings me to a last issue.

In my code, each chunk has a name&gt;
```{r filtering}
blabla
```
Not in yours:
```{R}
```
This is syntactically correct, however, it makes debugging very difficult. If you name the chunks like I do, then you get an error message that, for example, the Price vignette stopped at the plot chunk.  In your case, it will say that a vignette stopped at the unnamed-12 chunk, which is far harder to detect.

I hope this helps, if not, then just make the chunk that makes a problem (plotting) eval=FALSE.  I cannot think of any reason now other than package versions , because everything worked very well on my end.

Best regards,

Hi all,



I hope you're all well!



I'm writing to connect on the topic of background music / in-store music / public performances of recorded music, which SOZA indicated at the Bergfest as a priority for the forthcoming surveying.



SINUS will include a few questions on this topic in the general population survey we will conduct in January. However, there are some questions that this type of survey can't answer: e.g., the economic added value of background music (hypothetical questions like "how much more would you pay for a cup of coffee in a shop with great music" do not work in practice).



The HEARDIS research — which will be conducted in-store — could be a much better vector to get at these questions.



If we could get representatives from both partners into either the WP3 meeting on Friday at 9am or into a separate a call next week, that would be fantastic. We'd like to:

  *   Get a more precise view of exactly what SOZA needs / wants to learn about background music

  *   Run through the SINUS survey questions on background music

  *   Check in re: the progress of the HEARDIS research design and your fieldwork plans

My schedule next week is flexible so far, with the exception of Weds afternoon.



Thank you and best regards,

James

Dear all,

The ECHOES Policy Event 'Toward the Cultural Heritage Cloud' and a workshop on 'Onboarding communities into the Cultural Heritage Cloud' will take place in Brussels and online on 12 - 13 December 2024, and will officially launch the European Collaborative Cloud for cultural heritage!

The Cloud is envisaged as a shared platform for heritage professionals, scientists and researchers to access data, innovative scientific and training resources and advanced digital tools in collaboration with and for the cultural heritage communities, so it may be of interest to you as a Member of the EuropeanaTech Community.

Find out more and register: https://www.echoes-eccch.eu/registration-opens-for-echoes-policy-event/

Best,

Antoine

Hi Tamas and Attila,



Here is the 'formal' briefing! Please let us know if you have any questions.



Best regards,

James



==



Dear Kantar-Hoffmann team,

I am writing with an inquiry on survey research on behalf of the Horizon Europe project Open Music Europe (www.openmuse.eu&lt;http://www.openmuse.eu&gt;). Our aim is to better assess the economic and non-economic contributions of music to European society.To this end, we will conduct a nationally representative music audience survey within Germany, Hungary, Italy, and Slovakia. The parameters are as follows:

·        Fieldwork timeframe — two possibilities:

o   Mid- to late January 2025, OR

o   Rolling sample, January to March 2025 – open to discussion

·        Target countries: Germany, Hungary, Italy, Slovakia

·        Probability sample – sampling frame / method to-be-discussed with fieldwork provider

·        Age: 15 or 16 and above, depending on cost – to-be-discussed with fieldwork partner

·        Mode: CAPI or mixed-mode (CAPI, CATI, and/or CAWI) – to-be-discussed with fieldwork provider – mode need not be identical in all countries

·        Sample size: min. N=1000 per country

·        Length: max 30 min

·        Boosts:

o   Attended a live music concert / event, past 3 months: N=250 per country. Incidence rate in 2013 was approx. 11% (EU average).

o   Earned any income from any musical activities, past 12 months: N=100 per country on best-effort basis. Incidence rate is unknown, but expected to be low.

We would like two cost quotes:

Subject: RE: request for indicative price



Dear James,



Please find my answers. The circle of information as below reflect the research frame of 2019 yet the basic approaches hardly changed during the years in order to ensure comparability.



  1.  F2F CAPI
  2.  According to the agreement, the basic population investigated as a minimum was the Hungarian population aged 15-69, at the same time, the commitment referred to the ESSNet Culture recommendations and undertook to follow the best practice. ESSNet's recommendation was to examine the 15-75 age group as a minimum, but preferably the age group older than six years.
  3.  We therefore supplemented the primary base population with the 10-14 year old age group on the one hand, and the 70+ year old age group on the other hand. The sociodemographic characteristics of the basic population were defined on the basis of the data of the 2011 Census for easier comparability with the previous surveys, and taking into account the data of the later microcensus would have caused a very small, unnoticeable deviation from this. So the sampling frame is the population aged 10+ living in Hungarian households. Since the basic unit of analysis is the individual, we accordingly took a personal sample (as in previous years).
  4.  The method used was the disproportionately stratified random sample, in which the 10-14-year-old and 70+-year-old age groups were present in different (lower) proportions than in the basic population.
  5.  The settlements were selected randomly. Within the settlement, households were selected by random walking. Within a household, the interviewees were selected according to quota criteria. The 10-17-year-olds came from households where we also asked someone from among the adults. (Sampling aimed at random selection of minors would have increased the costs of the research to an unrealistic extent.) The selection of the minor respondents was made with the consent of the parents. We asked a maximum of one adult and one minor in a household.
  6.  The sample consisted of three parts: 1) base sample aged 15-69: N=~1000 people; 2) boosted sample of 10-14 year olds: N=~50 people; 3) boosted sample of 70+ year olds: N=~50 people.
  7.  In the sample, marginal quotas are applied taking into account the following aspects: region, type of settlement, gender and age. In determining the quotas, we used the data of the latest Population Census.



I do hope that above information would support your job.



Best regards,



Tamás

Dear Mr. Tamás,



I hope that you have been well, and I apologize for the long delay in replying to your indicative cost quote. As always, it took the European Commission a bit of time to evaluate the proposal. Fortunately, however, we were chosen to be invited to the grant agreement process. Currently, we’re reworking the proposal text into an agreement.



So, first off: thank you for your fast response to our initial inquiry, which was very helpful in putting our proposal on a solid enough foundation to be chosen!



Pursuant the grant agreement process, we’d like to ask a question about surveying mode. While the proposal was well-evaluated, the reviewers expressed concern about the fieldwork cost. We recognize that face-to-face surveying remains the “gold standard” for high-quality data; however, quite a bit has been learned during the SERISS (https://seriss.eu/) and CRONOS projects and the COVID-19 pandemic about effective non-f2f sampling and fieldwork, mode effects and how to compensate for them, etc. As you may have read, the European Social Survey has even announced a forthcoming change in data collection mode from face-to-face interviews to online and paper self-completion surveys (https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/singlenew.html?a=/about/news/essnews0130.html).



Given the rapidly progressing state of the art, we wonder what options Kantar Hoffmann might be able to offer with regard to a mixed-mode, or even entirely self-completion-based, survey. A probability rather than quota sample would still be strongly preferred. We are happy to keep conversing by email, or alternatively, to set up a call once Daniel is back from holiday later this month.



Again, many thanks, and best regards,

James

We would like to replicate the surveys we have conducted in 2015, 2017,2018,2019 with you with mainly the same questionnaire and sampling for comparability, because our work was seen as a best practice by the European Commission and relevant bodies in post-Brexit UK.

We are applying for an EU research and innovation grant with leading experts in this field, the Information Law Research Center of the University of Amsterdam, the University of Turku Data Science Group, the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies, Sinus and my company, and Artisjus and its sister societies.  We would like to show to the European Commission, Eurostat, and the scientific community that our work is not only the best example in this field but it is replicable.

Dear all,

The ECHOES Policy Event 'Toward the Cultural Heritage Cloud' and a workshop on 'Onboarding communities into the Cultural Heritage Cloud' will take place in Brussels and online on 12 - 13 December 2024, and will officially launch the European Collaborative Cloud for cultural heritage!

The Cloud is envisaged as a shared platform for heritage professionals, scientists and researchers to access data, innovative scientific and training resources and advanced digital tools in collaboration with and for the cultural heritage communities, so it may be of interest to you as a Member of the EuropeanaTech Community.

Find out more and register: https://www.echoes-eccch.eu/registration-opens-for-echoes-policy-event/

Best,

Antoine

==



Dear Kantar-Hoffmann team,

I am writing with an inquiry on survey research on behalf of the Horizon Europe project Open Music Europe (www.openmuse.eu&lt;http://www.openmuse.eu&gt;). Our aim is to better assess the economic and non-economic contributions of music to European society.To this end, we will conduct a nationally representative music audience survey within Germany, Hungary, Italy, and Slovakia. The parameters are as follows:

•        Fieldwork timeframe — two possibilities:

o   Mid- to late January 2025, OR

o   Rolling sample, January to March 2025 – open to discussion

•        Target countries: Germany, Hungary, Italy, Slovakia

•        Probability sample – sampling frame / method to-be-discussed with fieldwork provider

•        Age: 15 or 16 and above, depending on cost – to-be-discussed with fieldwork partner

•        Mode: CAPI or mixed-mode (CAPI, CATI, and/or CAWI) – to-be-discussed with fieldwork provider – mode need not be identical in all countries

•        Sample size: min. N=1000 per country

•        Length: max 30 min

•        Boosts:

o   Attended a live music concert / event, past 3 months: N=250 per country. Incidence rate in 2013 was approx. 11% (EU average).

o   Earned any income from any musical activities, past 12 months: N=100 per country on best-effort basis. Incidence rate is unknown, but expected to be low.

We would like two cost quotes:

•        WITH questionnaire programming and hosting. Outputs = quality controlled dataset in CSV / SAV formats and technical report detailing the sampling frame / method, fieldwork procedures, data quality control procedures, etc.

•         FIELDWORK ONLY (we would program and host the questionnaire). Output = technical report detailing the sampling frame / method, fieldwork procedures, etc.

As our project is funded by the European Commission, we must justify best service for cost, and thus request you send along some material on your experience conducting multi-country CAPI or mixed-mode studies.

Is this the kind of project that might interest you? If so, we would greatly appreciate the chance to discuss by phone or email.

Thank you, and best regards,

James Edwards
Project Director, Open Music Europe (www.openmuse.eu&lt;http://www.openmuse.eu&gt;)
Senior Research, SINUS Markt- und Sozialforschung GmbH (www.sinus-institut.de&lt;http://www.sinus-institut.de&gt;)

Subject: RE: request for indicative price



Dear James,



Please find my answers. The circle of information as below reflect the research frame of 2019 yet the basic approaches hardly changed during the years in order to ensure comparability.



  1.  F2F CAPI
  2.  According to the agreement, the basic population investigated as a minimum was the Hungarian population aged 15-69, at the same time, the commitment referred to the ESSNet Culture recommendations and undertook to follow the best practice. ESSNet's recommendation was to examine the 15-75 age group as a minimum, but preferably the age group older than six years.
  3.  We therefore supplemented the primary base population with the 10-14 year old age group on the one hand, and the 70+ year old age group on the other hand. The sociodemographic characteristics of the basic population were defined on the basis of the data of the 2011 Census for easier comparability with the previous surveys, and taking into account the data of the later microcensus would have caused a very small, unnoticeable deviation from this. So the sampling frame is the population aged 10+ living in Hungarian households. Since the basic unit of analysis is the individual, we accordingly took a personal sample (as in previous years).
  4.  The method used was the disproportionately stratified random sample, in which the 10-14-year-old and 70+-year-old age groups were present in different (lower) proportions than in the basic population.
  5.  The settlements were selected randomly. Within the settlement, households were selected by random walking. Within a household, the interviewees were selected according to quota criteria. The 10-17-year-olds came from households where we also asked someone from among the adults. (Sampling aimed at random selection of minors would have increased the costs of the research to an unrealistic extent.) The selection of the minor respondents was made with the consent of the parents. We asked a maximum of one adult and one minor in a household.
  6.  The sample consisted of three parts: 1) base sample aged 15-69: N=~1000 people; 2) boosted sample of 10-14 year olds: N=~50 people; 3) boosted sample of 70+ year olds: N=~50 people.
  7.  In the sample, marginal quotas are applied taking into account the following aspects: region, type of settlement, gender and age. In determining the quotas, we used the data of the latest Population Census.



I do hope that above information would support your job.



Best regards,



Tamás

Pursuant the grant agreement process, we’d like to ask a question about surveying mode. While the proposal was well-evaluated, the reviewers expressed concern about the fieldwork cost. We recognize that face-to-face surveying remains the “gold standard” for high-quality data; however, quite a bit has been learned during the SERISS (https://seriss.eu/) and CRONOS projects and the COVID-19 pandemic about effective non-f2f sampling and fieldwork, mode effects and how to compensate for them, etc. As you may have read, the European Social Survey has even announced a forthcoming change in data collection mode from face-to-face interviews to online and paper self-completion surveys (https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/singlenew.html?a=/about/news/essnews0130.html).



Given the rapidly progressing state of the art, we wonder what options Kantar Hoffmann might be able to offer with regard to a mixed-mode, or even entirely self-completion-based, survey. We are happy to keep conversing by email, or alternatively, to set up a call once Daniel is back from holiday later this month.



Again, many thanks, and best regards,

James

We would like to replicate the surveys we have conducted in 2015, 2017,2018,2019 with you with mainly the same questionnaire and sampling for comparability, because our work was seen as a best practice by the European Commission and relevant bodies in post-Brexit UK.

We are applying for an EU research and innovation grant with leading experts in this field, the Information Law Research Center of the University of Amsterdam, the University of Turku Data Science Group, the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies, Sinus and my company, and Artisjus and its sister societies.  We would like to show to the European Commission, Eurostat, and the scientific community that our work is not only the best example in this field but it is replicable.

We would like to have indicative budgets from you for the following countries, either separately, or together (if there is a cost saving):

Dear Eszter and Balazs, Tomas and Richard, and Daniel,

I hope you are all well!

During our prior call on the 2025 cultural access and participation survey, both ARTISJUS and SOZA indicated that this survey data would not be used in legal proceedings (as was originally considered when the project was planned). I'd like to ask you to confirm this.

The reason is that we have been discussing options with fieldwork providers Kantar and Ipsos, and both have urged us to consider online self-completion rather than face-to-face surveying or mixed f2f / telephone.

The traditional consensus in the surveying world is that face-to-face surveying is the modal "gold standard" and yields higher quality data (though this has been disputed in debates post-COVID). If you are planning to use the survey data to back up legal claims, we should stick to f2f / telephone (at least in Hungary and/or Slovakia).

However, if your aim is simply to support business planning with audience insight, our instinct is to go with the mode recommended by the fieldwork providers. We could use the substantial cost saving to: 1) significantly increase the sample per country, and 2) expand the survey to additional countries. Increasing the sample per country would allow more analytical possibilities, while expanding to include additional countries would improve project visibility and impact.

Please let us know as soon as you have a chance. I am also open to an ad-hoc call anytime today, Monday afternoon, or anytime Tuesday.

Thank you and best regards,
James

### Re: 2015 questionnaire {#email-815}

**From:** James Rhys Edwards &lt;JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&gt;  
**To:** Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;, Dr. Kabai Eszter &lt;ekabai@artisjus.com&gt;, Mikš Tomáš &lt;tomas.miks@soza.sk&gt;, Richard Demčák &lt;richard.demcak@soza.sk&gt;, Balázs Huszák &lt;bhuszak@artisjus.com&gt;, Isabella Tautscher &lt;Isabella.Tautscher@sinus-institut.de&gt;, marian.jankovic@soza.sk &lt;Marian.Jankovic@soza.sk&gt;  
**Date:** 12/06/2024 11:11:55

<!-- source: OpenMuse_20261009-2156/OpenMuse/messages/202412061111-Re_ 2015 questionnaire-579.txt -->

Hi Daniel,

Thank you for your considered response. In principle, I agree that CAPI / CATI produces better data.

In practice however, I raise XX points:

First, as you note, nobody in the Consortium has provided guidance on the use of survey data in valuations. We've been asking for inputs in this regard for months. I'm not an economist — nor is SINUS a partner in WP1 — so I am not positioned to conduct a literature review on this topic, much less adapt or develop a model. I've done my best by adapting the UK Live Music Census method, which is simple enough for me to grasp, but I'm not terribly confident in it.

Second, you are correct that online self-completion is poorly suited to collecting complex data, e.g., anything on spending. However, due to our lack of a valuation model, we don't even know what spending figures we would ask for anyway. In my opinion, spending 30-40k per country for "gold standard" data that was not collected with any specified valuation model in mind, is fiscally irresponsible.

Accordingly, I would like to pivot the survey toward simple usage and attitude questions, with a "sustainability" twist. Online is adequate for this. We can expand our scope to include several more countries: at least ES and FR. This would give us 60% EU population coverage and its four largest music markets. We could credibly claim to be an "EU music audience survey".

We can still ask the spending questions we inherited from the 2015 ARTISJUS survey and if ARTISJUS and SOZA prefer, we can still conduct classic CAPI / CATI fieldwork in HU and SK. It is entirely your decision.

However, I won't waste money on DE / IT "valuation" data collected without any particular model in mind. I would prefer to give the Commission something more modest in claim, but broader in scope.

Best regards,
James


________________________________
From: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
Sent: 06 December 2024 10:34
To: James Rhys Edwards &lt;JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&gt;; Dr. Kabai Eszter &lt;ekabai@artisjus.com&gt;; Mikš Tomáš &lt;tomas.miks@soza.sk&gt;; Richard Demčák &lt;richard.demcak@soza.sk&gt;; Balázs Huszák &lt;bhuszak@artisjus.com&gt;; Isabella Tautscher &lt;Isabella.Tautscher@sinus-institut.de&gt;; marian.jankovic@soza.sk &lt;Marian.Jankovic@soza.sk&gt;
Subject: Re: 2015 questionnaire


Dear James, Eszter, and Tomas,
In my opinion, Artisjus’ concern is to verify that an anyhow improved version of our valuations augmented with surveys is indeed the best practice.  Given the size of our grant, and that this is one of the remaining original goals and possible usable outcomes, I think that only the merit of best practice should be considered, not potential cost savings.
In my opinion, the survey must be carried out based on official statistical recommendations and scientific literature. The statistical recommendations that I am aware of do not use self-administered online surveys, particularly for such complex topics. In my opinion, switching away from the ESSNet recommendations should be justified with a short literature review of statistical papers, recommendations that prove the need to move away from face-to-face interviews. If we do not do this, then we can only claim that we are making a demonstration of Artisjus’s and SOZA’s normal work in a cost-saving, downgraded version.  I have a fear that this consortium with 2000% larger budget will replicate only a part of the work that we did on a shoestring budget better 5-10 years ago, both in terms of surveying and economics application.
To me the question is: what is the scientifically, statistically proven best method in 2024 to carry out a cultural access and participation survey? And what is the scientifically proven best method to use this data in valuations?

Best regards,
Daniel
