Hi Daniel,

I am confused.

For several months, you've suggested that we DO NOT have a fit-for-purpose valuation model that represents a scientifically significant improvement on the models you already developed for ARTISJUS in 2015/2018. In response, I asked the broad round whether anyone felt capable of working on such a task, esp. regarding live music. There was some lukewarm response, but nobody with the relevant competences stepped forward to own the task.

You also argued that it WAS NOT scientifically significant to merely conduct new surveys using the old model.

Just today, you seemed to repeat this standpoint, arguing that a literature review on the topic was urgently needed. Hence my reluctance to invest in CAPI on data collection not guided by any model or theory.

==

However, in your email just now, you suggest that we DO have a fit-for-purpose valuation model, as well as prior questionnaires that represent its effective operationalisation. Does this mean that you now think it IS scientifically significant to go forward with surveys based on the old model?

If so, I'm happy to use the old question batteries as a basis, make some cuts/additions to other sections of the surveys, and stick to the ESSnet-Culture recommendation for CAPI / CATI in Hungary and Slovakia.

==

The cost of CAPI / CATI is well over 30k per country. Please tell me clearly, with full confidence, that feeding new survey data based on the old questions into the old model (or whatever model you have on hand) is meaningful from a scientific and a business perspective. Then I will gladly spend it! Otherwise, we must discuss the real added value.

And I agree that this discussion must take absolute priority.

Best regards,
James

I am not a scientist, and I do not want to do scientific work, however, what we expected from this consortium to do whatever scientific work , but provide a scientific validation and if possible, improvement of the work that we had carried out with our modest means before winning this grant with the very same results of that work.

On Fri, Dec 6, 2024 at 11:11 AM James Rhys Edwards &lt;JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&lt;mailto:JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&gt;&gt; wrote:
Hi Daniel,

Thank you for your considered response. In principle, I agree that CAPI / CATI produces better data.

In practice however, I raise XX points:

First, as you note, nobody in the Consortium has provided guidance on the use of survey data in valuations. We've been asking for inputs in this regard for months. I'm not an economist — nor is SINUS a partner in WP1 — so I am not positioned to conduct a literature review on this topic, much less adapt or develop a model. I've done my best by adapting the UK Live Music Census method, which is simple enough for me to grasp, but I'm not terribly confident in it.

Second, you are correct that online self-completion is poorly suited to collecting complex data, e.g., anything on spending. However, due to our lack of a valuation model, we don't even know what spending figures we would ask for anyway. In my opinion, spending 30-40k per country for "gold standard" data that was not collected with any specified valuation model in mind, is fiscally irresponsible.

Accordingly, I would like to pivot the survey toward simple usage and attitude questions, with a "sustainability" twist. Online is adequate for this. We can expand our scope to include several more countries: at least ES and FR. This would give us 60% EU population coverage and its four largest music markets. We could credibly claim to be an "EU music audience survey".

We can still ask the spending questions we inherited from the 2015 ARTISJUS survey and if ARTISJUS and SOZA prefer, we can still conduct classic CAPI / CATI fieldwork in HU and SK. It is entirely your decision.

However, I won't waste money on DE / IT "valuation" data collected without any particular model in mind. I would prefer to give the Commission something more modest in claim, but broader in scope.

Best regards,
James

Subject: Re: 2015 questionnaire


Dear James, Eszter, and Tomas,
In my opinion, Artisjus’ concern is to verify that an anyhow improved version of our valuations augmented with surveys is indeed the best practice.  Given the size of our grant, and that this is one of the remaining original goals and possible usable outcomes, I think that only the merit of best practice should be considered, not potential cost savings.
In my opinion, the survey must be carried out based on official statistical recommendations and scientific literature. The statistical recommendations that I am aware of do not use self-administered online surveys, particularly for such complex topics. In my opinion, switching away from the ESSNet recommendations should be justified with a short literature review of statistical papers, recommendations that prove the need to move away from face-to-face interviews. If we do not do this, then we can only claim that we are making a demonstration of Artisjus’s and SOZA’s normal work in a cost-saving, downgraded version.  I have a fear that this consortium with 2000% larger budget will replicate only a part of the work that we did on a shoestring budget better 5-10 years ago, both in terms of surveying and economics application.
To me the question is: what is the scientifically, statistically proven best method in 2024 to carry out a cultural access and participation survey? And what is the scientifically proven best method to use this data in valuations?

Best regards,
Daniel

On 06/12/2024 10:23, James Rhys Edwards wrote:
Dear Eszter and Balazs, Tomas and Richard, and Daniel,

I hope you are all well!

During our prior call on the 2025 cultural access and participation survey, both ARTISJUS and SOZA indicated that this survey data would not be used in legal proceedings (as was originally considered when the project was planned). I'd like to ask you to confirm this.

The reason is that we have been discussing options with fieldwork providers Kantar and Ipsos, and both have urged us to consider online self-completion rather than face-to-face surveying or mixed f2f / telephone.

The traditional consensus in the surveying world is that face-to-face surveying is the modal "gold standard" and yields higher quality data (though this has been disputed in debates post-COVID). If you are planning to use the survey data to back up legal claims, we should stick to f2f / telephone (at least in Hungary and/or Slovakia).

However, if your aim is simply to support business planning with audience insight, our instinct is to go with the mode recommended by the fieldwork providers. We could use the substantial cost saving to: 1) significantly increase the sample per country, and 2) expand the survey to additional countries. Increasing the sample per country would allow more analytical possibilities, while expanding to include additional countries would improve project visibility and impact.

Please let us know as soon as you have a chance. I am also open to an ad-hoc call anytime today, Monday afternoon, or anytime Tuesday.

Thank you and best regards,
James

Dear Kantar-Hoffmann team,

I am writing with an inquiry on survey research on behalf of the Horizon Europe project Open Music Europe (www.openmuse.eu&lt;http://www.openmuse.eu&gt;). Our aim is to better assess the economic and non-economic contributions of music to European society.To this end, we will conduct a nationally representative music audience survey within Germany, Hungary, Italy, and Slovakia. The parameters are as follows:

·        Fieldwork timeframe — two possibilities:

o   Mid- to late January 2025, OR

o   Rolling sample, January to March 2025 – open to discussion

·        Target countries: Germany, Hungary, Italy, Slovakia

·        Probability sample – sampling frame / method to-be-discussed with fieldwork provider

·        Age: 15 or 16 and above, depending on cost – to-be-discussed with fieldwork partner

·        Mode: CAPI or mixed-mode (CAPI, CATI, and/or CAWI) – to-be-discussed with fieldwork provider – mode need not be identical in all countries

·        Sample size: min. N=1000 per country

·        Length: max 30 min

·        Boosts:

o   Attended a live music concert / event, past 3 months: N=250 per country. Incidence rate in 2013 was approx. 11% (EU average).

o   Earned any income from any musical activities, past 12 months: N=100 per country on best-effort basis. Incidence rate is unknown, but expected to be low.

We would like two cost quotes:

·        WITH questionnaire programming and hosting. Outputs = quality controlled dataset in CSV / SAV formats and technical report detailing the sampling frame / method, fieldwork procedures, data quality control procedures, etc.

·         FIELDWORK ONLY (we would program and host the questionnaire). Output = technical report detailing the sampling frame / method, fieldwork procedures, etc.

As our project is funded by the European Commission, we must justify best service for cost, and thus request you send along some material on your experience conducting multi-country CAPI or mixed-mode studies.

Is this the kind of project that might interest you? If so, we would greatly appreciate the chance to discuss by phone or email.

Thank you, and best regards,

James Edwards
Project Director, Open Music Europe (www.openmuse.eu&lt;http://www.openmuse.eu&gt;)
Senior Research, SINUS Markt- und Sozialforschung GmbH (www.sinus-institut.de&lt;http://www.sinus-institut.de&gt;)

Dear James,



Please find my answers. The circle of information as below reflect the research frame of 2019 yet the basic approaches hardly changed during the years in order to ensure comparability.



  1.  F2F CAPI
  2.  According to the agreement, the basic population investigated as a minimum was the Hungarian population aged 15-69, at the same time, the commitment referred to the ESSNet Culture recommendations and undertook to follow the best practice. ESSNet's recommendation was to examine the 15-75 age group as a minimum, but preferably the age group older than six years.
  3.  We therefore supplemented the primary base population with the 10-14 year old age group on the one hand, and the 70+ year old age group on the other hand. The sociodemographic characteristics of the basic population were defined on the basis of the data of the 2011 Census for easier comparability with the previous surveys, and taking into account the data of the later microcensus would have caused a very small, unnoticeable deviation from this. So the sampling frame is the population aged 10+ living in Hungarian households. Since the basic unit of analysis is the individual, we accordingly took a personal sample (as in previous years).
  4.  The method used was the disproportionately stratified random sample, in which the 10-14-year-old and 70+-year-old age groups were present in different (lower) proportions than in the basic population.
  5.  The settlements were selected randomly. Within the settlement, households were selected by random walking. Within a household, the interviewees were selected according to quota criteria. The 10-17-year-olds came from households where we also asked someone from among the adults. (Sampling aimed at random selection of minors would have increased the costs of the research to an unrealistic extent.) The selection of the minor respondents was made with the consent of the parents. We asked a maximum of one adult and one minor in a household.
  6.  The sample consisted of three parts: 1) base sample aged 15-69: N=~1000 people; 2) boosted sample of 10-14 year olds: N=~50 people; 3) boosted sample of 70+ year olds: N=~50 people.
  7.  In the sample, marginal quotas are applied taking into account the following aspects: region, type of settlement, gender and age. In determining the quotas, we used the data of the latest Population Census.



I do hope that above information would support your job.



Best regards,



Tamás

Subject: Re: 2015 questionnaire


Dear James, Eszter, and Tomas,
In my opinion, Artisjus’ concern is to verify that an anyhow improved version of our valuations augmented with surveys is indeed the best practice.  Given the size of our grant, and that this is one of the remaining original goals and possible usable outcomes, I think that only the merit of best practice should be considered, not potential cost savings.
In my opinion, the survey must be carried out based on official statistical recommendations and scientific literature. The statistical recommendations that I am aware of do not use self-administered online surveys, particularly for such complex topics. In my opinion, switching away from the ESSNet recommendations should be justified with a short literature review of statistical papers, recommendations that prove the need to move away from face-to-face interviews. If we do not do this, then we can only claim that we are making a demonstration of Artisjus’s and SOZA’s normal work in a cost-saving, downgraded version.  I have a fear that this consortium with 2000% larger budget will replicate only a part of the work that we did on a shoestring budget better 5-10 years ago, both in terms of surveying and economics application.
To me the question is: what is the scientifically, statistically proven best method in 2024 to carry out a cultural access and participation survey? And what is the scientifically proven best method to use this data in valuations?

Best regards,
Daniel

Subject: Re: 2015 questionnaire

Hi James,

It may not be feasible to do valuations at this point. Still, Artisjus and SOZA require at least a validation of their pricing, which is complex and, to some extent, contains elements from valuation methodology. The complexity arises because most music prices are shadow, i.e., not expressed with a unit price. Such shadow prices are implied from the total licensing fee and can be determined by observing the unknown quantities of the licensed use, using the simple licencing fee = quantity x price
equation.

This means that to accomplish the minimal tasks we had foreseen in the grant agreement, we must utilise the background developed by Daniel  Antal for Artisjus and SOZA to observe unknown quantities and prices, and compare them. It is likely that this work can be published in academic journals, particularly with at least some real-time, realistic data.

The following timeline is roughly in line with the timelines experiences in Hungary and Slovakia.  You must beware that in those cases practically one person, i.e., me carried out the work without background.  Now we have an entire consortium and we already have a very much developed background, so the following time frame should be easy to follow.

Survey methodology
We must consistently survey music creators (MSME survey) and audiences to collect revenues, prices, or quantities we do not know.  We have followed the best practices published around 2012, and the scientific partners must ensure that this methodology is updated with recent developments in survey harmonisation and generally surveying cultural access, participation, and microenterprises.
• Literature review of the novelties since 2015 [we did not find major novelties till 2019]
• Documenting and critical revision of existing surveying methods and questionnaires
• Methodology update to reflect the best practice as of 2025
• Working paper ready: 25 January
• Preparation of article: till April 2025
• Article manuscript: as soon as data is processed
It is possible to publish 2 articles from this. Reprex has created a software that handles the data processing tasks related to retrospective harmonisation, and we will be ready with a new package handling ex ante harmonisation.  This can result in a data science publication (provided Fabio or UTU gives meaningful support) and a CAP harmonised surveying  article (with James)

Economic statistics methodology
• Literature review of the novelties since 2020
• Documenting and critical revision of observing revenues, prices and quantities
• Methodology update to estimate shadow prices (so-called zero price uses of music)
• Working paper ready: 25 January
• Preparation of article: till April 2025
• Article manuscript: as soon as data is processed
It is possible to publish 3 articles from this, perhaps even three, because there is very little reliable, and empirically supported articles on the topic.  An article could be written about the estimation of shadow prices (or zero-price use of music), which is the most frequent form. Another article could be written about an analysis of price observations in Europe, as in my opinion nobody has any clue on this, and it would be an interesting topic. A third article could be written about the R packages that handle the data integration for this work; they already went through initial peer review.

  Expected outcomes:
• A working paper on the best practices, including the existing description from our background, and recent developments: 25 January
• A working paper on the best practices of price comparisons, with a special attention given to shadow price comparisons and estimations: 25 January
• Questionnaire designed based on novel methodological expectations: 20 Februrary
• Questionnaire programming: 20 March
• Survey period: April/May 2025.
• Data processing: May/June 2025.
• Manuscripts finished for publication: ~July, August 2025 after processing the data.


We would like to work similarly to the WP2 tasks lead by Tomas and Daniel: have a weekly fixed meeting where all team members arrive prepared, the day before latest send in their work, and we review out together.  We would have a similar weekly call where we would ask Richard (SOZA) and Balazs (Artisjus), Anna (Reprex) to be present with the scientists who are working on the scientific valuation in a fixed time every week.

Repex as a task leader, and we can supervise the academic work, and give a very substantial background, as we have researched the topic with academic rigour, but without any aim of academic publication.  This supervision can also include the organisation of consultation or receiving feedback, data samples, etc, from Artisjus and SOZA colleagues (and ZAiKS, if they decide to do this work.) Reprex works However, the entire publication process must be in the hands of academics (paper structure, literature review, bibliography management, hypothesis testing, etc.)

Reprex is also developing R packages that can be published in data science literature.  Some of them have already passed peer review and are ready for publication, others will be ready by around April. Any academic can be a co-author who contributes to the testing, documentation of the packages, and the publication process (paper structure, literature review, bibliography management, hypothesis testing, etc.)

Best regards,
Daniel

Subject: Re: 2015 questionnaire


Dear James, Eszter, and Tomas,
In my opinion, Artisjus’ concern is to verify that an anyhow improved version of our valuations augmented with surveys is indeed the best practice.  Given the size of our grant, and that this is one of the remaining original goals and possible usable outcomes, I think that only the merit of best practice should be considered, not potential cost savings.
In my opinion, the survey must be carried out based on official statistical recommendations and scientific literature. The statistical recommendations that I am aware of do not use self-administered online surveys, particularly for such complex topics. In my opinion, switching away from the ESSNet recommendations should be justified with a short literature review of statistical papers, recommendations that prove the need to move away from face-to-face interviews. If we do not do this, then we can only claim that we are making a demonstration of Artisjus’s and SOZA’s normal work in a cost-saving, downgraded version.  I have a fear that this consortium with 2000% larger budget will replicate only a part of the work that we did on a shoestring budget better 5-10 years ago, both in terms of surveying and economics application.
To me the question is: what is the scientifically, statistically proven best method in 2024 to carry out a cultural access and participation survey? And what is the scientifically proven best method to use this data in valuations?

Best regards,
Daniel

On 06/12/2024 10:23, James Rhys Edwards wrote:
Dear Eszter and Balazs, Tomas and Richard, and Daniel,

I hope you are all well!

During our prior call on the 2025 cultural access and participation survey, both ARTISJUS and SOZA indicated that this survey data would not be used in legal proceedings (as was originally considered when the project was planned). I'd like to ask you to confirm this.

The reason is that we have been discussing options with fieldwork providers Kantar and Ipsos, and both have urged us to consider online self-completion rather than face-to-face surveying or mixed f2f / telephone.

The traditional consensus in the surveying world is that face-to-face surveying is the modal "gold standard" and yields higher quality data (though this has been disputed in debates post-COVID). If you are planning to use the survey data to back up legal claims, we should stick to f2f / telephone (at least in Hungary and/or Slovakia).

However, if your aim is simply to support business planning with audience insight, our instinct is to go with the mode recommended by the fieldwork providers. We could use the substantial cost saving to: 1) significantly increase the sample per country, and 2) expand the survey to additional countries. Increasing the sample per country would allow more analytical possibilities, while expanding to include additional countries would improve project visibility and impact.

Please let us know as soon as you have a chance. I am also open to an ad-hoc call anytime today, Monday afternoon, or anytime Tuesday.

Thank you and best regards,
James

Subject: Re: 2015 questionnaire

Hi James,

It may not be feasible to do valuations at this point. Still, Artisjus and SOZA require at least a validation of their pricing, which is complex and, to some extent, contains elements from valuation methodology. The complexity arises because most music prices are shadow, i.e., not expressed with a unit price. Such shadow prices are implied from the total licensing fee and can be determined by observing the unknown quantities of the licensed use, using the simple licencing fee = quantity x price
equation.

This means that to accomplish the minimal tasks we had foreseen in the grant agreement, we must utilise the background developed by Daniel  Antal for Artisjus and SOZA to observe unknown quantities and prices, and compare them. It is likely that this work can be published in academic journals, particularly with at least some real-time, realistic data.

The following timeline is roughly in line with the timelines experiences in Hungary and Slovakia.  You must beware that in those cases practically one person, i.e., me carried out the work without background.  Now we have an entire consortium and we already have a very much developed background, so the following time frame should be easy to follow.

Survey methodology
We must consistently survey music creators (MSME survey) and audiences to collect revenues, prices, or quantities we do not know.  We have followed the best practices published around 2012, and the scientific partners must ensure that this methodology is updated with recent developments in survey harmonisation and generally surveying cultural access, participation, and microenterprises.
• Literature review of the novelties since 2015 [we did not find major novelties till 2019]
• Documenting and critical revision of existing surveying methods and questionnaires
• Methodology update to reflect the best practice as of 2025
• Working paper ready: 25 January
• Preparation of article: till April 2025
• Article manuscript: as soon as data is processed
It is possible to publish 2 articles from this. Reprex has created a software that handles the data processing tasks related to retrospective harmonisation, and we will be ready with a new package handling ex ante harmonisation.  This can result in a data science publication (provided Fabio or UTU gives meaningful support) and a CAP harmonised surveying  article (with James)

Economic statistics methodology
• Literature review of the novelties since 2020
• Documenting and critical revision of observing revenues, prices and quantities
• Methodology update to estimate shadow prices (so-called zero price uses of music)
• Working paper ready: 25 January
• Preparation of article: till April 2025
• Article manuscript: as soon as data is processed
It is possible to publish 3 articles from this, perhaps even three, because there is very little reliable, and empirically supported articles on the topic.  An article could be written about the estimation of shadow prices (or zero-price use of music), which is the most frequent form. Another article could be written about an analysis of price observations in Europe, as in my opinion nobody has any clue on this, and it would be an interesting topic. A third article could be written about the R packages that handle the data integration for this work; they already went through initial peer review.

  Expected outcomes:
• A working paper on the best practices, including the existing description from our background, and recent developments: 25 January
• A working paper on the best practices of price comparisons, with a special attention given to shadow price comparisons and estimations: 25 January
• Questionnaire designed based on novel methodological expectations: 20 Februrary
• Questionnaire programming: 20 March
• Survey period: April/May 2025.
• Data processing: May/June 2025.
• Manuscripts finished for publication: ~July, August 2025 after processing the data.


We would like to work similarly to the WP2 tasks lead by Tomas and Daniel: have a weekly fixed meeting where all team members arrive prepared, the day before latest send in their work, and we review out together.  We would have a similar weekly call where we would ask Richard (SOZA) and Balazs (Artisjus), Anna (Reprex) to be present with the scientists who are working on the scientific valuation in a fixed time every week.

Repex as a task leader, and we can supervise the academic work, and give a very substantial background, as we have researched the topic with academic rigour, but without any aim of academic publication.  This supervision can also include the organisation of consultation or receiving feedback, data samples, etc, from Artisjus and SOZA colleagues (and ZAiKS, if they decide to do this work.) Reprex works However, the entire publication process must be in the hands of academics (paper structure, literature review, bibliography management, hypothesis testing, etc.)

Reprex is also developing R packages that can be published in data science literature.  Some of them have already passed peer review and are ready for publication, others will be ready by around April. Any academic can be a co-author who contributes to the testing, documentation of the packages, and the publication process (paper structure, literature review, bibliography management, hypothesis testing, etc.)

Best regards,
Daniel

Subject: Re: 2015 questionnaire


Dear James, Eszter, and Tomas,
In my opinion, Artisjus’ concern is to verify that an anyhow improved version of our valuations augmented with surveys is indeed the best practice.  Given the size of our grant, and that this is one of the remaining original goals and possible usable outcomes, I think that only the merit of best practice should be considered, not potential cost savings.
In my opinion, the survey must be carried out based on official statistical recommendations and scientific literature. The statistical recommendations that I am aware of do not use self-administered online surveys, particularly for such complex topics. In my opinion, switching away from the ESSNet recommendations should be justified with a short literature review of statistical papers, recommendations that prove the need to move away from face-to-face interviews. If we do not do this, then we can only claim that we are making a demonstration of Artisjus’s and SOZA’s normal work in a cost-saving, downgraded version.  I have a fear that this consortium with 2000% larger budget will replicate only a part of the work that we did on a shoestring budget better 5-10 years ago, both in terms of surveying and economics application.
To me the question is: what is the scientifically, statistically proven best method in 2024 to carry out a cultural access and participation survey? And what is the scientifically proven best method to use this data in valuations?

Best regards,
Daniel

On 06/12/2024 10:23, James Rhys Edwards wrote:
Dear Eszter and Balazs, Tomas and Richard, and Daniel,

I hope you are all well!

During our prior call on the 2025 cultural access and participation survey, both ARTISJUS and SOZA indicated that this survey data would not be used in legal proceedings (as was originally considered when the project was planned). I'd like to ask you to confirm this.

The reason is that we have been discussing options with fieldwork providers Kantar and Ipsos, and both have urged us to consider online self-completion rather than face-to-face surveying or mixed f2f / telephone.

The traditional consensus in the surveying world is that face-to-face surveying is the modal "gold standard" and yields higher quality data (though this has been disputed in debates post-COVID). If you are planning to use the survey data to back up legal claims, we should stick to f2f / telephone (at least in Hungary and/or Slovakia).

However, if your aim is simply to support business planning with audience insight, our instinct is to go with the mode recommended by the fieldwork providers. We could use the substantial cost saving to: 1) significantly increase the sample per country, and 2) expand the survey to additional countries. Increasing the sample per country would allow more analytical possibilities, while expanding to include additional countries would improve project visibility and impact.

Please let us know as soon as you have a chance. I am also open to an ad-hoc call anytime today, Monday afternoon, or anytime Tuesday.

Thank you and best regards,
James

==



Dear Kantar-Hoffmann team,

I am writing with an inquiry on survey research on behalf of the Horizon Europe project Open Music Europe (www.openmuse.eu&lt;http://www.openmuse.eu&gt;). Our aim is to better assess the economic and non-economic contributions of music to European society.To this end, we will conduct a nationally representative music audience survey within Germany, Hungary, Italy, and Slovakia. The parameters are as follows:

·        Fieldwork timeframe — two possibilities:

o   Mid- to late January 2025, OR

o   Rolling sample, January to March 2025 – open to discussion

·        Target countries: Germany, Hungary, Italy, Slovakia

·        Probability sample – sampling frame / method to-be-discussed with fieldwork provider

·        Age: 15 or 16 and above, depending on cost – to-be-discussed with fieldwork partner

·        Mode: CAPI or mixed-mode (CAPI, CATI, and/or CAWI) – to-be-discussed with fieldwork provider – mode need not be identical in all countries

·        Sample size: min. N=1000 per country

·        Length: max 30 min

·        Boosts:

o   Attended a live music concert / event, past 3 months: N=250 per country. Incidence rate in 2013 was approx. 11% (EU average).

o   Earned any income from any musical activities, past 12 months: N=100 per country on best-effort basis. Incidence rate is unknown, but expected to be low.

We would like two cost quotes:

·        WITH questionnaire programming and hosting. Outputs = quality controlled dataset in CSV / SAV formats and technical report detailing the sampling frame / method, fieldwork procedures, data quality control procedures, etc.

·         FIELDWORK ONLY (we would program and host the questionnaire). Output = technical report detailing the sampling frame / method, fieldwork procedures, etc.

As our project is funded by the European Commission, we must justify best service for cost, and thus request you send along some material on your experience conducting multi-country CAPI or mixed-mode studies.

Is this the kind of project that might interest you? If so, we would greatly appreciate the chance to discuss by phone or email.

Thank you, and best regards,

James Edwards
Project Director, Open Music Europe (www.openmuse.eu&lt;http://www.openmuse.eu&gt;)
Senior Research, SINUS Markt- und Sozialforschung GmbH (www.sinus-institut.de&lt;http://www.sinus-institut.de&gt;)

Dear James,



Please find my answers. The circle of information as below reflect the research frame of 2019 yet the basic approaches hardly changed during the years in order to ensure comparability.



  1.  F2F CAPI
  2.  According to the agreement, the basic population investigated as a minimum was the Hungarian population aged 15-69, at the same time, the commitment referred to the ESSNet Culture recommendations and undertook to follow the best practice. ESSNet's recommendation was to examine the 15-75 age group as a minimum, but preferably the age group older than six years.
  3.  We therefore supplemented the primary base population with the 10-14 year old age group on the one hand, and the 70+ year old age group on the other hand. The sociodemographic characteristics of the basic population were defined on the basis of the data of the 2011 Census for easier comparability with the previous surveys, and taking into account the data of the later microcensus would have caused a very small, unnoticeable deviation from this. So the sampling frame is the population aged 10+ living in Hungarian households. Since the basic unit of analysis is the individual, we accordingly took a personal sample (as in previous years).
  4.  The method used was the disproportionately stratified random sample, in which the 10-14-year-old and 70+-year-old age groups were present in different (lower) proportions than in the basic population.
  5.  The settlements were selected randomly. Within the settlement, households were selected by random walking. Within a household, the interviewees were selected according to quota criteria. The 10-17-year-olds came from households where we also asked someone from among the adults. (Sampling aimed at random selection of minors would have increased the costs of the research to an unrealistic extent.) The selection of the minor respondents was made with the consent of the parents. We asked a maximum of one adult and one minor in a household.
  6.  The sample consisted of three parts: 1) base sample aged 15-69: N=~1000 people; 2) boosted sample of 10-14 year olds: N=~50 people; 3) boosted sample of 70+ year olds: N=~50 people.
  7.  In the sample, marginal quotas are applied taking into account the following aspects: region, type of settlement, gender and age. In determining the quotas, we used the data of the latest Population Census.



I do hope that above information would support your job.



Best regards,



Tamás

So, first off: thank you for your fast response to our initial inquiry, which was very helpful in putting our proposal on a solid enough foundation to be chosen!



Pursuant the grant agreement process, we’d like to ask a question about surveying mode. While the proposal was well-evaluated, the reviewers expressed concern about the fieldwork cost. We recognize that face-to-face surveying remains the “gold standard” for high-quality data; however, quite a bit has been learned during the SERISS (https://seriss.eu/) and CRONOS projects and the COVID-19 pandemic about effective non-f2f sampling and fieldwork, mode effects and how to compensate for them, etc. As you may have read, the European Social Survey has even announced a forthcoming change in data collection mode from face-to-face interviews to online and paper self-completion surveys (https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/singlenew.html?a=/about/news/essnews0130.html).



Given the rapidly progressing state of the art, we wonder what options Kantar Hoffmann might be able to offer with regard to a mixed-mode, or even entirely self-completion-based, survey. The code is available here: https://esomar.org/code-and-guidelines/icc-esomar-code

<!-- source: OpenMuse_20261009-2156/OpenMuse/messages/202501101555-OpenMusE -- survey planning-839.txt -->


Hi Daniel,

I hope your winter holiday was relaxing!

Olga and I are working on several aspects of the OpenMusE music professional and MSME survey, and would like to finish a questionnaire draft as soon as possible especially to plan the ethical committee application. We know we are still in the evaluation of the survey methods and variables but we would like to proceed with application as the whole procedure can be lengthy. As it has happened in the past we can submit to the ethical committee a longer list of questions for the approval and skim through it later in the actual execution or if we will add new questions we can have a faster amendment procedure later.

For this, we need to:
-look at the prior music professional and MSME surveys that REPREX conducted with its CEEMID partner
-discuss with you and them which questions should be carried over to the present round (definite yes, maybe yes, no, undecided)

I know we are still in the evaluation of the survey methods and variables but

James already requested permission for this in July 2024, and both ARTISJUS and SOZA are OK with sharing this material. The signed requests are reattached.

Would you available next week, possibly towards the end (Thursday or Friday) to discuss it?

Best Regards
Arianna

### OPENMUSE - Sharing a structure for the WG on methodology {#email-829}

**From:** Arianna Martinelli &lt;arianna.martinelli@santannapisa.it&gt;  
**To:** Joost Poort &lt;j.p.poort@uva.nl&gt;, Olga Kavkaeva &lt;Olga.Kavkaeva@santannapisa.it&gt;, Mária Kmety Barteková &lt;maria.bartekova@euba.sk&gt;  
**Cc:** James Rhys Edwards &lt;JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&gt;, Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;  
**Date:** 01/16/2025 15:48:50

<!-- source: OpenMuse_20261009-2156/OpenMuse/messages/202501161548-OPENMUSE - Sharing a structure for the WG on metho-841.txt -->

Dear all,

Following our meeting, I am sharing a basic document structure for everyone to fill in.

At the beginning of Section Two, I have included a list of bullet points summarizing what I think we should report for each method. The first two points are more “theoretical,” while the others are more practical, in line with the “hitchhiking guide” logic we discussed on Tuesday.
The PWC report follows a rather similar structure, but we can differentiate ourselves in two ways: first, by adopting a stronger scientific focus in addressing all the points; and second, by noting that the PWC report is quite dated, and there may have been progress since then.

If you think additional bullet points are needed, please feel free to add them. The idea is to establish a uniform set of minimum contents to provide for each method. Afterward, I will work on harmonizing the text and consider how to structure it in a way that aligns with some models from the industry. We will have time to discuss this further.

Here the link: https://alumnisssup-my.sharepoint.com/:w:/g/personal/arianna_martinelli_santannapisa_it/EdPzeJU0MNFPrvreLNwJ4zQBpEr5Ha8GXP0emAIX1HKglw?e=S8L7xk

Here the link to the meeting recording if someone needs a refresh :) https://alumnisssup-my.sharepoint.com/:v:/g/personal/arianna_martinelli_santannapisa_it/EbG3aI-2kWRHglUlbek-VBwB5OJQJynxnMDD1v-YTkkCug?e=Xy1TUU


@Daniel: I hope you’re feeling better. It would be great if you could share in the reader the material you mentioned during the call.

Best regards,
Arianna

Hello LMMP team,

Happy New Year!

First off, @Patrycja Rozbicka&lt;mailto:p.rozbicka@aston.ac.uk&gt; thank you again for your comments! We're working on a second questionnaire draft now.

Second, during our call, you mentioned that you'd been working on a taxonomy of actors in UK music ecosystems. My colleagues at Reprex, @Daniel Antal&lt;mailto:daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;, and Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna, @Arianna Martinelli&lt;mailto:Arianna.Martinelli@santannapisa.it&gt; and @Olga Kavkaeva&lt;mailto:Olga.Kavkaeva@santannapisa.it&gt;, are doing something similar, in preparation for running a survey of music professionals and music MSMEs. Their taxonomy of job roles will be cross-referenced with ISCO / ESCO while the taxonomy of legal entity roles will be cross-references with ISIC / NACE (with one purpose being to better understand / quantify the gaps in this system). I just wanted to put you in touch, in case of potential synergies in this work.

We'll keep you abreast of other 2025 plans as they come together in more detail!

Best regards,
James

Hey James,

As promised some of the comments on the survey. Most are ok, but there are few things requiring fixes, as you probably know yourself. Here few more general points:

  *
Try shortening the survey and replace it with short boosts of shorter questionnaires. Yes, you will risk varied response rates, but there will be more responses in general. Do not tell ppl it will take 30min. They will be discouraged at the start.
  *
One point of significance, it isn't clear at whom is the survey aimed. I am assuming general public, but you also have quite specific employment questions linked with music industry (example about playing instruments or income from 'musicking' activities). At the same time, you are missing a whole group of professionals working on the gigs: sound/video/light engineers, professional staff at the bar and security).

All comments and suggestions inserted in the text, especially if you need an extra example for rewarding from other sources. All suggestions aimed with good intentions 🙂

Pat

Hi all,

Ahead of our call, here's the questionnaire draft so far. As the call is short, I'd like to focus on Section 2 "Engaging with Live Music: Experiences, Preferences, and Challenges". However, if we have time, I'd also be very interested in hearing your thoughts on the other sections in the coming days!

The total length of interview is around 30 min, so we will have to either 1) go with F2F (CAPI) and/or telephone (CATI) as a survey mode; 2) go with online self-completion (CAWI), but split the sample so that the total length of interview for any given respondent is around 15 min; or 3) make some radical cuts.

CAPI/CATI is much more cost- and effort-intensive, but is preferred by some of our partners (in line with the ESSnet-Culture 2012 recommendations). Option 2 is our preference, as we conduct many online surveys on non-sensitive topics and usually find the data quality acceptable. But, we'd be curious to hear your input.

I've also attached an adapted version of the UK LMC economic methodology, which cross-maps our live music valuation data sources to yours.

Thank you again for taking the time! Best regards,
James

From: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
Sent: Monday, January 13, 2025 1:26 PM
To: Joost Poort &lt;j.p.poort@uva.nl&gt;; Fábio Generoso Vieira &lt;f.v.vieira@uva.nl&gt;
Subject: Reading in ALOADED's data

Dear Fabio and Joost,

I have written this more or less up for the consultation, and this is what I would have wanted to ask from Fabio.

I would like to ask Fabio to remove all content from the alluded repository that is not related to creating datasets. There should be no other dependencies than tidyverse packages, and dataset package (which is compatible with tidyverse) and is going to be used for putting our data out to the scientific repositories.

Task 1

There should be only one vignette: how does the function create a datacube (a standard, multidimensional dataset) from ALOADED's csv files.

The csv files should be transformed to a tidy dataset in R following the datacube specifications without slicing.

They should have the following dimensions:
- price
- currency [choose one functional currency, for example, SKK or EUR]
- territory
- time period
- service provider (Apple, Spotify)
- service name (Family Package, etc)
- exchange rates to the functional currency
- unit of measure (is this 1 unit of the currency, or 1/100th of the currency)

there should be unit test(s) which check the logical consistency of Fabio's work:
- is there only one price observation for one combination of the dimensions, i.e., geo, time_period, service_provider, etc.

Such unit tests should check for data derived from rows that are not single data points. A single data point is, for example, if the Spotify Family package has only one single sales in Namibia for a given time period.

I would consider this done if I can run the same code with the same aloaded CSV file and receive the same dataset.

Whatever functions you create for these tasks, they should have their standard roxygen documentation. If creating the dataset from the file requires explanation, it should be a "vignette", which does not use any further dependencies beyond tidyverse and kntir (knitr is required for vignettes.)

Part of this task is simple data wrangling: identifying, selecting, filtering the rows and columns from ALOADED's data. But some of this is statistical work, because you may need to handle missing variables, or average data points over a time period. Those steps will require sound decisions.

Reading:
- https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-data-cube/ The definition of a data cube that can be shared on the internet (for example, in a data repository)
- Wikipedia on Datacube https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_cube

Task 2

Create a function that reads in all CSV files from a folder, and creates one datacube. For example, if ALOADED has each time period in a separate file, then add them time periods from separate files in a directory.

I would like to see how much data and in what quality are we able to retrieve from 1 ALOADED file, and from several files.  How much the files overlap or add new information?

- Can you come up with other unit tests that verify that you read in the data from ALOADED in a safe and sound way?
- Is there any contradictory information in the ALOADED dataset, regarding the unit price of music in a given territory, counted in a given currency, for a specific service?

Best regards,


Daniel Antal, CFA
co-founder

From: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
Sent: Thursday, January 16, 2025 9:24 AM
To: Fábio Generoso Vieira &lt;f.v.vieira@uva.nl&gt;
Cc: Joost Poort &lt;j.p.poort@uva.nl&gt;
Subject: Re: Reading in ALOADED's data

Hi Fábió,

I reviewed your work, and as you can see, going step by step makes a lot of sense.  There are problems with reading in the dataset which are at this point not explained. Also, if we want to get more data from ALOADED, we must have functions that repeat the tasks and retrieve guaranteed good data from their accounts.  Their accounting system (until changed) will always export the data in the same format, so we have to get it right with only one file.

Because we do not yet get the price data correctly, we need to go step by step.

1. The get_aloaded_price_data should end in a dataset that contains all variables in a tidy dataset which are needed to create the statistical dataset.  Its input should be an aloaded datafile.
2. This is how you add a testing dataset to your package: https://r-pkgs.org/data.html  I would add here one of the ALOADED files, perhaps reduced in size to 100 rows; your function should be tested against this.
3. The create_aloaded_price_dataset should process (with only tidyverse functions) the microdata produced by get_aloaded_price_data() to a statistical, multi-dimensional dataset, which has the following dimensions: territory, time period, currency unit, sales platform, sales configuration, price.
4. It should have a boolean parameter if you want to impute missing data or not.  In my opinion, it is easier to trace data problems if you did not impute them.
5. You already added the unit test infrastructure, which is very good.  Both functions should have sensible unit tests, which we will expand if we try them on more files and more problems arise.

Best regards,
Daniel

**From:** Isabella Tautscher &lt;Isabella.Tautscher@sinus-institut.de&gt;

**Date:** 01/27/2025 17:56:41

<!-- source: OpenMuse_20261009-2156/OpenMuse/messages/202501271756-Clarification Reporting Periods-855.txt -->

Dear all,

I hope you had a good start into the new year!

We have received a couple of questions concerning financial reporting, so there seems to be a need for clarification.

Good news, we do not need to repeat last year's reporting process until end of next year!
The reporting periods, which are set by the European commission, are M1 to M12, and M13 to M36, i.e. reporting period 1 was the entire year of 2023, and reporting period 2 will be 2024 and 2025 together.
This means that we do not need to hand in any financial statements, timesheets or other, until end of this year.

If you have already put together any information on 2024, this will certainly help you during the final reporting.
Please also note that you need to keep your timesheets throughout the entire project duration. Richard shared timesheet suggestions in the beginning of the project, which you can also find on the Sinus Cloud&lt;https://cloud.sinus-institut.de/public/c0402d&gt;.

I hope this clears things up! Please let me know if you have any other questions.

Best regards,

Hi Daniel,

I agree that sampling, target concepts, variables, etc. should be defined before we move to the level of individual survey question phrasing. However, laying eyes on a "nuts and bolts" questionnaire in parallel would give the team a more concrete idea of how this must all come together in the end.

Within the team, you are the only one who has conducted a music MSME survey — I've done music surveys, and Arianna has done MSME surveys, but having experience in both is very rare. I would hazard to say there are only a handful of good practices worldwide, and none of them have publicly available questionnaires. This is why the conversation until now has remained abstract, and why the workflow suffers from chicken-and-egg syndrome.

An inelegant metaphor: If asked to build an aircraft, a thorough study of aerodynamic theory is of course necessary, but in parallel, it would also be helpful to see a bird.

As per the background form, we can set restrictions on usage (e.g., no reuse of individual questions without explicit permission).

Just my two cents!

Best regards,
James

Subject: Re: OpenMusE -- survey planning

Hi James,

CEEMID did conduct 10 MSME surveys, following whatever methodologies we found out to be the best, with a very special sampling to ensure representativity.  I think that before going into details with our questionnaires, perhaps the methodology of the MSME survey should be fixed, including its sampling, target concepts, variables, and mapping, etc. We agreed to have a review of how we would like to represent DDI in our questionbank where we place the questions, but that is waiting for review since early November.  I think that since the kick off meeting in 2023 I wrote tons of descriptions on our methodology, approach, etc.

Given that currently there is nothing written yet about what economic models will use the survey data and which aspect of it, I find it a bit early to start dealing with a questionnaire.

Best regards,
Daniel

Hello LMMP team,

Happy New Year!

First off, @Patrycja Rozbicka&lt;mailto:p.rozbicka@aston.ac.uk&gt; thank you again for your comments! We're working on a second questionnaire draft now.

Second, during our call, you mentioned that you'd been working on a taxonomy of actors in UK music ecosystems. My colleagues at Reprex, @Daniel Antal&lt;mailto:daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;, and Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna, @Arianna Martinelli&lt;mailto:Arianna.Martinelli@santannapisa.it&gt; and @Olga Kavkaeva&lt;mailto:Olga.Kavkaeva@santannapisa.it&gt;, are doing something similar, in preparation for running a survey of music professionals and music MSMEs. Their taxonomy of job roles will be cross-referenced with ISCO / ESCO while the taxonomy of legal entity roles will be cross-references with ISIC / NACE (with one purpose being to better understand / quantify the gaps in this system). I just wanted to put you in touch, in case of potential synergies in this work.

We'll keep you abreast of other 2025 plans as they come together in more detail!

Best regards,
James

Hey James,

As promised some of the comments on the survey. Most are ok, but there are few things requiring fixes, as you probably know yourself. Here few more general points:

  *
Try shortening the survey and replace it with short boosts of shorter questionnaires. Yes, you will risk varied response rates, but there will be more responses in general. Do not tell ppl it will take 30min. They will be discouraged at the start.
  *
One point of significance, it isn't clear at whom is the survey aimed. I am assuming general public, but you also have quite specific employment questions linked with music industry (example about playing instruments or income from 'musicking' activities). At the same time, you are missing a whole group of professionals working on the gigs: sound/video/light engineers, professional staff at the bar and security).

All comments and suggestions inserted in the text, especially if you need an extra example for rewarding from other sources. All suggestions aimed with good intentions 🙂

Pat

Hi all,

Ahead of our call, here's the questionnaire draft so far. As the call is short, I'd like to focus on Section 2 "Engaging with Live Music: Experiences, Preferences, and Challenges". However, if we have time, I'd also be very interested in hearing your thoughts on the other sections in the coming days!

The total length of interview is around 30 min, so we will have to either 1) go with F2F (CAPI) and/or telephone (CATI) as a survey mode; 2) go with online self-completion (CAWI), but split the sample so that the total length of interview for any given respondent is around 15 min; or 3) make some radical cuts.

CAPI/CATI is much more cost- and effort-intensive, but is preferred by some of our partners (in line with the ESSnet-Culture 2012 recommendations). Option 2 is our preference, as we conduct many online surveys on non-sensitive topics and usually find the data quality acceptable. But, we'd be curious to hear your input.

I've also attached an adapted version of the UK LMC economic methodology, which cross-maps our live music valuation data sources to yours.

Thank you again for taking the time! Best regards,
James

From: Daniel Antal &lt;daniel.antal@reprex.nl&gt;
Sent: 20 January 2025 13:40
To: James Rhys Edwards &lt;JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&gt;
Cc: Joost Poort &lt;j.p.poort@uva.nl&gt;; Arianna Martinelli &lt;Arianna.Martinelli@santannapisa.it&gt;; Olga Kavkaeva &lt;Olga.Kavkaeva@santannapisa.it&gt;; AnnA Mester &lt;anna.mester@reprex.nl&gt;
Subject: Re: OpenMusE -- survey planning

Hi James,

Here is the English version of the 2019 survey. It was not intended to be used in English, and it has standard .po files that translators use to translate technical text in 12 languages. We will place them into the questionbank as soon as we understand how they will be used and for what.

On 9 November we have placed this to the open repository, and we have been waiting for feedback on how to upload the questions so that they can actually be imported to the fieldwork program and into the statistical application that will analyse them: https://zenodo.org/records/14059450

"Thank you for your answer. Like I wrote earlier, before an intern gets to work, we need to agree on the final structure of the data, which I started to document here&lt;https://zenodo.org/records/14059450&gt; and here&lt;https://github.com/dataobservatory-eu/questionbank_papers/&gt;. The best would be if you would be able to fork this repository and work in the source file in RStudio. It is only text, no programming is involved. "

To me, sharing my 10-years old questionnaires is not a new contribution, and at least I would like to finalise some of the work that we originally promised with UTU in the grant agreement, and release a new software and a question bank as an enriched dataset.  I would expect that this would be used by the researchers of this consortium to prove that there was some connection with our work and not only the background was reused.

However, as it came out today in the meeting, there is a more fundamental problem here, I am still not convinced that SSSA colleagues have a realistic idea about what an MSME survey is and how it can be conducted.  The Orbis database looks like a good idea, but I have extremely high doubts that it will actually overlap with our target audience, and that the overlap can be exploited.  Our worst survey response rate was below 2% and the best 25%.  Also, it is methodologically and practically very challenging to differentiate between a population and a microenterprise survey, after all, who will respond in the name of a microenterprise? In our target countries, I doubt that we will have a single respondent who reaches the size of a small enterprise.

I think that we should have as a starting point the following:

- Exactly what information should be collected and from whom
- What can be collected with survey(s)
- Who is the target population of the survey(s), how can we reach them
- How do we care for the duality of a population- enterprise question in case of highly informal small enterprises and microenterprises, including exclusion of dual responses, ensuring that we have questionnaire(s) that make sense in a population and enterprise survey, etc.
- What is the best way to administer the survey to the target population(s), who will administer it, with what means?
- How will you create a sampling and data collection that ensures that a certain degree of representativeness is present?

If we would have this in writing, say, in a 10-12 working paper with methodological literature survey, at least some hypotheses, etc, then I think we could talk about variables, questions, and the representation of question output (for which our system is ready to be finalised since 9 November.)

Best regards,
Daniel

On Thu, Jan 16, 2025 at 3:30 PM James Rhys Edwards &lt;JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&lt;mailto:JamesRhys.Edwards@sinus-institut.de&gt;&gt; wrote:
Hi Daniel,

I agree that sampling, target concepts, variables, etc. should be defined before we move to the level of individual survey question phrasing. However, laying eyes on a "nuts and bolts" questionnaire in parallel would give the team a more concrete idea of how this must all come together in the end.

Within the team, you are the only one who has conducted a music MSME survey — I've done music surveys, and Arianna has done MSME surveys, but having experience in both is very rare. I would hazard to say there are only a handful of good practices worldwide, and none of them have publicly available questionnaires. This is why the conversation until now has remained abstract, and why the workflow suffers from chicken-and-egg syndrome.

An inelegant metaphor: If asked to build an aircraft, a thorough study of aerodynamic theory is of course necessary, but in parallel, it would also be helpful to see a bird.

As per the background form, we can set restrictions on usage (e.g., no reuse of individual questions without explicit permission).

Just my two cents!

Best regards,
James

Hey James,



As promised some of the comments on the survey. Most are ok, but there are few things requiring fixes, as you probably know yourself. Here few more general points:

  *   Try shortening the survey and replace it with short boosts of shorter questionnaires. Yes, you will risk varied response rates, but there will be more responses in general. Do not tell ppl it will take 30min. They will be discouraged at the start.

  *   One point of significance, it isn't clear at whom is the survey aimed. I am assuming general public, but you also have quite specific employment questions linked with music industry (example about playing instruments or income from 'musicking' activities). At the same time, you are missing a whole group of professionals working on the gigs: sound/video/light engineers, professional staff at the bar and security).

All comments and suggestions inserted in the text, especially if you need an extra example for rewarding from other sources. All suggestions aimed with good intentions 🙂



Pat

Hi all,



Ahead of our call, here's the questionnaire draft so far. As the call is short, I'd like to focus on Section 2 "Engaging with Live Music: Experiences, Preferences, and Challenges". However, if we have time, I'd also be very interested in hearing your thoughts on the other sections in the coming days!



The total length of interview is around 30 min, so we will have to either 1) go with F2F (CAPI) and/or telephone (CATI) as a survey mode; 2) go with online self-completion (CAWI), but split the sample so that the total length of interview for any given respondent is around 15 min; or 3) make some radical cuts.



CAPI/CATI is much more cost- and effort-intensive, but is preferred by some of our partners (in line with the ESSnet-Culture 2012 recommendations). Option 2 is our preference, as we conduct many online surveys on non-sensitive topics and usually find the data quality acceptable. But, we'd be curious to hear your input.



I've also attached an adapted version of the UK LMC economic methodology, which cross-maps our live music valuation data sources to yours.



Thank you again for taking the time! Best regards,

James

Dear Joost and Arianna,

I did apologise in front of the people in CC, but I must emphasise that these people were under the impression yesterday that they received a document from Arianna that seems to disregard their work that they thought they were doing for Arianna.  They thought that they have to provide a survey frame for Arianna, and they also think that they have to administer survey(s) for them.

From Arianna's reply we had the impression that no MSME survey available for their deliverable.  This means that we have to work from two personal surveys: the one that needs to be administered by the CMOs and the one that is carried out by James.

  With Aritsjus, SOZA, and ZAIKS or MusicAutor we have to prepare two deliverables: one of the survey frames and one actual use of the surveys.

  1.  For Hungary and Slovakia we have everything ready and programmed as far as I understand.
  2.  I do not know what is the latest status with Bulgaria but we do have a translated, tested and programmed survey for Bulgaria.
  3.  For Poland, we have a translated, programmed, but not tested survey.

We can do this without any input from SSSA regarding data, surveys, however, the two deliverables do have to look as if they were prepared in a Consortium and went beyond the 5-10 years old background. That means that some scientific underpinning must be found and put into a public document.

In our last meeting about methodology, only James and I got an assignment, and I find it problematic.  Neither the CMOs or Reprex have the research capacity to do that. I think that the cooperative attitude in your criticism in this regard should go both ways.

Best regards,
Daniel

From: Daniel Antal
Sent: Thursday, January 23, 2025 19:19
To: Arianna Martinelli
Cc: Jankovič Marián; Tomas Miks; Rosina Petrova; Dr. Kabai Eszter; Demčák Richard; Dr. Huszák Balázs; Olga Kavkaeva; Joost Poort; James Rhys Edwards
Subject: Re: OPENMUSE - List of target and request of a meeting

Hi Arianna,

The document that you sent to us today is something that cannot be connected to our work. We cannot design and build a survey frame and register for such a broad target group so late in the project. The reasons I well explained in the document that I created as a step-in for SSSA and submitted for the interim review in D1.1, which explains generally the enterprise surveying difficulties of a highly informal music sector.

I still have not seen in the last 2 years any written document about what you call "Orbis survey", so I can rely only on fragments of oral statements which make me think that the Orbis survey falls into the category that we described in D1.1 as a faulty approach that resulted in not having enterprise data in the last 15 years. (i.e., a NACE-based, random sample, online administered survey among enterprises.) As far as I understand, this is supposed to be added to the project as a comparator, a benchmark of "bad surveying" so that we can show how "good surveying" can improve.

In short, so that we do not have to come back in circles:
- NACE codes are useless, so administering a survey with a population frame based on NACE codes must overshoot its target response by at least 300-400%
- This means that your online survey response rate goes down from 2-3% to an inferred 0.5%.
- When you have a target population of 58, for example, then you have a chance to get 0 or 1 examples. This means that if you have 58 music publishing entities in a country, then an online survey sent out to addresses of all of them has a chance of 0 to 1 answers.
- No statistics can be made from less than 10 responses.

We were offered to participate in the enterprise surveying scheme of Slovakia in the cultural sector in both 2024 and 2025. Because those surveys come with a legal mandate, a fine for non-response, and a well-designed survey frame, they are useful, and they result in a 90%+ coverage. Also, there was a candidate who had to leave the Slovak ministry, and who had a PhD, had working experience with the enterprise survey administration and the register, and would have been available for this project, but she was not hired.   Apart from this, in various projects, we administered enterprise surveys with organisations, and it was a huge undertaking, and I do not think that either SOZA or Artisjus or MusicAutor or MusicExport Poland or Reprex would consider administering such a survey.  In some of our works in HU, SK and CZ we relied on cooperation with IFPI. The IFPI surveys among sound recording companies have about 90% coverage, for example, and they are done with great care. Usually one person who is already knowledgeable about the topic works part time about 3 months on the administration, per country, so the effective PM input, in true, calendar months, is 1.5PM, but that is like working 20 hours dedicated per week on it. And for two countries, that is 3 PMs, but calculated in calendar months.   In my opinion, you had more than 10 PMs for the enterprise survey, so an enterprise survey could have been designed and administered.

There are several tasks and deliverables in this project that require usable survey data, and in my understanding, SSSA and Sinus are responsible for designing and administering those surveys, and they are supposed to be an improvement to what we have done in Slovakia and Hungary with 5% of the budget of this project.

If we will not get suitable data for our tasks, we can think of the following alternatives
a) we present our deliverables with old data
b) we present our deliverables with simulated data
c) Reprex runs a survey for the societies, if we get a public, academic document stating that we have been doing it always the best possible way and there was no room for improvement.

Best regards,
Daniel

1. Two samples are going to be built, one based on ORBIS (done by SSSA) and one based on CMOs registers (T1.2 done by REPREX)
2. SSSA is going to design two questionnaires, one for professionals and one for MSMEs, and some survey design that was going to ensure that each respondent was going to get the “right” questionnaire
3. SSSA was going to administer the survey to the ORBIS sample and take care of non-response bias with available variables

Hi Arianna,

The document that you sent to us today is something that cannot be connected to our work. We cannot design and build a survey frame and register for such a broad target group so late in the project. I still have not seen in the last 2 years any written document about what you call "Orbis survey", so I can rely only on fragments of oral statements which make me think that the Orbis survey falls into the category that we described in D1.1 as a faulty approach that resulted in not having enterprise data in the last 15 years. (i.e., a NACE-based, random sample, online administered survey among enterprises.) As far as I understand, this is supposed to be added to the project as a comparator, a benchmark of "bad surveying" so that we can show how "good surveying" can improve.

In short, so that we do not have to come back in circles:
- NACE codes are useless, so administering a survey with a population frame based on NACE codes must overshoot its target response by at least 300-400%
- This means that your online survey response rate goes down from 2-3% to an inferred 0.5%.
- When you have a target population of 58, for example, then you have a chance to get 0 or 1 examples. This means that if you have 58 music publishing entities in a country, then an online survey sent out to addresses of all of them has a chance of 0 to 1 answers.
- No statistics can be made from less than 10 responses.

We were offered to participate in the enterprise surveying scheme of Slovakia in the cultural sector in both 2024 and 2025. Because those surveys come with a legal mandate, a fine for non-response, and a well-designed survey frame, they are useful, and they result in a 90%+ coverage. Also, there was a candidate who had to leave the Slovak ministry, and who had a PhD, had working experience with the enterprise survey administration and the register, and would have been available for this project, but she was not hired.   Apart from this, in various projects, we administered enterprise surveys with organisations, and it was a huge undertaking, and I do not think that either SOZA or Artisjus or MusicAutor or MusicExport Poland or Reprex would consider administering such a survey.  In some of our works in HU, SK and CZ we relied on cooperation with IFPI. The IFPI surveys among sound recording companies have about 90% coverage, for example, and they are done with great care. Usually one person who is already knowledgeable about the topic works part time about 3 months on the administration, per country, so the effective PM input, in true, calendar months, is 1.5PM, but that is like working 20 hours dedicated per week on it. And for two countries, that is 3 PMs, but calculated in calendar months.   In my opinion, you had more than 10 PMs for the enterprise survey, so an enterprise survey could have been designed and administered.

There are several tasks and deliverables in this project that require usable survey data, and in my understanding, SSSA and Sinus are responsible for designing and administering those surveys, and they are supposed to be an improvement to what we have done in Slovakia and Hungary with 5% of the budget of this project.

If we will not get suitable data for our tasks, we can think of the following alternatives
a) we present our deliverables with old data
b) we present our deliverables with simulated data
c) Reprex runs a survey for the societies, if we get a public, academic document stating that we have been doing it always the best possible way and there was no room for improvement.

Best regards,
Daniel

- This means that your online survey response rate goes down from 2-3% to an inferred 0.5%.
- When you have a target population of 58, for example, then you have a chance to get 0 or 1 examples. This means that if you have 58 music publishing entities in a country, then an online survey sent out to addresses of all of them has a chance of 0 to 1 answers.
- No statistics can be made from less than 10 responses.

We were offered to participate in the enterprise surveying scheme of Slovakia in the cultural sector in both 2024 and 2025. Because those surveys come with a legal mandate, a fine for non-response, and a well-designed survey frame, they are useful, and they result in a 90%+ coverage. Also, there was a candidate who had to leave the Slovak ministry, and who had a PhD, had working experience with the enterprise survey administration and the register, and would have been available for this project, but she was not hired.   Apart from this, in various projects, we administered enterprise surveys with organisations, and it was a huge undertaking, and I do not think that either SOZA or Artisjus or MusicAutor or MusicExport Poland or Reprex would consider administering such a survey.  In some of our works in HU, SK and CZ we relied on cooperation with IFPI. The IFPI surveys among sound recording companies have about 90% coverage, for example, and they are done with great care. Usually one person who is already knowledgeable about the topic works part time about 3 months on the administration, per country, so the effective PM input, in true, calendar months, is 1.5PM, but that is like working 20 hours dedicated per week on it. And for two countries, that is 3 PMs, but calculated in calendar months.   In my opinion, you had more than 10 PMs for the enterprise survey, so an enterprise survey could have been designed and administered.

There are several tasks and deliverables in this project that require usable survey data, and in my understanding, SSSA and Sinus are responsible for designing and administering those surveys, and they are supposed to be an improvement to what we have done in Slovakia and Hungary with 5% of the budget of this project.

If we will not get suitable data for our tasks, we can think of the following alternatives
a) we present our deliverables with old data
b) we present our deliverables with simulated data
c) Reprex runs a survey for the societies, if we get a public, academic document stating that we have been doing it always the best possible way and there was no room for improvement.

Best regards,
Daniel

Hi  Isabella &amp; James,

I wrote a more personal note to Joost, partly explaining my edgy behavior for the repeated lateness of the partners, but I realised that I may need to make my situation clear to you, and perhaps others in the Consortium.

As you know, we won a competition of the EIT, which is technically financed by Horizon Europe (although it is a very different program than our RIA action.)  It is a startup prize, supposed to provide alternative, investment-type funding for startups working on a really big puzzle. We won with our ESG calculator, and the prize is partly an investment, and partly a grant. (There were 307 applicants in 5 sectors, and we won the Audiovisual prize.) In the granted period, the for-profit startups must work on a non-profit basis, and practically they cannot solicit other work. Because we still have some commitment to OpenMusE, and we have some smaller commercial work, we offered all our remaining capacity to them for a year ahead.

Because there was fraudulent misconduct in the EIT KIC the grant payments are prolonged or perhaps even cancelled, and may need to go through the anti-fraud authority and courts.  The misconduct also affected us: they tried to manipulate our score and give our money to somebody else, but we successfully appealed that. Unfortunately, in other parts of the KIC there was money going to pockets that they could not keep under the carpet.

There had always been questions about the financial stability of Reprex. Now the worst possible thing happened: we are entering the period when we are crediting the Horizon program, but at the same time, the Horizon program reserved most of our capacities and failed to pay for us. We should be receiving about 150,000 euros in the coming days, but it may take years as I see that we actually get this money; and this is of course just a first advance (this program has much lower advance rates.)  If Reprex will become insolvent, it will be because of "irregularities" committed on the EU side, and we are (acknowledged by their supervisory report) all but completely innocent victims.

Tomorrow I will go public with this problem, because we need to ask help from our partners, investors, and the least that we want to have is quarrelling within OpenMusE.  I am very edgy, but partly also because I feel that we put more work in than others, and in these extremely challenging times our schedule is often disrupted. I think that we can meet all our commitments in OpenMusE, but we do not want to put more work into the deliverables than others and we want to avoid any quarrelling.

I am doing the best that I can do, and I am by now thinking that Reprex will go under, but the next 3-6 months will be extremely challenging for us.  I think that it would be appropriate to communicate at one point to the PO and other WP leaders. I think that PO is critical; I think it is rather unprecedented that a fraud in the HE program makes a HE beneficiary insolvent, but it may happen.

Best regards,
